There are references to Ahikar in the apocryphal book of Tobit, the works of the Greek philosopher Democritus, the apocalyptic Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, and the Qur’an. The original story was written in Aramaic but later appeared in many other languages, including Syriac, Arabic, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Greek. These versions differ from one another in various ways.

See also Apocrypha.

BOOK OF AMOS

The book of Amos contains the messages of the prophet Amos. He was one of the twelve minor prophets in the Hebrew Old Testament. These prophets are called “minor” because their books are short, not because their messages are less important.

Amos gives one of the Bible’s strongest warnings about God’s judgment against injustice, oppression, and religious hypocrisy. Religious hypocrisy means pretending to honor God while living in ways that disobey him.

The book mainly contains messages that Amos preached at Bethel. Bethel was an important place of worship for the kings and people of the northern kingdom of Israel. Amos preached there during the eighth century BC, about 800 years before the birth of Jesus Christ.

Who Wrote the Book of Amos?

Amos was undoubtedly the preacher of the messages, or oracles, in the book. He was a herdsman and a farmer who cared for fig trees. He came from Tekoa, a village south of Jerusalem.

God gave Amos a vision of judgment against Israel. Amos then traveled north to Bethel, near the border between Judah and Israel, to deliver God’s messages.

Everything we know about Amos comes from three sources:

the book’s opening statement (Amos 1:1–2), 

a section that describes events from his life (Amos 7:10–14), and

what we can learn from the style and content of the rest of the book.

Did Amos write down his own prophecies? Scholars have raised many questions about who wrote the book of Amos. However, there is no strong reason to think that someone else wrote it.

Some scholars suggest that people passed Amos’s messages on by word of mouth for many years before someone wrote them in their final form. However, the Hebrew text is in better condition than we would expect after such a long period of oral transmission. The book also contains many statements in the first person and uses strong, lively language. This evidence suggests that Amos himself wrote down much of his prophecy soon after he spoke it at Bethel.

One possible view is that Amos collected the visions before he began his ministry in the northern kingdom of Israel (Amos 7:1–9; 8:1–3; 9:1–4). He may then have written the spoken messages, or oracles, after his ministry began (Amos 1–6). . Another possibility is that someone joined the two sections into one book much later, during or after the Babylonian exile. Some passages may also have been added at that time.

However, this proposal is uncertain. Other prophetic books, such as Ezekiel and Jeremiah, also contain both spoken messages and visions. Scholars have not generally divided those books on this basis. The evidence within Amos does not require such a division either.

The two sections also share similar concerns. In both the visions (Amos 7:1–3) and the oracles (5:1–7), Amos acts as an intercessor, someone who pleads with God on behalf of Israel.

When and Where Was the Book of Amos Written? Who Was It Written For?

The opening statement of the book says that Amos prophesied during the reigns of Uzziah, king of Judah, and Jeroboam II, king of Israel (Amos 1:1). This places his ministry sometime between 792 and 740 BC. His message fits what is known about conditions in Israel during that period. However, it is difficult to identify the exact years when his ministry began and ended.

Amos received his vision "two years before the earthquake" (1:1). Another biblical passage probably refers to the same earthquake and says that it happened during the reign of King Uzziah of Judah (Zechariah 14:5). Excavations at Hazor may also show evidence of an earthquake around 760 BC.

Amos also refers to a solar eclipse as a sign of coming judgment (Amos 8:9). Scholars have identified an eclipse that occurred around 763 BC as a possible background for this passage.

After Uzziah developed a serious skin disease, he lived apart from others. His son then helped govern Judah with him (2 Chronicles 26:21). For this reason, Amos’s reference to Uzziah as king (Amos 1:1) may suggest that Amos’s ministry took place no later than about 760 BC.

After Amos gave his prophecies, disaster came upon Israel through the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III, who ruled from 745 to 727 BC. Amos warned that Israel would go into captivity, but he did not name Assyria as the nation that would capture Israel. He only said that the people would be taken to a land east of Damascus (Amos 5:27). 

Amos may not have been thinking specifically about the growing power of Assyria. Instead, he may have been warning about the certain results of Israel’s idolatry and hypocrisy.

Based on the available evidence, Amos probably began his prophetic ministry at Bethel around 760 BC. This was near the middle of the period when Uzziah ruled Judah and Jeroboam II ruled Israel. We do not know how long Amos’s ministry lasted. It may have continued for only a few months.

Amos had been caring for his flocks in the hills of Judah, south of Jerusalem. Then God told him, “Go, prophesy to My people Israel” (Amos 7:15). Amos may have already known the more developed cities of the northern kingdom. He may have traveled there before to sell wool or fruit. It is also possible that he became deeply aware of the false worship and social injustice there after God called him to prophesy.

His writings show both his rural background in Judah and his direct knowledge of life in the northern kingdom of Israel. Most of his prophecies were directed against Israel. However, he also condemned Judah’s sin and said that Jerusalem, its capital city, would be destroyed by fire (Amos 2:4–5). 

Several passages speak directly to the people of Samaria, the capital of Israel (Amos 4:1, 11; 6:1). Amos may have traveled there from Bethel. He may also have learned about the city’s wealth from people who lived there. Another possibility is that he spoke to people from Samaria when they came to worship at Bethel.

What Was the Background of the Book of Amos?

The eighth century BC was an important time in the history of Israel and Judah. Both kingdoms had become very prosperous. They had not known such wealth since the time of Solomon.

However, both kingdoms were becoming weaker because their people were turning away from God. Their societies were also becoming less fair. A new wealthy class gained more and more wealth, while poor people became even poorer.

In 803 BC, the Assyrian king Adad-nirari III conquered Damascus in Syria. This weakened one of Israel’s main enemies. Israel was then able to regain territory under King Joash (2 Kings 13:25). For a time, Assyria also reduced its military activity in the west. Israel and Judah entered a period with less warfare. This allowed both kingdoms to give more attention to matters within their own borders.

Joash’s son, Jeroboam II, became king of Israel in 793 BC and ruled until 753 BC. Uzziah ruled Judah from 792 to 740 BC. During the reigns of these two kings, Israel and Judah controlled almost as much land as Solomon’s kingdom had controlled. Their wealth increased because trade expanded and because they gained goods from conquered lands.

Archaeological discoveries show that Israel and Judah had active industries. For example, Debir had an important dye-making industry. Excavations at Samaria have also uncovered many ivory decorations. These findings support Amos’s description of the wealthy people in the capital city (Amos 6:4). Samaria was protected by a very thick double wall. A large palace, probably built for King Jeroboam II, stood above the city. The palace also had a strong tower.

However, the wealth and success of this period hid serious problems within the nation. Many wealthy people treated the poor unfairly. This weakened the unity of the nation and broke God’s laws. Amos condemned this harsh treatment of the poor. He warned that God would punish the people for disobeying his commands (Amos 5:11–13; 8:4–10).

The nation of Israel was guilty of more than social sins against its covenant with God. The people were also adopting the religious practices of the Canaanites.

Archaeologists found many ostraca in a palace storehouse at Samaria. Ostraca are broken pieces of pottery that people used for short written messages, such as letters and receipts. Many of these pieces contain Hebrew names that include the name Baal. Baal was a major god in the Canaanite religion. The Canaanites connected him with fertility and worshiped him as a god. The Israelites, however, regarded Baal as a false god.

Although the nation was slowly becoming weaker, many people remained falsely confident. Amos met people who looked forward to the day of the Lord (Amos 5:18). They believed it would bring them hope and rescue. Amos corrected this misunderstanding. He warned that the day of the Lord would bring God’s judgment on sinners.

A more immediate judgment was also approaching. Assyria was becoming powerful again and was expanding its territory. Under Tiglath-pileser III, who ruled from 745 to 727 BC, Assyria regained its place as the leading power in the region.

Later, the Assyrian king Shalmaneser V attacked Israel. Samaria, the capital of Israel, fell to the Assyrians in 722 BC. As the Assyrian army entered Israel, many people who had ignored Amos’s message may have realized that God had sent a prophet to warn them. Assyria’s attack showed that God was judging Israel for its sins.

What Is the Content of the Book of Amos?

Superscription (1:1)

The prophet introduces himself as a shepherd. This may suggest that he wants to keep not only sheep, but also people, from going astray.

Prophetic Oracles (1:2–6:14)

This section begins by showing God’s great power. God acts in history to judge the nations (Amos 1:2).

Judgment on Surrounding Nations (1:3–2:3)

The prophet first speaks against Damascus. He then announces judgment on other nations, moving step by step closer to Israel. The people of Israel may have welcomed God’s judgment on their enemies. Then Amos shocks them by accusing Israel of similar sins.

Damascus was the capital of Syria, northeast of Israel. It was also the center of Syrian power. During the reign of King Hazael of Damascus, from 842 to 806 BC, Syria repeatedly attacked Israel. These attacks greatly weakened Israel (2 Kings 10:32–33; 13:3–5, 22–24). 

When the Syrian army entered Gilead, it nearly destroyed Israel’s army. The Bible compares this destruction to dust on a threshing floor (2 Kings 13:7). Amos uses a similar picture when he says that Syria threshed Gilead with "sledges of iron" (Amos 1:3). This means that Syria treated the people of Gilead with extreme cruelty.

Amos also says that Syria would be destroyed and that its people would be taken to Kir. Amos understood Kir to be the place where the Syrians had come from (Amos 9:7). This prophecy was later fulfilled when the Assyrians captured Damascus and sent its people to Kir (2 Kings 16:9).

Amos next spoke against Gaza, a Philistine city in southwest Palestine. Gaza probably represents all the Philistines because Amos also names three of their other four major cities (Amos 1:8). The fifth city, Gath, had already been conquered by Hazael (2 Kings 12:17). Amos condemned the Philistines for raiding Israel’s border. During this attack, they captured many people and sold them into slavery (Amos 1:6).

Amos next spoke against the Phoenician city of Tyre. Tyre stood on the Mediterranean coast, north of Israel and southwest of Damascus. Amos said that Tyre would be destroyed, just as the Philistine cities would be. This judgment would come because the people of Tyre had captured Israelites and sold them into slavery.

Amos next spoke against Edom, a nation south of the Dead Sea. The people of Edom had often attacked and troubled Israel. The Old Testament speaks negatively about Edom many times. Amos says that Edom showed no mercy to Israel, even though the two nations were closely related (Amos 1:11).

Amos also announced judgment against Ammon, a nation southeast of Israel. The violent act he describes probably happened during one of Ammon’s attempts to take control of Gilead, an Israelite region to the north (Amos 1:13).

Moab was the last nearby nation Amos condemned. He referred to what may have been a well-known act of disrespect toward the dead (Amos 2:1–3).

Oracles against Israel and Judah (2:4–16)

Although Judah and Israel were at peace at this time, they had remained enemies after the united kingdom divided. Amos accused Judah of rejecting “the law of the Lord.” He also said that Jerusalem would be destroyed by fire.

The message against Israel is longer than the messages against the other nations. Amos clearly explains that Israel’s sins were social sins. He shows that Israel was no better than the nations around it and deserved the same punishment.

Some nations had sold captured people into slavery. In a similar way, the Israelites were selling poor people who could not repay their debts (Amos 2:6). 

The law of Moses said that a lender must return a garment taken as security before nightfall. The garment might be the debtor’s only protection from the cold (Exodus 22:26–27). However, wealthy Israelites wore these garments at religious feasts, even though they had taken them unfairly from the poor (Amos 2:8).

Amos reminds the people of Israel about all the good things God had done for them (Amos 2:9–11). However, Israel continued to disobey God. Therefore, the nation would not escape the judgment that was coming (Amos 2:12–16).

Judgment and Warning against Israel (3:1–6:14)

Amos explains why he has authority to speak as a prophet. He does this by showing how causes lead to results (Amos 3:1–8). A lion roars when it has caught its prey. People become afraid when a trumpet sounds a warning. In the same way, when disaster comes to a city, God has allowed it. God reveals his plans to his prophets. God has announced judgment against Israel, so Amos must proclaim the message.

Amos calls on Egypt and Assyria to witness Israel’s sins. These nations were known for oppression and cruelty, yet Amos suggests that even they would be shocked by what they saw in Israel (Amos 3:9–10). Only a small group of survivors would remain after the coming judgment (Amos 3:11–12). God’s judgment would fall on the objects connected with Israel’s false worship (Amos 3:14). It would also fall on the signs of wealth that had drawn the people away from the Lord (Amos 3:15).

Amos strongly condemns the wealthy people who lived in comfort while the poor suffered (Amos 4:1–3). He especially speaks against rich women whose desire for luxury led their husbands to oppress the poor. Amos compares these women to well-fed cattle and warns that they will one day be treated like cattle.

Amos then speaks against the people who worshiped at Bethel. They took part in religious ceremonies, but their hearts and actions did not honor God (Amos 4:4–5).

In the rest of the fourth chapter, Amos reminds Israel of disasters that should have led the people back to God. These included hunger, drought, disease, and the destruction of some cities. Even after these events, the people did not turn back to God. Amos then warns them, “Prepare to meet your God!” He follows this warning with a song that praises God’s great power (Amos 4:6–13).

The fifth chapter begins like a funeral song. Amos speaks as though Israel were already dead (Amos 5:1–2). No one will be able to rescue the nation. When disaster comes, most of Israel’s soldiers will be killed (Amos 5:3). 

Yet God still offers hope: “Seek Me and live” (Amos 5:4–6). This promise of life stands in strong contrast to the picture of Israel’s death. The idols at Bethel and Gilgal cannot save the people (Amos 5:5). Amos then calls the people to seek the Lord. After this, he praises God’s great power (Amos 5:8–9).

Although Amos offers Israel some hope, he still describes a dark future (Amos 5:10–13). The courts are corrupt. Taxes and high interest rates place a heavy burden on the poor. The people could correct these wrongs if they would "hate evil and love good" (Amos 5:15). However, judgment is already coming (Amos 5:16–17).

The people were acting with hypocrisy. They claimed to look forward to the day of the Lord, but Amos warned that this day would bring judgment on their sins. God did not want empty offerings or songs of praise. He wanted justice to flow like water and righteousness, or right living, to continue like a never-ending stream (Amos 5:18–24). 

Their disobedience had begun long ago. Even during the exodus from Egypt, the people were drawn to false gods. The Lord God of Hosts would send those false gods into captivity together with the people who trusted in them (Amos 5:25–27).

The wealthy people of Israel felt secure and satisfied with themselves. This attitude had also spread to Judah, so Amos spoke harshly to both Samaria and Jerusalem (Amos 6:1). Amos told those who lived in luxury to look at three nearby kingdoms: 

Calneh,

Hamath, and

Gath.

Judgment had already come upon them. Israel should not think that it would escape the same fate. When the day of judgment came, the rich people who had enjoyed the greatest comfort would be the first to be taken away (Amos 6:2–7). The destruction would leave only a few survivors. Those who remained would understand that the punishment had come from God (Amos 6:8–11). Israel was foolish to be proud. The people believed they were strong, but they had deceived themselves (Amos 6:12–14).

Prophetic Visions (7:1–9:10)

Amos then describes three visions that God gave him. Through these visions, he clearly communicates God’s message.

Israel’s Destruction (7:1–9)

The first vision has three parts.

Amos sees a locust plague that threatens the land. He prays for the people, and God decides not to send the disaster (Amos 7:1–3). 

Amos sees a fire that could destroy everything. Again, he prays, and God stops the disaster (Amos 7:4–6). 

Amos sees the Lord standing beside a wall with a plumb line, a tool used to test whether a wall is straight. The plumb line shows that God has a standard for his people. They have failed to meet that standard, so this time the judgment will not be stopped (Amos 7:7–9).

Historical Interlude (7:10–17)

At this point, Amos meets Amaziah, the priest at Bethel. Amos has explained that the vision of the plumb line means that Israel’s false altars and places of worship will be destroyed. He has also said that the royal family of Jeroboam will die by the sword.

Amaziah sends a message to King Jeroboam. He accuses Amos of plotting against the king and tells him to return to Judah.

Amos replies that he is not a professional prophet and does not belong to a group of prophets. Then he announces that judgment will also come upon Amaziah’s family as part of Israel’s coming disaster.

The Ripe Fruit (8:1–14)

In the second vision, Amos sees a basket of ripe summer fruit. In Hebrew, the word for “summer fruit” sounds almost the same as the word for “end.” This wordplay shows that Israel’s end is near. The nation is ripe for judgment because its people have become morally corrupt.

Greedy merchants can hardly wait for the religious festivals to end. Then they can return to cheating the poor. They use dishonest weights, sell poor-quality goods, and take property from people who cannot pay their debts.

When Israel goes into captivity, its celebrations will become times of mourning. God will also send a famine. This will not be a shortage of food or water, but a lack of hearing the words of the Lord. Even strong young people will collapse because they cannot find God’s message.

Destruction of the Temple (Amos 9:1–10)

In the third vision, Amos sees the Lord destroy the place of worship at Bethel. It is full of people taking part in worship that does not honor God. The place where they expected to be safe becomes the place of their destruction.

The people outside the shrine will not escape either. No matter where they run, they cannot hide from God. They cannot hide in Sheol, the place of the dead, on the heights of Mount Carmel, or in the depths of the sea (Amos 9:1–4). After this vision, Amos gives another song that praises God’s great power (Amos 9:5–6).

The final words of judgment in Amos appear in 9:7–10. However, they prepare the way for a message of hope. Amos shows that Israel is not better than other nations in God’s sight. God brought Israel out of Egypt, but he also brought the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir. Because of Israel’s sin, the people have lost the special meaning of the exodus. Most of the nation will be destroyed, but a faithful group will remain.

The idea of a faithful remnant, a small group that survives, was important in the preaching of the prophets in the eighth century BC (compare Isaiah 6:12–13; Micah 6:7–9). It pointed back to God’s promise to preserve Israel because of the covenant he made with the patriarchs, the early ancestors of Israel (Leviticus 26:44–45). 

In Amos’s prophecy, God will sift Israel among the nations like grain in a sieve. The wicked will be scattered like chaff, the useless outer part of the grain. However, the faithful people will be preserved like good grain.

Israel’s Hope (9:11–15)

In the final section of the book, Amos expands this message of hope through a series of powerful and beautiful metaphors.

Restoration of the City of David (9:11–12)

The first metaphor is of the city (literally “house”) of David, which means David’s royal family and kingdom. Amos describes it as a house that has fallen into ruin. The kingdom had become weak because of problems within the nation and attacks from outside enemies. Amos pictures God restoring it to its former strength and honor. He also says that the restored kingdom of David will include people from every nation who belong to the Lord.

In the New Testament, James quotes this passage to support including Gentiles in God’s promise (Acts 15:16–18). The wording in Acts is slightly different from the wording in Amos because James uses the Septuagint, an early Greek translation of the Old Testament.

The people who are called by God’s name include more than nations or territories. They also include individuals from any nation who belong to God.

James understood Amos to mean that Gentiles would be included in the kingdom of God. This kingdom is much greater than the early kingdom ruled by David’s descendants. Christians believe that this prophecy has been partly fulfilled in the church.

Restoration of Israel’s Fortunes (9:13–15)

The book of Amos ends with metaphors about farming and country life. show the rich blessings of God’s coming kingdom. God will restore Israel after the terrible events of Amos’s time.

Christians understand this prophecy in different ways. Some believe it describes the present age of the church. In this view, the church receives these blessings as God’s spiritual people. Others believe it describes the future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth. In this view, the prophecy shows what will happen during that future kingdom.

The Bible also speaks about the earth being renewed (Romans 8:20–22). Micah uses language similar to Amos when he describes the restoration of Jerusalem (Micah 3:12–4:4). Some Christians believe the final prophecy in Amos points to the complete restoration that will happen when Christ returns. Christians differ on the exact meaning of the passage. However, the faithful remnant includes the followers of Jesus Christ, and the promised blessings are for all who belong to the kingdom of God.

Why Is the Book of Amos Important?

The main purpose of Amos’s prophecies was to condemn Israel for disobeying its covenant with God. Amos does not directly mention the promise God gave to Abraham (Genesis 22:15–18). However, that promise is present throughout the message of the book.

Amos teaches that the covenant was spiritual in nature. He also stresses that the people would receive its blessings only as they obeyed God.

Amos saw both disobedience and hypocrisy among the people. One of his main teachings was that religious ceremonies are not enough when people do not truly obey God.

God’s law taught the people to love him and to care for others (Exodus 23:1–13). In Amos’s time, many wealthy people ignored these commands. At the same time, they continued to take part in religious rituals.

Amos condemned this behavior. He taught that religious acts can become sinful when people perform them without a sincere desire to honor God and treat others rightly (Amos 4:4). Worship can become a false display when it does not reflect the will of a holy God.

Amos taught that Israel’s disobedience and hypocrisy would lead to national disaster. His prophecy warned the nation that judgment was coming.

Amos also taught that God held other nations responsible for how they treated people (Amos 1:3–2:3). God judged their violence and injustice through events in history.

This shows that God’s moral law applied not only to Israel and Judah but also to other nations. They were accountable to God and were judged for serious wrongs against other people.

The people in Amos’s time believed that the day of the Lord would bring victory and justice for Israel. Amos taught something different. He said that the day of the Lord would bring punishment on all sinners, including the people of Israel.

However, Amos did more than condemn Israel’s sins. He also announced a future hope for the nation. He said that God would restore the kingdom of David, probably under the Messiah, during a time of peace (Amos 9:8–15). The connection between David’s kingdom and the Messiah’s kingdom comes from God’s promise to David (2 Samuel 7:8–16). Other nations were accountable to God’s moral law and judgment. In the same way, people from other nations who belonged to God would also share in the blessings of his promise (Amos 9:12).

The book of Amos gives special attention to two truths about God: his authority over all things and his righteousness. God rules over every nation. Amos shows this through God’s judgment on the nations around Israel (Amos 1:3–2:3). God also rules over the natural world. He has power over the heavens, the earth, and the forces of nature (Amos 4:13; 5:8; 9:13–14). 

Because God is righteous, he cannot allow people to keep breaking his law without judgment. However, his righteousness also gives hope to the faithful remnant, the small group of Israelites who continue to trust him. God will keep his promise to preserve Israel as a nation (Leviticus 26:44–45).

Amos said that Israel could still avoid the national disaster that was approaching. However, he described the nation’s social problems and the people’s stubborn hearts in very dark terms. This suggests that he did not expect them to repent or escape the coming judgment.

Amos presented his message through strong metaphors that were easy to remember. His message is still relevant today because many of the same sins continue in modern society and in individual lives. People still mistreat others in the twenty-first century AD, just as they did in the eighth century BC.

People today should notice four main themes in the book of Amos:

sin has consequences, 

privilege brings responsibility, 

God remains faithful, and 

there is hope.

Christians believe this hope is now seen in part through the church.

The book of Amos may seem gloomy, but Amos was describing a very serious situation. He saw a nation falling apart because the people had been unfaithful to God. Yet Amos also looked beyond Israel’s coming disaster. He saw a new kingdom of peace in which God’s people would receive the fulfillment of his promises.

BOOK OF BARUCH

The book of Baruch is named after Baruch. Baruch was the secretary of the prophet Jeremiah. This book is included in some Christian Old Testaments as part of the Deuterocanon.

In ancient times, people wrote several books but said Baruch wrote them. People knew Baruch worked with Jeremiah, so these books were popular.

The Book of Baruch talks about how God is right and wise in all that God does. It also says God will listen when people are sorry for their sins. The book says the Jewish people deserve to be punished by God because they have sinned. But it also says God is kind. At the end, the book tells the people of Israel not to be sad. It says God will care for them and make them great again.

Introduction

The book of Baruch tells the story of the Jewish exiles in Babylon. They fast, weep, and pray over their difficult position, and remember their disobedience to God. They plan to raise money to send to the high priest in Jerusalem so offerings can be made for the exiles. They also send the book of Baruch. The book has been read to the Jews in Babylon. The exiles ask that the book be read on feast days, on “appointed seasons”, and be added to the liturgy (the formal arrangement of prayers, hymns, and other practices used in worship). They ask that the high priest prays for the wellbeing of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar his son so “the Lord will give us strength, and he will give light to our eyes, and we shall live under the protection of… Belshazzar his son, and we shall serve them many days and find favor in their sight” (Baruch 1:12, Revised Standard Version).

A Confession and Prayer for Mercy

A confession and prayer for mercy follow the introduction. The Jewish people agree that their misfortune is a result of their own sin. They admit that God is just, and they ask for his mercy and forgiveness. “Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God, but confusion of face to us and our fathers, as at this day” (Baruch 2:6, Revised Standard Version). The Jewish people ask God not to punish them for their disobedience. In particular, they ask that they aren't punished for not having served the king of Babylon. “Hear, O Lord, our prayer and our supplication, and for thy own sake deliver us, and grant us favor in the sight of those who have carried us into exile” (Baruch 2:14, Revised Standard Version).

A Call to Seek Wisdom Again

The Jews are then told to follow God’s law and rediscover the wisdom that comes from the Torah. They are instructed to follow God and not trust in wealth. This wisdom is not abstract but practical, as they might find in the Old Testament. The purpose of this section was to establish that the exiles were still special to God and had a future ministry.

A Lament That Leads to Hope

The final section is a lamentation (an expression of deep sorrow) followed by hope for the glory God has planned for Israel: “Take off the garment of your sorrow and affliction, O Jerusalem, and put on forever the beauty of the glory from God. Put on the robe of righteousness from God; put on your head the diadem of the glory of the Everlasting” (Baruch 5:1–2, Revised Standard Version).

The Letter of Jeremiah

In the Latin Vulgate, “The Letter of Jeremiah” is added after the fifth chapter. This document is actually a religious document condemning idolatry. It was supposedly sent to the Judeans being taken into exile in Babylon.

Who Wrote the Book of Baruch? When Was It Written?

The book of Baruch was probably written by several authors. It might have been edited by the writer of the introduction. The "confession" borrows from Daniel 9. The following prayers for forgiveness are similar to the prophetic texts in the Old Testament. The section of wisdom poetry is very different as it is similar to Job 28–29. The final call for hope probably used Isaiah 40–45 as inspiration.

The date of the book has been widely discussed. The book was probably written in Hebrew and translated into Greek. The translator was probably the same person who translated the book of Jeremiah for the Septuagint (an ancient Greek version of the Old Testament). The date of 582 BC has been suggested based on internal evidence from the first section. However, later dates are more likely, possibly even as late as the second century BC.

How Did the Book of Baruch Influence the Church?

Although the book was popular with Jewish people who did not live in the land of Israel, its influence was greater in the early Christian church. Early theologians quoted the book often. The Roman Catholic Church accepted the book of Baruch into their canon at the Council of Trent (1545–1563).

BOOK OF DANIEL

The fourth book of the Major Prophets in the Old Testament features vivid symbolism and highlights heroic events during the Babylonian exile of the Jewish people. Daniel is a complex book, so understanding it requires careful study and reflection. Daniel himself wrote about one of his visions, saying, “I was confounded by the vision; it was beyond understanding” (Daniel 8:27).

In the old Jewish division of the Old Testament, Daniel is part of the third section, called the Writings. This section also includes books like Psalms, Proverbs, and Job. Daniel is not included in the second section of the Old Testament, called the Prophets. Although some parts of his book can be seen as prophetic, Daniel is not clearly identified as a prophet. The book has two main parts: 

Stories about Daniel’s life (Daniel 1–6) 

Daniel’s visions (Daniel 7–12)

Who Wrote the Book of Daniel?

The book of Daniel does not have a known author, like many ancient texts. The title, "Daniel," refers to the main subject of the book: the man Daniel.

The first six chapters of the book describe Daniel in the third person. Starting in Daniel 7:2, the book claims to include Daniel's words in the first person. Traditionally, Judaism, later followed by Christianity, believed Daniel wrote the entire book. However, there is little evidence to confirm this. Jesus’s reference to things “spoken of by the prophet Daniel” (Matthew 24:15) does not clarify the authorship of the entire book. These words appear in the second half of the book, clearly marked as Daniel's. Therefore, the question of who wrote the first part remains unresolved.

Daniel is the most important character in the book, whether or not he wrote it. The book itself is the only source of information about him. Daniel was a Hebrew from Judah, likely of royal descent, born in the late seventh century BC. As a young boy, he was taken from his homeland to Babylon (now southern Iraq) around 605 BC. After three years of formal education in language and literature (Daniel 1:4–5), he became an official in the royal household. The first six chapters describe specific events in Daniel's life but do not give a complete biography.

Daniel's name means "God is my judge." In Babylon, where he lived as a foreigner, he received another name, Belteshazzar. This name might have meant "may Bel (a god) protect his life" in the Babylonian language.

When Was the Book of Daniel Written?

Uncertainty about who wrote the book of Daniel also creates uncertainty about when it was written. If Daniel wrote the entire book, it was likely written in the second half of the sixth century BC. If he did not write it, it could have been written later. The conservative view is that the book was written in the sixth century BC. Another view is that it was written around 165 BC.

There is evidence for both early and late dates of the Book of Daniel. People who support a late date and a different author usually use historical and language-based arguments. However, those who support an earlier date have counterarguments, which are discussed below.

Historical Argument

The historical argument suggests the writer knew a lot about Near Eastern empires from the sixth to the second centuries. However, the writer misunderstood some historical details from the second half of the sixth century, which is Daniel's time. This uneven knowledge suggests the writing happened later.

People with a conservative view must agree on the first part of the historical argument. The book of Daniel shows a deep understanding of Near Eastern history. The main question is whether this knowledge was gained after the events or revealed to Daniel beforehand. Different people answer this question in various ways, depending on their beliefs about prophecy and other factors.

The second part of the historical argument is more complex. Was the writer's knowledge of history in the late sixth century BC really wrong? The main issue is the identity of Darius the Mede (Daniel 5:30–31). The book of Daniel claims that Darius the Mede conquered Babylon and was later succeeded by Cyrus. However, external historical sources do not mention a Darius at that time. They clearly show that Cyrus conquered Babylon. Those who support a late date see this as strong evidence. Those who support an early date have no simple solution. 

One proposed solution is that Darius and Cyrus are two names for the same person. This idea is based on the translation of Daniel 6:28: “So Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” A similar case is the use of the names Pul and Tiglath-pileser in 1 Chronicles 5:26. In summary, dating Daniel based on the writer's historical knowledge is challenging, whether suggesting an early or late date.

Linguistic Argument

The arguments about when the Book of Daniel was written are complex, especially for those unfamiliar with Hebrew and Aramaic. Supporters of a later date use three main points: 

The Aramaic in the book resembles late Aramaic from the second century BC and later

The book contains Persian loan words, suggesting a later date for its Aramaic

The presence of Greek loan words indicates the language dates after Alexander the Great's conquest of the East around 330 BC. 

For those who support a later date, the third point is the strongest. They argue it would be impossible to find Greek loan words in Aramaic two centuries before Alexander's time.

At first, the arguments seem convincing, but they are less persuasive to conservatives upon closer examination. Each part of the argument has been addressed.

People commonly used Aramaic in the Near East from the ninth century BC. It became an official language in Assyria in the eighth century BC. Ninety percent of the Aramaic words in the Book of Daniel were from the older language, including both Old and Imperial Aramaic dialects. The remaining ten percent, known only from later texts based on current evidence, might suggest a late date. However, they could also be early uses of those words.

The presence of Persian loan words in Aramaic can be surprising. Later Aramaic includes many Persian loan words, with about 19 appearing in the book of Daniel. However, there is another explanation for these words in Daniel from an earlier time. The story of Daniel partly takes place in a Persian-controlled court. The Persians used Aramaic for managing their empire, so their language naturally influenced Aramaic. If we assume an early date for the book of Daniel, it was written when Persian had the most impact on Aramaic.

The evidence of Greek words in Daniel’s Aramaic is not very strong. Greek traders traveled in the Near East from the eighth century BC. Greek soldiers fought for Near Eastern states from the seventh century BC. During Daniel’s time, King Nebuchadnezzar hired Greek artisans in Babylon. Therefore, Greek influence on the Aramaic language could have happened before Alexander the Great. He was not the first Greek in the East.

Conclusion

The arguments about when the Book of Daniel was written are not clear for either an early or late date. Dating the book depends on factors like who wrote it, the purpose, and whether you see parts as prophetic. Saying Daniel wrote it fits with the current evidence. Some material from the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran does not support a late date. All Daniel manuscripts and fragments are copies from the second century BC, suggesting the original is older. One manuscript, similar to the large Isaiah Scroll, likely comes from the same time, several centuries before the Qumran copy of Isaiah. Other Qumran manuscripts show that no Old Testament material was written after the Persian period. Therefore, no manuscript evidence supports a second-century BC date for Daniel.

What Languages Is the Book of Daniel Written In?

The book of Daniel has an interesting feature that is not obvious in the English Bible. It is bilingual. Daniel 1:1–2:4a and Daniel 8–12 are in Hebrew, like other Old Testament books. The middle part (Daniel 2:4b–7:28) is in Aramaic, a related language. People have different ideas about why this is. Some think a Hebrew writer added to an original Aramaic book, adding parts at the start and end. Others believe a part of the original Hebrew book was lost, so they replaced it with an Aramaic translation. There are more complex theories, but none are widely accepted.

Another suggestion is possible. The book of Daniel, regardless of the date, may reflect the bilingual nature of its cultural setting. (For example, many written materials in Canada appear in both English and French.) Finally, one can see the bilingual nature as another mysterious aspect of the book that makes its interpretation difficult.

What Is the Background of the Book of Daniel?

We can look at the background of the book of Daniel in two ways. First, we can see it from the Babylonian exile, which Daniel experienced in the early sixth century BC. Second, we can view it in light of future events in the second century BC, which the visions in the book's second half seem to predict.

The Babylonian Exile

Daniel was exiled around 605 BC, but the main phase of the Babylonian exile started in 586 BC. This followed the defeat of Judah and the destruction of Jerusalem. The story covers the reigns of Nebuchadnezzar (also known as Nebuchadrezzar) and Belshazzar. It ends in the early years of the Persian king Cyrus, who captured Babylon in 539 BC. For the Jews, the exile was a time of hardship and renewed religious understanding. Both aspects are shown in the book of Daniel.

The Seleucid Period in Palestine

Daniel's visions in the second half of the book seem to refer to the Seleucid period in Palestine. This was when Antiochus Epiphanes, a member of the Seleucid dynasty, ruled the Jews from 175 to 163 BC. Whether these visions predicted future events or reflected the culture of the time, the Seleucid period is crucial for fully understanding the book.

Under Antiochus, Palestinian Jews faced significant hardship. Their ancient faith was greatly weakened, the high priesthood in Jerusalem was sold to the highest bidder, and the temple was desecrated in many ways. Jews were pressured to change their lives and faith to fit Hellenistic (Greek-influenced) culture. 

Some gave in, but others held firmly to their old faith. A rebellion against Antiochus's oppressive measures began in 168 BC. By 164 BC, the rebels largely removed the objectionable practices. However, the Seleucid period was generally difficult for faithful Jews, as historical forces seemed to oppose their true faith. Part of the book of Daniel's greatness is its theological understanding of history, which helped people continue living in faith during a time of severe crisis.

Why Was the Book of Daniel Written? What Does It Teach Us About God?

The section of the Old Testament called the Writings had many purposes. The psalms were mainly used in Israel's worship. The proverbs might have been part of Israel's school lessons. The book of Job dealt with a specific human and religious problem.

The purpose of the book of Daniel is not easy to determine. It is mainly a story and a partial biography of Daniel. It is not strictly a prophetic book or history in the modern sense. Much of it focuses on dreams and their interpretations.

The word "history" hints at its purpose. Daniel aims to explain history through theology. The first six chapters focus on Daniel and his friends. This is not just to satisfy curiosity but to teach readers. Old Testament theology emphasized that the God of Israel was involved in human life and history. Reading biblical history reveals God's role in human events and teaches how God and people interact. The opening chapters of Daniel describe events in the life of a man with strong faith. This type of history offers lessons on how to live.

The last six chapters focus on Daniel’s dreams. Although the dreams and their interpretations are complex, a theme of history emerges. Daniel 7–12 emphasize the meaning of history and the world's future, not just past events. From a biblical view, the movements of human societies now and in the future are as important as past history. Daniel’s visions focus on nations and superpowers but highlight a key theme: God’s power over humans and nations. 

History often seems chaotic and full of conflict, but God ultimately controls it and guides it toward a goal. Despite unclear details at the book's end, Daniel offers hope to those in crisis. Even if the “the time of the end” is not understood now (Daniel 12:9), the end of history is hopeful for those with faith in God (12:13). The book of Daniel explores the meaning of history, teaching lessons from the past and offering hope for the present and future.

The book includes specific religious ideas about: 

Human faith

Divine salvation

The nature of revelation

One important topic in Daniel is the belief in resurrection.

The New Testament clearly teaches resurrection followed by judgment, but this is not a main theme in the Old Testament. The Hebrews mainly focused on earthly life. Many texts suggest hope for life after death, but it is not clear. Only in the later Old Testament writings, especially Ezekiel and Daniel, does a clearer doctrine of resurrection appear.

The main idea of this doctrine in the book of Daniel is found in Daniel 12:2: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” The belief in personal resurrection gives individuals hope for the future. Nations may fight each other, creating chaos. People believe God controls everything, but what happens to those who die during these events? According to Daniel, the dead will rise again and be judged based on their actions. Some will receive everlasting life, while others will face shame.

For readers of the book of Daniel, the idea of resurrection gave hope in a bleak world. It reminded them that actions in life matter and shape future judgment. Life extends beyond physical death. Justice will eventually prevail, even if it is rare now. Evildoers might escape punishment now, but after death, God's justice will bring final judgment.

The book of Daniel is about history and hope. We must live life now, and the first six chapters offer insights from Daniel's experience. Life happens amid war and international chaos, and Daniel 7–12 show God's control and his plans in history. Individual life leads to death, and the writer discusses resurrection and judgment.

What Happens in the Book of Daniel? Stories about Daniel (1–6)

Daniel and His Companions (1:1–21)

Daniel and his companions—Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah—were exiled to Babylon about 19 years before the main exile after Jerusalem's destruction. The king selected these four healthy young men from many Jewish exiles. King Nebuchadnezzar assigned them to a special three-year training program to become court aides.

When the four Jewish youths joined Babylon's high society, they encountered a dietary issue. The king offered them the finest food and wine from the royal kitchens. However, Jewish dietary laws, as outlined in Deuteronomy 14, restricted their diet. The four requested a diet of vegetables and water. They did this not to be picky or ungrateful, but to stay faithful to their God. The story explains how they resolved the dietary issue and follows their education and Daniel's appointment as a royal counselor.

The first episode focuses on a key issue for all Jewish exiles: How can one live in a foreign land with different food and customs, yet stay faithful to God and his laws? Daniel serves as a model. He was brave enough not to compromise and wise enough to find a solution acceptable to everyone. God rewarded his faithfulness. By the end of the episode, people see Daniel as someone with special wisdom and gifts from God. He used these gifts throughout his life.

Nebuchadnezzar’s Dream (2:1–49)

The king had a dream that troubled him, but he could not remember it. When his interpreters failed to help, he ordered their execution. This order included Daniel and his friends, who were also interpreters. Daniel asked for more time and offered to interpret the dream. After praying, Daniel received the dream and its meaning from God and shared it with the king. Grateful, Nebuchadnezzar promoted Daniel and his friends to important positions in Babylon.

The writer documented both the king’s dream and Daniel’s interpretation. The challenge for modern readers is understanding the interpretation. In the dream, the king saw a statue with a gold head, silver chest and arms, brass belly and thighs, iron legs, and feet made of part iron and part clay. The interpretation identified Nebuchadnezzar as the gold head. His kingdom would be followed by three other kingdoms, each symbolized by different parts and materials of the statue. Modern interpretations vary from this point.

A common view of the four kingdoms is: 

Chaldean Empire (gold)

Medo-Persian Empire (silver)

Greece (brass)

Rome (iron and clay)

Others suggest: 

Chaldean Empire (gold)

Media (silver)

Persia (brass)

Greece (iron and clay)

Focusing too much on identifying these kingdoms can distract from the chapter's main point. Among these human kingdoms, "In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will shatter all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but will itself stand forever" (Daniel 2:44). The Babylonian king's dream predicted the arrival of a greater kingdom, that of Jesus Christ.

The Fiery Furnace (3:1–30)

The story continues with Daniel's three friends, using their Babylonian names—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. King Nebuchadnezzar built a huge gold statue, 27.4 meters (90 feet) tall. At its dedication ceremony, everyone had to bow down and worship when the band played. The three young Hebrews refused to worship and were called before the king. Their firm refusal led to a death sentence, and they were thrown into a fiercely burning furnace. Remarkably, they did not burn, and a fourth being appeared with them in the furnace. As they emerged unharmed, the king recognized God's power to save and rewarded them.

The story shows another problem faced by the Jews in exile. Staying true to God's first commandment, "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Deuteronomy 5:7), could mean risking death. The three young men stayed faithful, not because they were sure God would save them, but regardless of whether he chose to save them or not (Daniel 3:17–18). God did save them; they were thrown into the furnace tied up, but they came out as free men. The message was clear: Jews should believe in a God who can save them from persecution, but they should remain faithful even if they cannot see a way out of their troubles.

Nebuchadnezzar’s Second Dream and Madness (4:1–37)

Nebuchadnezzar admitted belief in the living God twice: 

When Daniel explained his dream about the statue (Daniel 2:47)

When Daniel’s three friends were freed from the furnace (Daniel 3:28)

However, the king’s belief was weak. Daniel 4 tells of a faith lapse that led to severe consequences. After eight years, when these consequences ended, the king again recognized God (Daniel 4:37).

The story is a proclamation by Nebuchadnezzar, shared widely after the events occurred. The king dreamed of a tall tree growing higher in a field. A divine messenger ordered the tree to be cut down, leaving only a stump and roots. The stump and roots then turned into a man, but his mind became like an animal's. For seven years, this semihuman creature acted like a beast.

Daniel explained to the king that the dream was about him. Nebuchadnezzar was the great tree that would be cut down. He would act like a beast in the field for seven years. One year after hearing this interpretation, the judgment happened. For seven years, he acted like an animal until his sanity returned.

The moral of the king’s story is that his madness was not an accident but divine judgment. His arrogant belief in having God's power led to severe punishment (Daniel 4:30). The king likely suffered from a rare mental illness now called “boanthropy.” The deeper meaning of the story is that believing oneself to be God, with total power and control over one's life, is madness. This madness can only be cured by realizing that only God has absolute power and authority.

Belshazzar’s Feast (5:1–31)

The scene shifts to the reign of a later king in Babylon, Belshazzar. He was the son of Nabonidus and likely co-ruled with him from around 555 to 539 BC. He had special authority in Babylon. His story is similar to Daniel 4. During a large feast, Belshazzar used sacred vessels taken from the Jerusalem temple. The Babylonians used these vessels to toast their gods, a disrespectful act that invited divine judgment. This judgment appeared as words written on the wall by a hand, which Daniel interpreted as a warning (Daniel 5:26–28). 

Although Belshazzar praised Daniel for his interpretation, he failed to understand the true meaning and the lesson taught to Nebuchadnezzar, his predecessor (Daniel 5:18–22). Belshazzar was killed that night when Darius the Mede entered and captured the city. The theme continues relentlessly: human pride and arrogance do not go unnoticed by the God of history, who guides human events to fulfill his purpose.

The Den of Lions (6:1–28)

The theme of Daniel 6 is similar to Daniel 3, but Daniel is the main character. He refuses to compromise and obeys Darius as long as it aligns with God's law. Daniel knowingly breaks a royal decree that bans prayer to anyone but the king. Despite knowing the risks, Daniel stays loyal to God. When his enemies report him, he faces execution and is thrown to the lions. However, he survives, and the king, relieved from a difficult situation, punishes the plotters.

The story conveys two messages. First, God's servant should remain faithful in prayer and worship, no matter the result. God saved Daniel from disaster. Second, Daniel's faithfulness taught the king, who wanted his subjects to worship him, about true worship (Daniel 6:25–27). Faithfulness, like ripples from a pebble in water, impacts more than just the faithful person.

What Happens In the Book of Daniel? Daniel’s Visions (7–12)

At the start of Daniel 7, the timeline in the book of Daniel shifts. Daniel's first vision goes back to Belshazzar's first year (Daniel 7:1), but later visions occur during the reign of Cyrus, the Persian king (Daniel 10:1). Daniel 7–12 focus on the meaning of history and God's control over it, shown through the mysterious symbols in dreams. This section divides into: 

The vision of four beasts (Daniel 7:1–28)

The vision of the ram and the goat (Daniel 8:1–27)

Daniel’s prayer (Daniel 9:1–27)

The vision of the end times (Daniel 10:1–12:13)

The first vision revisits the theme of four kingdoms, as seen in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream (Daniel 2). The second vision narrows the focus to two kingdoms, Persia and Greece. Much of the final vision about the end times covers events during the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes in the second century BC. All the visions share the same theme. Although human kingdoms may show their power in a chaotic world, the sovereign God works through history's apparent chaos toward a final goal of salvation.

The primary interpretation of the visions can relate to past historical events. However, a further messianic aspect appears in the New Testament. This aspect is most evident in Daniel 7. In the context of the four kingdoms, a divine court of judgment is established, led by the “Ancient of Days”—the almighty God (Daniel 7:9). Then Daniel sees the arrival of “One like the Son of Man” (Daniel 7:13). Although the phrase “Son of Man” was later seen as a messianic title, it did not technically have that meaning in the book of Daniel. Daniel 7:13 is a main source for the title “Son of Man,” which Jesus often used to refer to himself. His most significant use of that term was at his trial, where he directly linked his title with Daniel 7 (Matthew 26:63–64).

BOOK OF ECCLESIASTES

Ecclesiastes is an Old Testament book of wisdom literature. Wisdom literature includes biblical writings that reflect on how to live wisely. The book is philosophical. It asks deep questions about the meaning of life and the nature of human existence.

The Greek title “Ecclesiastes” comes from the Septuagint, which is the Greek translation of the Old Testament. Early Jewish tradition named books after their first few words. So, the Hebrew title of Ecclesiastes is The Words of Qoheleth, the Son of David, King in Jerusalem. It is also called Qoheleth.

The term “Qoheleth” is the author's title for himself throughout the book (Ecclesiastes 1:1–2, 12; 7:27; 12:8–10). It is the Hebrew participial form of a verb meaning “to assemble,” and it likely refers to someone who speaks in a gathering. The word is often translated as "the Preacher" in English. Due to the book's philosophical nature, the title might also indicate the author's role as a leader among wise men.

What Is the Book of Ecclesiastes About?

Who Wrote the Book of Ecclesiastes?

The authorship of Ecclesiastes raises complex questions, and biblical scholars do not agree. Early Jewish tradition was also divided. Some attributed the book to King Hezekiah and the scribes who worked with him, while others credited King Solomon.

People often use internal evidence to support the idea that Solomon wrote Ecclesiastes. The first verse credits the book to “the son of David.” Other passages (such as Ecclesiastes 1:16–17 and 2:6–7) also seem to refer to Solomon, who became king after David in the united kingdom of Israel. Those who disagree with Solomon's authorship see these references as literary tools. They believe a later unknown author used Solomon's devotion to wisdom to express his own thoughts on life's purpose and meaning.

Some scholars point to several passages in Ecclesiastes as evidence that Solomon did not write the book. For example, they argue that if Solomon were the author, he would not have used the past tense in speaking of his reign “over Israel in Jerusalem” (Ecclesiastes 1:12). Scholars who support Solomon as the author respond that the Hebrew verb translated “was” can also mean “became,” indicating that Solomon had become king in Jerusalem.

Some people claim that Ecclesiastes 1:16 suggests the text was written by someone who lived much later than Solomon. They argue that Solomon could not have claimed to be wiser than “all those before me who were over Jerusalem.” Such a claim, they say, points to a long line of kings before him. However, the author might have referred to prominent wise men rather than kings (see 1 Kings 4:31).

The strongest argument against Solomon as the author comes from a difference between the book and what we know about his life. Ecclesiastes reflects on life and calls people back to God and his commandments. Solomon, however, turned away from God as he grew older. His rule ended with idolatry (worship of other gods) and the oppression of his people. Some of the author’s statements also do not sound like a king describing his own reign.

These concerns are important, but they do not settle the question. The following points help answer these objections:

Solomon ruled for 40 years, and his turning away from God came late in life. He could have written the book after many years of experience, but before his final failure.

The historical books of the Old Testament do not focus on personal spiritual struggles. They mainly describe events that affected the whole nation and God’s plan for his people. For this reason, they would not likely record the kind of personal reflection found in Ecclesiastes, even if it happened.

Solomon had contact with many foreign nations. Because of this, some observations in the book may describe life outside Israel, not just conditions during his own rule.

It is difficult to determine the author, but there seems to be no conclusive evidence against Solomon as the author of Ecclesiastes.

When Was the Book of Ecclesiastes Written?

Most scholars who believe Solomon wrote Ecclesiastes think he did so in his last years as king, around 940 BC. This would place the book in the golden age of Israelite wisdom, authored by a leading teacher of wisdom.

Those who deny that Solomon wrote the book disagree on its date, but most think it was written after the exile in Babylon. The Maccabean period was around 165 BC. A date that late is hard to support because fragments of Ecclesiastes from the second century BC were found at Qumran, the site near the Dead Sea where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found. Also, the apocryphal book of Ecclesiasticus, which is not part of the Hebrew Bible, was strongly influenced by Ecclesiastes. Ecclesiasticus was probably written in the early second century BC. These factors leave little time for the book to be written and spread during the Maccabean period.

Some conservative scholars, like Franz Delitzsch and E. J. Young, believe the book dates to the fifth century BC. Many others think it is from the third century BC.

Internal Evidence

People have tried to date the book of Ecclesiastes using supposed historical references. However, the gloomy observations in passages like Ecclesiastes 1:2–11 and 3:1–15 might just reflect the author's views on life's emptiness. These do not necessarily mean the book was written during a period of national decline or social decay in Israel, which would not match Solomon's reign.

Some people believe that Ecclesiastes refers to Greek philosophical ideas. This may suggest that the book was written after the conquests of Alexander the Great spread Greek culture into Syria and Palestine. Alexander the Great lived from 356 to 323 BC. His conquests helped spread Greek culture throughout this region.

One important philosophical idea is the “golden mean” proposed by Aristotle. The golden mean suggests avoiding extremes to find satisfaction in life. It appears in Ecclesiastes 7:14–18. This idea is also present in Egyptian wisdom literature (Instruction of Amen-em-opet 9.14) and Aramaic wisdom literature. The Words of Ahiqar is a notable example of Aramaic wisdom. It expresses the golden mean this way: “Be not (too) sweet, lest they [swallow you]; be not (too) bitter [lest they spit you out].” The golden mean does not belong to one specific time or culture. It represents a basic wisdom shared by people across different eras and backgrounds.

Linguistic Considerations

The main challenge in dating Ecclesiastes is its language. The Hebrew used in Ecclesiastes is unique. It is different in style and language from fifth-century Old Testament books like Ezra and Nehemiah.

Some scholars believe that Aramaic heavily influenced the language of Ecclesiastes. They suggest the book was written when Aramaic was influential among Hebrew speakers. Others argue that the unique Hebrew features show similarities with Canaanite-Phoenician dialects.

People often say the Hebrew in the book is like later Mishnaic Hebrew, especially in its use of the relative pronoun. The Mishnah is the earliest written collection of Jewish oral traditions. However, the language of Ecclesiastes differs from the Mishnah in other aspects.

The language used might suggest the book was written later. However, Solomon might have used a literary style influenced by Phoenician literature. This style could have become standard for the genre of Ecclesiastes. During Solomon's reign, interactions between Palestine and Phoenicia were common.

What Is the Purpose of the Book of Ecclesiastes? What Does It Teach Us About God?

The book of Ecclesiastes shows that a worldview which leaves God out is meaningless. It seeks to show that a person may still find real satisfaction in a world that seems like nothing more than endless, tiring cycles. People feel trapped in this world with no way out. According to Qoheleth, we can find freedom by fearing God (living in awe of God and obeying God) and trusting that God will judge everything fairly. Therefore, life has a goal and purpose, even if it does not always seem that way in history and nature.

The book's main teaching about God is that God cares about human events and their injustices. He will judge every action. Therefore, life has a purpose, and human actions matter.

People often say Qoheleth has a negative view of life. In passages like Ecclesiastes 1:12–14, 18 and 2:1–9, 18–23, we can feel his sense of helplessness about what seemed like an empty existence. However, Qoheleth's negative outlook was about life without God. To him, such a life had no meaning.

The book reveals a positive message, though it is often overlooked. Qoheleth speaks in absolutes as he presents his argument. There is an absolute good for people living in a seemingly meaningless world. This good is enjoying God's gifts. Thus, Qoheleth is not completely pessimistic. When he considers God's influence in the world, he becomes optimistic. However, when he views life without God, he feels pessimistic, as this perspective only leads to despair.

Qoheleth's theology of contentment is clear in passages like Ecclesiastes 2:24–25, 3:10–13, and 3:22. The first passage seems to show a view of life focused on pleasure, making eating and drinking the main purpose. The phrase "eat and drink" is a Semitic idiom that represents daily life routines (see Jeremiah 22:15; Luke 17:27–28). Qoheleth uses this phrase to mean that one should enjoy God's gifts. Life is meant to be enjoyed, not just endured.

In Ecclesiastes 3:10–13, Qoheleth presents a major mystery of humanity: God has placed the knowledge of eternity in the human mind (“hearts” in the Berean Standard Bible). That is, God has made the mind able to think beyond the limits of physical existence. However, this ability does not reveal all of God's plans. Therefore, it is wise for a person to accept human limits and appreciate the knowledge God provides.

Ecclesiastes 3:16–4:3 is a challenging part of the book. Qoheleth observes life's unfairness. He concludes that God allows it to sift people, showing them that in themselves they are no more than animals. The same idea appears in Ecclesiastes 8:11, where Qoheleth notes that when evil is not punished, it encourages more wrongdoing. 

In Ecclesiastes 3:18, he claims injustice exists to separate the good from the wicked. The Hebrew phrase in that verse should be translated as “in and of themselves,” meaning that without God, humans are no better than animals. Without a belief in God, one cannot know what happens after death (Ecclesiastes 3:21). Qoheleth believes these injustices will be fixed only on the day of judgment. Therefore, it is wise to be content with God's plan and not worry about the future (Ecclesiastes 3:22).

The key to understanding the book of Ecclesiastes is the repeated phrase “under the sun.” This phrase shows Qoheleth's perspective. He is not saying all human experiences are pointless. Instead, he observes that life “under the sun,” or without God, is pointless. The apostle Paul gave a similar view of the world in Romans 8:20–23. However, he added that God uses everything in the world for good outcomes for his people (Romans 8:28). Qoheleth's viewpoint serves the same purpose.

People often interpret Qoheleth as expressing an Epicurean view of life. Epicureanism was a Greek philosophy that viewed pleasure, especially freedom from pain and distress, as life’s highest good. In this interpretation, Qoheleth teaches that eating and drinking are humanity's highest good. However, in Ecclesiastes 2:1–8, he tests pleasure and finds it futile. He concludes that pleasure is not an absolute good. The passages about eating and drinking refer only to enjoying the good and necessary things that come from God's hand.

What Is the Book of Ecclesiastes About?

The Vanity of the Cycle of History and Nature (1:1–11)

Qoheleth starts by describing the vanity of life, that is, its emptiness, and the apparent lack of purpose in nature. Human work achieves nothing (Ecclesiastes 1:3), and life's endless cycle seems pointless (1:4–11).

The Vanity of Qoheleth's Own Experience (1:12–2:26)

In this dramatic section, Qoheleth reflects on the futility of parts of his life that others might value. He remembers his quest for wisdom but finds human philosophy pointless (Ecclesiastes 1:12–18). His pursuit of pleasure (Ecclesiastes 2:1–11) also ends in futility. Given this, Qoheleth does not see pleasure as life's greatest goal. 

The search for true philosophical truths is tiring and pointless (Ecclesiastes 2:12–17). Human work is also in vain (Ecclesiastes 2:18–23) because a person cannot know who will benefit from that work (Ecclesiastes 2:21). Qoheleth concludes that the greatest good is to joyfully accept God's guidance (Ecclesiastes 2:24–26), adding an optimistic note to his message.

The Plight of Humanity apart from God (3:1–22)

Qoheleth's well-known statement that everything in life has its time (Ecclesiastes 3:1–9) is often seen as fatalistic. However, these verses likely describe how life’s circumstances cannot change. Humans cannot escape this continuous cycle, yet they can think beyond the physical world (Ecclesiastes 3:11). This is the mystery of humanity. Without considering God, people are no better than animals (Ecclesiastes 3:19–20).

Conclusions Resulting from Qoheleth's Observations (4:1–16)

The author starts with a bleak view of life (Ecclesiastes 4:1–3) but then shares lasting insights. For example, he notes that facing life's challenges is easier with a partner than alone (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12).

The Vanity of Living Only for Oneself (5:1–6:12)

Qoheleth strongly criticizes a selfish life and calls people to focus on God instead (Ecclesiastes 5:1–2, 4–6). He condemns the misuse of wealth and shows concern for the poor (Ecclesiastes 5:8–6:9), themes later highlighted in the New Testament.

Wisdom for Living (7:1–8:17)

This example of Old Testament wisdom literature uses a proverbial pattern (Ecclesiastes 7:1–13) and personal references (Ecclesiastes 7:23–29) to show how to find true satisfaction. The passage highlights the value of godly wisdom. Qoheleth teaches that God is the source of both adversity and prosperity (Ecclesiastes 7:14). He advises accepting both as coming from God. 

When applying wisdom to government authority (Ecclesiastes 8:2–9), Qoheleth advises obeying the authorities. The apostle Paul gave similar advice in Romans 13. Qoheleth is optimistic (Ecclesiastes 8:13), emphasizing the importance of fearing God. The author is not entirely pessimistic, as he shows that fearing God leads to true satisfaction.

Observations on Life’s Seeming Injustices (9:1–18)

“Under the sun,” meaning apart from God, there seem to be no differences among people (Ecclesiastes 9:1–6, 11–12). People often fail to notice great deeds, and those who do them receive no thanks (Ecclesiastes 9:13–16). However, a person should still be content because life offers some benefits (Ecclesiastes 9:7–10).

Wisdom and Folly (10:1–20)

In the Old Testament, wisdom means knowing God, while folly means rejecting God. Qoheleth shows that wisdom leads to honor and satisfaction, and folly leads to ruin.

Qoheleth's Conclusion—Fear God (11:1–12:14)

The book of Ecclesiastes starts by declaring that everything is meaningless, but it ends with Qoheleth seeing God beyond his bleak views. Ecclesiastes 11 begins by saying humans cannot understand God's ways. People should enjoy life, but they must remember that God will judge them in the future (Ecclesiastes 11:9–10). After beautifully describing old age (Ecclesiastes 12:1–8) and urging the reader to fear God while young, Qoheleth shares his conclusion. A person's whole duty is to fear God (Ecclesiastes 12:13–14). The pleasures of youth do not last, and without God a person is finally left with nothing. True satisfaction comes only from fear of God. Life without God is the greatest emptiness.

See also Solomon (Person); Wisdom; Wisdom Literature.

BOOK OF ELDAD AND MEDAD

This is an ancient work that existed before the Roman Empire became Christian. It claims to include the prophecies of Eldad and Medad. These were two elders whom Moses appointed while the Israelites were in the wilderness (Numbers 11:26). The Bible says they prophesied, but it does not tell what they said.

Because of this gap, someone wrote a separate work about them. That book has not survived. The only known quotation from it appears in the Shepherd of Hermas: “The Lord is near to those who return to Him, as written in Eldad and Medad, who prophesied to the people in the wilderness” (Vision II, chapter 3). This is the only surviving sentence that tells us anything about the content of the book.

See also Apocrypha; Eldad; Medad; Shepherd of Hermas.

BOOK OF ESTHER

An Old Testament book telling the story of a Jewish woman’s protection of her people after her marriage to a non-Jewish king.
