They do not believe that Christ is present in or with the bread and wine. However, many believe that Christ is present with his people as they worship and that the Lord’s Supper can strengthen their faith.

These differences were sharply debated during the Reformation in the sixteenth century and remain important today. Most Christians agree, however, that the Lord’s Supper is an important act of worship connected to the death of Jesus and his promise of salvation.

See Lord’s Supper; Presence of God.

CHRISTIAN

The followers of Jesus Christ were first called Christians in Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). When the Christian message reached Antioch, believers preached the good news to Gentiles as well as to Jews. This showed that the movement was becoming more than a new form of Judaism.

The Gentiles in Antioch may have created the name “Christian” for this new group. The believers often spoke about Christ, so people called them Christians. The name may have meant “members of Christ’s household” or “supporters of Christ.”

The name may also have been intended as a joke or insult. For example, the “Augustinians” were an organized group that publicly praised the emperor Nero Augustus. The people of Antioch may have formed the name “Christian” in a similar Latin style. Another example was the Herodians, who were supporters of Herod.

The title “Christ” was unfamiliar to many gentiles and may not have had a clear meaning for them. However, Chrestos, which means “good” or “kind,” was a common name. For this reason, some non-Christians called the group “Chrestians.” The Roman writer Suetonius later wrote that Jews were expelled from Rome in AD 49 because of someone he called “Chrestus.”

The believers themselves may not have liked the name “Christian” at first. However, like many nicknames, the name continued to be used.

The word “Christian” appears only three times in the Greek New Testament. Acts 11:26 explains where the name began. In Acts 26:28, Herod Agrippa II says to Paul, “In such a short time, are you persuading me to become a Christian?” First Peter 4:16 instructs Christians not to feel ashamed if they suffer. This is because they "bear" the name of Christ. 

The name does not appear again in surviving records until the second century. Ignatius of Antioch was one of the first Christian writers to use the name "Christians" for believers (Letter to the Ephesians 11:2). Pliny, a Roman governor in the region addressed by First Peter, also wrote to Emperor Trajan about people who were accused of being Christians.

After that time, Christians used the name more often. The name clearly showed that they belonged to Christ.

CHRISTOLOGY

The study of who Jesus Christ is and what he did. The belief that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, was first boldly stated by Peter at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16:16). This is the central belief of the Christian faith. It is what makes someone a Christian. All Christian theology is centered around understanding the meaning of this belief.

The first significant theological decision in the church, based on this belief, was accepting that Jesus, the Son of God, is truly divine. This means he shares the same essence with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. This belief was made explicit in the doctrine of the Trinity at the Council of Nicaea in AD 325. Since this doctrine was applied to Jesus of Nazareth, it led to the question: How can one person be both God and man? How can someone infinite become finite? How can someone eternal become part of time? How can God become human?

To answer this, the church accepted the doctrine of the Incarnation, which says that God became a human being in Jesus. This doctrine was developed after a lot of discussion. During these debates, the church rejected certain ideas: 

Docetism denied Jesus’s humanity to emphasize his divinity 

Adoptionism denied his divinity to emphasize his humanity

The Apollinarians believed that Jesus only looked human, but his spirit was divine

Others believed that Jesus was human but became divine through moral development and then became God. This either happened at his baptism when he received the Holy Spirit or his resurrection, as suggested by Acts 13:33—“Today I have become Your Father”

Nestorianism believed that Jesus was two separate persons—one divine and one human

Monophysitism believed that Jesus had a mixed divine and human nature

The Chalcedonian Creed

At the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451, the church declared that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. The creed from this council stated:

"[He is] consubstantial with the Father as to his Godhead, and consubstantial also with us as to his manhood; like unto us in all things, yet without sin; as to his Godhead, begotten of the Father before all worlds; but as to his manhood, in these days, born for us men and for our salvation, of the virgin Mary, the mother of God, one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, known in two natures, without confusion, without conversion, without severance, and without division; the distinction of the natures being in no wise abolished by their union, but the peculiarity of each nature being maintained, and both concurring in one person and subsistence. We confess not a Son divided and sundered into two persons, but one and the same Son, and only-begotten, and God-Logos, our Lord Jesus Christ."

During the Reformation, the Protestant Reformers also accepted this confession.

This understanding of Christ does not explain the mystery of the Incarnation but defines how believers should think about Christ. This has been important in Christian thought throughout history.

Some key terms from the creed are:

Nature (from the Greek physis) 

This does not refer to physical things that can be studied through science. Instead, "nature" refers to a thing's essence. Jesus Christ's nature being "divine" means that all the qualities that define God also apply to him. He is not just like God, he is God. But, the same thing is true about his human nature—Jesus does not only look like a man, he is a man. He is not only a man or only God, he is the God who became a man. Jesus did not stop being God when he became a man, nor did he trade a divine spirit for a human one. Instead, he took on humanity, so now he is both divine and human.

Person (from the Greek hypostasis)

This describes Jesus Christ as a self-aware, free individual, someone who can refer to himself as "I" and relate to others as "you." As a connection between God and humanity, Jesus is a person with both divine and human natures. While there cannot be a "person" without a "nature," there can be a "nature" without a "person." For example, an object like a stone may have the "nature" of being gray, hard, round, and smooth, but it is not a "person" because it is not self-aware or free.

Christ is a "person" with both a "divine nature" and a "human nature." The church fathers taught that while Christ had all divine and human qualities (including physical human attributes—the Word “became flesh,” John 1:14), He was not "two persons." He is a divine person with a human nature. He is not a human person. All humans have a beginning. A human becomes self-aware at some point. However, Jesus said, "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58). This statement is the absolute truth. The person who preached on the mountainside and called fishermen to follow him by the sea is the same person who existed before there was any sea, mountain, or even fishermen.

Jesus is not only a human who was given insight by the Word of God. Jesus is the eternal Son of God who became a human being. The Son of God did not enter a human person. He added human nature to his divine person. He remains the same person, though he now shares in our humanity. Therefore, Jesus is living in history and transcends history. For example, he said, "I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do. And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:4–5). Jesus speaks as someone in the world who also existed before the world began and shared in the Father's glory.

Trying to understand this mystery usually results in oversimplifying it. Some attempts have been: 

Docetism: Christ is a divine being who only appears human.

Adoptionism: Christ is a human being who became divine.

Ritschlianism: Christ only has divine value for others.

To preserve Jesus Christ's two natures, the creed uses four phrases that tell us what is true about the Incarnation (when Christ became a man):

Without confusion 

Without conversion 

Without separation 

Without division

Some people have mocked these as "four simple negatives," but they are actually very important. If any of these are false, we will lose a central belief of the Christian faith—that Jesus Christ is fully both God and man.

The creed does not only say what did not happen in the Incarnation, it also tells us what did happen:

Jesus's two natures were unified.

The two natures occur in one person.

That person is the eternal Son of the Father. 

This union of the two natures was done by the Son of God. This is the primary mystery of the Incarnation: no one knows how an infinite God became a finite man. Theologians have thought deeply about this, and more explanations have been written since the Council of Chalcedon.

The union of the divine and human natures in Jesus is called the "hypostatic union." This term comes from a Greek word that means "person." The union is personal because it is the act of a Person—the Son of God, who became human. This means that Jesus is a divine person who is worthy of worship. He is not only a human like anyone else. Worshipping a human would be idolatry. Because Jesus's divine and human nature are united in one person, Jesus is one Person, not two. Worshipping two persons—one human and one divine—would be absurd. Therefore, this Person, who combines both divine and human natures, is often called the "God-man." As long as this term is understood to mean that Jesus Christ is fully both God and man, it is consistent with the creed's teaching.

Christology After Chalcedon

After the Council of Chalcedon, understanding Jesus's humanity became challenging, and there were not many agreements between theologians. However, the view that is most consistent with the Chalcedonian Creed and widely accepted by Protestants refers to the "impersonal humanity" of Jesus. Modern theologians like Karl Barth, Emil Brunner, and G. C. Berkouwer have also supported this view.

"Impersonal humanity" does not mean the incarnate Jesus lacked human qualities. Instead, it means his humanity only exists as part of the divine Person who took on human nature in the Incarnation. Jesus’s human nature exists in and through the Word (the Son of God), who is God. While God is present in all creation, God does not share his identity with anything. Even when the New Testament says that the Holy Spirit lives in Christians, it does not mean they are the same as God. The human and divine are not the same. However, Jesus Christ was unique: Jesus is identical with God because he is the Word made flesh. As Karl Barth says, Jesus is not just living through God or with God; he is God. His human nature is united with his divine nature, meaning his humanity is a characteristic of his divinity. His human nature only exists because of the divine Word acting in and through him.

Simply put, Jesus is so united with God that he can only exist as a man because he is God. This is confirmed by two doctrines:

Anhypostasy: Jesus's human nature does not exist by itself 

Enhypostasy: Jesus's human nature exists through its union with the divine Son of God. Jesus of Nazareth did not become the Son of God, the Son of God became Jesus of Nazareth 

The Incarnation is an act of a divine Person, not an experience of a human person becoming divine. In the Incarnation, the Son of God acted, but a human person was not acted upon. Because the divine Son acts to become the man, Jesus of Nazareth, this man is the Son of God in a way that no other human can be.

The scriptural proof for the doctrine of the Incarnation includes: 

The Gospels

Several passages in Paul’s letters, especially Philippians 2:6–8 which is the most important statement about Christ in the New Testament. Paul speaks of Jesus, "Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness."

The Chalcedonian Creed does not solve the mystery of the Incarnation, and theologians have made many efforts to understand it better. One well-known theory, based on the passage from Philippians mentioned earlier, is called "kenosis." It suggests that when the Son of God became human, he abandoned ("emptied himself") some aspects of his divinity. However, the text in Philippians does not say that he emptied himself of anything, but rather that he "emptied himself," which is a figure of speech meaning that he humbled himself (the King James Version says "made himself of no reputation"). Despite the difficulty of interpreting this statement, the theory of kenosis is still present, especially in British theology. Another interpretation suggests that Jesus's humanity was a disguise (a term used by the philosopher Søren Kierkegaard) that hid his divine identity from everyone except those with faith. According to this view, the Incarnation reveals the truth but also hides it.

See also Ascension of Christ; Christ; Incarnation; Jesus Christ, Life and Teachings of; Kingdom of God, Kingdom of Heaven; Messiah; Parable; Son of God; Son of Man; Virgin Birth of Jesus; Word.

t: Chronicles, Books of First and Second
c:
CHRONICLES, Books of First and Second

Two OT books, historical records of King David and his successors in the land of Judah. The books of Chronicles are among the most neglected books in the Bible, partly because most of the material can be found in Samuel, Kings, or elsewhere in the OT. Fourteen chapters (1 Chr 1–9; 23–27) are little more than lists of names; the rest of the material is primarily historical narrative, which some people find almost as boring as lists. Yet the content of Chronicles is not history in a professional or academic sense because the materials used are comparable to the annals compiled by ancient Near Eastern court scribes. Those sources recorded each year’s most important events and were frequently more propagandistic than objectively historical. The records in Chronicles, somewhat eclectic in nature and ignoring certain facets of national history while emphasizing others, deal with only a selected portion of the history of the Israelites. A good deal of the criticism that the work is historically unreliable has come from lack of understanding the book’s character. Chronicles is not so much a history as a metaphysical interpretation of events in Israelite life in light of covenantal values. It was not sufficient for the Chronicler that kings rose and fell; the events were interpreted from a special religious standpoint.

• Content

Author

In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Chronicles form a single book. The Bible does not say who wrote that book or when it was written. According to the Jewish Talmud, Ezra wrote “his book and Chronicles—the order of all generations down to himself.” Although many scholars defend the view that Ezra wrote Chronicles, there is still no general agreement about the date and authorship of the book.

The author is usually called “the Chronicler,” a title suggesting that he was a historian. It is possible that he was a scribe, priest, or Levite. Evidently the writer had access to government and temple archives, because repeated references are made to a number of official records of kings (1 Chr 9:1; 27:24; 2 Chr 16:11; 20:34; 25:26; 27:7; 28:26; 32:32; 33:18; 35:27; 36:8) and prophets (1 Chr 29:29; 2 Chr 9:29; 12:15; 13:22; 20:34; 26:22; 32:32; 33:19).

The evidence is suggestive, but not conclusive, that the author of Chronicles also wrote the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. The last two verses of Chronicles are almost the same as the first three verses of Ezra. The language and literary style of all three books are similar. The same theological concerns for the temple and its worship and the same interest in lists and genealogies appear in all three books. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra-Nehemiah is considered one book and stands before Chronicles. Chronicles stands at the very end of the Hebrew Bible.

Date

It is not possible to determine precisely when the book of Chronicles was written. The book ends with a reference to the decree of Cyrus, king of Persia, permitting the Jewish captives in Babylon to return to their homeland. Since Cyrus’s decree is usually dated about 538 BC, Chronicles could not have been written before that date. But if Ezra-Nehemiah is a part of the same work as Chronicles, the materials could not have been written until Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem in 444 BC.

Genealogies in Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah may shed some light on the dating of the books. In 1 Chronicles 3:10–24 the lineage of David and Solomon is traced through the sixth generation after the exile, which would make the date for Anani (the last person in the list) about 400 BC.

The language of Chronicles is definitely that of postexilic Hebrew. The use of the Persian word daric (1 Chr 29:7), plus a lack of any Greek words, places Chronicles in the Persian period (538–331 BC). The word midrash (“exposition”) appears in the OT only in Chronicles (2 Chr 13:22; 24:27) but is very common in postbiblical Hebrew. Around 400 BC is probably the best estimate for the date of Chronicles, based on evidence now available.

Background

During the Persian period, some of the Jews returned to Jerusalem from Babylon soon after Cyrus’s decree. They rebuilt the temple and waited for the messianic age to come. But with drought, economic hardships, and moral and spiritual laxness, their hopes faded. Judah was stable politically as a part of the large, dominant Persian Empire. There was not the slightest possibility of restoring the Davidic kingdom.

If the kingdom of David could not be restored politically, how was a Jew of the early fourth century BC to understand history and the place of the Jews in God’s plan? The Chronicler, living at that time, found the key to history in God’s covenant with David. The first 10 chapters of 1 Chronicles lead up to David; chapters 11–29 detail events of David’s rule. Moses is mentioned in Chronicles 31 times; David, more than 250 times. David planned the temple and collected money to build it. He appointed Levites, singers, and gatekeepers. He divided the priesthood into its orders. He was responsible for the temple worship, which was tremendously important to the Chronicler and his contemporaries.

The Persian period of Israel’s history is largely a silent one, both in other OT materials and in archaeological finds. Of course, all the evidence is not yet in, as archaeologists continue their investigations of the period.

Origin and Purpose

The Chronicler must have lived in Jerusalem and written for the Jewish community there. He refers to Jerusalem about 240 times and to Judah more than 225 times. A negative feeling toward the northern kingdom of Israel can be seen in the almost total lack of references to any northern king. The Chronicler’s attitude toward the north is clearly expressed in the two following verses: “The northern tribes of Israel have refused to be ruled by a descendant of David to this day” (2 Chr 10:19, nlt) and “Don’t you realize that the Lord, the God of Israel, made an unbreakable covenant with David, giving him and his descendants the throne of Israel forever?” (13:5, nlt).

The Chronicler wanted the Jewish people to see that God was sovereign over all things. For example, he includes David’s affirmation: “Yours, O Lord, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty. Everything in the heavens and on earth is yours, O Lord, and this is your kingdom. We adore you as the one who is over all things. Riches and honor come from you alone, for you rule over everything. Power and might are in your hand, and it is at your discretion that people are made great and given strength” (1 Chr 29:11–12, nlt).

Compiled in the postexilic period, Chronicles was meant to emphasize the significance of the theocracy seen in light of earlier history. The theocracy was a social configuration God planned for postexilic Judah, a religious rather than secular community. Instead of a king, the Jews had a priesthood of which the Lord approved (as distinct from the corrupt priests who had been to a large extent responsible for the preexilic moral and spiritual collapse of the nation).

The postexilic Judeans were to live as a holy nation, not as people with political and nationalistic ambitions. Therefore, the Chronicler demanded implicit obedience to the Mosaic covenant so that the returning Jews could find prosperity, divine blessing, and grace. The Jews were still the chosen people, purged by the experience of exile, with a new opportunity to fulfill the Sinai covenant.

The Chronicler gave great weight to divine retribution and was insistent that all action be guided by specific moral principles, to reflect God’s character clearly in his people. Because the writer saw God’s hand in all history, punishing the apostate and being gracious to the penitent, he saw in the chastened remnant of the exile the true spiritual heirs of the house of David. He insisted that the postexilic community adhere rigorously to the morality of Sinai, guarding against preexilic apostasy and ensuring divine blessing.

The writer wanted the Jews to know God’s power. He also wanted them to believe in the Lord so that they would be “established.” If they believed God’s messengers, they would succeed (2 Chr 20:20). He also wanted the people to know that Jerusalem was God’s chosen place of worship (2 Chr 5–6), and that the temple, priests, singers, Levites, and gatekeepers had been divinely appointed (1 Chr 28:19). The temple was meant to be a place where all their needs could be met (2 Chr 6:19–7:3).

Content

Chronicles can be briefly outlined as follows: 1 Chronicles—genealogies (1–9); the reign of David (10–29); 2 Chronicles—the reign of Solomon (1–9); the kings of Judah (10:1–36:21); epilogue on the exile and return (36:22–23). Since the Chronicler’s writings do not have a didactic format, the reader must draw out those ideas and principles that are prominent and basic.

One important idea running through Chronicles is the greatness, power, and uniqueness of God. It is expressed most beautifully and forcefully in 1 Chronicles 29:11–12, which declares that everything in heaven and earth belongs to God and he is head over all. Other passages make a similar claim. When Sennacherib, king of Assyria, attacked Judah and Jerusalem, King Hezekiah of Judah admonished his people not to fear the king of Assyria.

Several times the Chronicler repeats the idea that Israel’s God is unique: there is no other God like the Lord. In 1 Chronicles 16:25–26, Psalm 96:4–5 is quoted: “Great is the Lord! He is most worthy of praise! He is to be revered above all gods. The gods of other nations are merely idols, but the Lord made the heavens!” (nlt). Both David and Solomon are quoted as saying that there is no other God but the Lord (1 Chr 17:20; 2 Chr 6:14).

Chronicles emphasizes that the Lord is “greater than all gods” (2 Chr 2:5). The classic passage that stresses the differences between God and the “god” of a nation is in 2 Chronicles 32. When Sennacherib attacked Jerusalem, he asked the people what they were relying on to withstand the siege in Jerusalem. Sennacherib was saying, in effect, “Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you by telling you that your God will deliver you. No god of any nation so far has been able to stand against me. Your God is like the gods of all the other nations. He will not be able to deliver you from me.” The Chronicler observes that the Assyrians spoke of the God of Jerusalem as they spoke of the gods of the peoples of the earth. But God did deliver Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from Sennacherib.

Several passages declare that God rules over the nations (1 Chr 17:21; 2 Chr 20:6). In fact, the Chronicler saw the Lord as the one who directs history. The Lord brought Israel out of Egypt and drove the Canaanites out of their land (1 Chr 17:21; 2 Chr 6:5; 20:7). Some seeming quirks of history are explained with such phrases as “it was ordained by God” (2 Chr 22:7, rsv). Over and over in telling the story of the struggles of the kings of Judah with other nations, Chronicles points out that the Lord always decided the battle (1 Chr 10:13–14; 18:6; 2 Chr 12:2; 13:15; 20:15; 21:11–14; 24:18; 28:1, 5–6, 19).

To the Chronicler the Lord was a covenant-keeping God (2 Chr 6:14). He was the God of justice and righteousness (12:6), so human judges must judge honestly and fairly (19:7). The Chronicler made it clear that no individual or nation could succeed by opposing God (24:20); not only would people fail against God, but they were powerless without him (1 Chr 29:14; 2 Chr 20:12).

The Lord is seen not only as a unique, righteous, and powerful God, but also as a wise God. God tests the human heart and knows when he finds integrity (1 Chr 29:17). Solomon prayed for God to “hear thou from heaven thy dwelling place, and forgive, and render unto every man according unto all his ways, whose heart thou knowest; (for thou only knowest the hearts of the children of men)” (2 Chr 6:30, kjv).

Although God knows all about human beings, and has supreme power in heaven and on earth, men and women are still free to obey or disobey the Lord. The stories in Chronicles depict people who chose to obey or disobey God. Those who obeyed succeeded; but to the extent that others, even kings, disobeyed God, they failed. Three of the Chronicler’s heroes were Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah. Each was a great reformer, and each was commended for obeying the Lord. But each one sinned near the end of his life and incurred the disfavor of God. Jehoshaphat joined an alliance with a wicked king from the north (2 Chr 20:35–37). Hezekiah sinned in receiving envoys from Babylon and “God left him to himself” (32:31). Josiah did not obey the word of God spoken by Pharaoh Neco and was killed (35:21–24).

The Chronicler believed that all human beings have sinned (2 Chr 6:36), and should repent with all their mind and heart (6:38). One of the greatest passages on repentance in all the Bible is in 2 Chronicles 7:14.

A prominent theme in Chronicles is the importance of the temple as the place to meet God in worship. One could say that almost everything in Chronicles is related to the temple in one way or another. For a person living in Jerusalem in the fourth century BC under the domination of the Persians, temple worship was very significant. The Chronicler expressed the importance of true community and institutional worship.

Worship was the dominant attitude of the Chronicler, whose God was worthy to be praised. A worship service is described in 2 Chronicles 29:20–30. Hezekiah commanded a burnt offering and a sin offering to be made for all Israel. The Levites were stationed in the house of the Lord with cymbals, harps, and lyres. The priests had trumpets. “Then Hezekiah ordered that the burnt offering be placed on the altar. As the burnt offering was presented, songs of praise to the Lord were begun, accompanied by the trumpets and other instruments of David, king of Israel. The entire assembly worshiped the Lord as the singers sang and the trumpets blew, until all the burnt offerings were finished. Then the king and everyone with him bowed down in worship. King Hezekiah and the officials ordered the Levites to praise the Lord with the psalms of David and Asaph the seer. So they offered joyous praise and bowed down in worship” (2 Chr 29:27–30, nlt).

See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Israel, History of; King; Kings, Books of First and Second.

CHRONOLOGY OF THE BIBLE (New Testament)

Chronology is a part of biblical studies that tries to find the order of New Testament events and the time between them. Chronology is important for historians, who need to figure out the causes and effects of past events. For historians, knowing the order of events and how they influenced each other is more important than assigning exact dates. In fact, very few New Testament events can be dated precisely.

Christianity's influence is evident in how the Western world divides history into BC (before Christ) and AD (anno Domini, “in the year of the Lord”). Before this dating system became common in the Middle Ages, people dated events by their relation to other major events, such as the founding of Rome or the start of a king's reign. In the sixth century, a monk named Dionysius Exiguus created the dating system now widely used in the West. He used the birth of Christ as the dividing point. However, he made a calculation error, leading to the odd fact that Jesus was born at least four years "before Christ."

Preview

The Life of Jesus

The Life of Jesus

The Birth of Jesus

According to Matthew 2:1, Jesus was born during the time of King Herod. A historian from the first century AD, Josephus, noted that Herod died in the spring of 4 BC. So, Jesus was born before that year, but we do not know exactly when. Luke 2:1–2 mentions that Jesus was born when "Caesar Augustus," the Roman emperor, ordered a census (population count) across the nation. This was the first census taken when Quirinius was governor of Syria. These statements lead to two questions: When was this census taken, and when did Quirinius govern Syria? Neither question has a completely clear answer.

Along with earlier references, census records found in Egypt suggest enrollments took place every 14 years. This would place a census around 8 or 9 BC. Time was needed to complete the census because it required people to travel to their birthplace. So, the birth of Jesus might have been a bit later than the decree, possibly in 7 BC.

Josephus noted that Quirinius became governor of Syria in AD 6. This date is too late to fit the time of the birth of Jesus. However, some scholars have argued from ancient inscriptions that Quirinius also served in Syria before 6 BC. During that earlier period, he was a special representative of Emperor Augustus, not the regular governor. This earlier service might be the period mentioned in Luke 2:2. 

Why did Luke mention Quirinius instead of the regular governor of Syria then? Perhaps Luke wanted to give a more exact date for the birth of Jesus. Quirinius held power for a shorter time than the regular governor, so the time frame would have been more exact.

Jesus was likely born around 7 or 6 BC. This aligns with Matthew 2:16, the verse that suggests Jesus was born at least two years before Herod's death in 4 BC. There is no clear evidence about the exact day and month of his birth. The celebration of December 25 as Christmas began in the fourth century. It was probably a Christian alternative to the pagan winter solstice festival, Saturnalia.

The Beginning of Public Ministry

Luke 3:23 states that Jesus was "about thirty years old" when he started his ministry. This age is an estimate, so he could have been a few years older or younger (compare the Testament of Levi 2:2; 12:5, an ancient Jewish writing that is not part of the Bible). If we add 30 years to the suggested birth date, we get AD 24. 

This date cannot be right, however, because Jesus began his ministry after John the Baptist was known. Luke 3:1–3 specifies that John the Baptist appeared publicly in "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" when Pilate was governor of Judea. Pilate governed from AD 26 to 36, and the 15th year of Tiberius was likely AD 27. Therefore, Jesus did not start his ministry before AD 27. If only a short time passed between the ministry of John and the ministry of Jesus, Jesus likely began in AD 27 or 28, around 33 years old.

The Crucifixion of Jesus

All four Gospel accounts suggest that Jesus had the Last Supper with his disciples on Thursday evening. He was crucified on Friday, and rose from the dead early Sunday morning (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:1; Luke 24:1). The idea that Jesus rose on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:4) comes from the Jewish tradition of counting part of a day as a full day. According to Matthew (26:19), Mark (14:12), and Luke (22:15), the Last Supper was the Passover meal, an annual celebration of Israel’s escape from Egypt (Exodus 12–15). However, according to John 13:1 and 19:14, the Passover meal had not yet been eaten on Friday, so the Last Supper in John was not the Passover meal. 

No one has fully explained the apparent discrepancy. Some scholars suggest that using two different calendars caused the confusion. According to this theory, Jesus followed a calendar that placed the Passover meal on Thursday night. Temple officials, however, used a different calendar. According to this calendar the sacrificial killings were scheduled for the next day. John may have used the second system to emphasize that Christ was offered as the Passover sacrifice (compare John 19:36; 1 Corinthians 5:7). 

To determine how long the public ministry of Jesus lasted and the year he died, we can look at time references in John's Gospel. John mentions at least three Passovers (John 2:13; 6:4; 13:1) and possibly four (5:1). Since Passover was an annual event, the ministry of Jesus lasted at least two, possibly three years. In Matthew, Mark, and Luke, Jesus died on a Friday, the 15th of the Jewish month Nisan (which overlaps March and April). According to John, Jesus died on 14 Nisan. The question is: Between 26 and 36 (when Pilate governed Judea), when did 14 or 15 Nisan fall on a Friday? The answer is AD 27, 29, 30, and 33. Of these, 27 is too early and 33 is likely too late. Therefore, Jesus was probably crucified in 29 or 30, his public ministry lasted two or three years, and he was 35 or 36 years old when he died.

Events from AD 30 to 50

Acts is the only New Testament book that records how much time passed between the death of Jesus and his return to heaven. Acts 1:3 says, "After His suffering, He presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive. He appeared to them over a span of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God." 

The next important event after Jesus went to heaven was Pentecost (Acts 2:1). Pentecost, a Greek word meaning "fiftieth," was a celebration of the Feast of Weeks or Harvest. The Feast happened 50 days after Passover (see Exodus 34:22; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). Jesus was crucified during Passover in AD 29 or 30. The Pentecost in Acts 2:1, when the disciples received the Holy Spirit, took place about 50 days after the crucifixion. This would also have been around 10 days after the ascension, when Jesus went up to heaven. 

After that, it is hard to know the exact dates of events in the early chapters of Acts because there are no specific timeframes. To date events in the time of the apostles, we first find at least one event with a known date from sources outside the New Testament. Then, we estimate the time between events before and after that event. Sometimes, Acts tells us how much time passes between two events, but usually it does not, so the dates are only approximate.

One key event is the great famine predicted by Agabus, which occurred in Palestine during the rule of Roman Emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28–29). Josephus, alive during that time, provides enough details to place the famine between 46 and 48 AD. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish laws, tells us that from autumn 47 to autumn 48 was a sabbatical year. During this time, Jews let the land rest and did not harvest crops (see Leviticus 25:2–7). This practice could have worsened and extended the famine. However, it is unclear when the famine started. Some scholars suggest 46 AD, while others propose 47 AD.

It might seem strange that Luke, the author of Acts, mentions the famine (Acts 11:28) before describing the death of Herod Agrippa (12:20–23). The Jewish historian Josephus says that Herod Agrippa, the grandson of Herod the Great, died in about AD 44, probably in the spring. If so, Herod died several years before the famine that Luke mentioned earlier.

Some scholars think Luke placed these events in the wrong order. Others believe Acts 12:1–24 returns to an earlier event so that Luke can complete the account of the church in Jerusalem. Ancient historians often organized their writing this way by following one source to a suitable stopping point before turning to another. According to this view, Luke's order of events reflects an accepted writing method rather than a mistake in dating.

Herod Agrippa died in AD 44 (Acts 12:23). The apostle James, whom Herod killed with a sword (verse 2), likely died shortly before AD 44, possibly during Passover in AD 43 (verse 3). The apostle Peter was imprisoned and miraculously escaped during this time (verses 3–17).

Christians in Antioch decided to help those in Jerusalem during a severe famine (Acts 11:29), choosing Barnabas and Paul to deliver the money. This was Paul's second trip to Jerusalem after he became a Christian. Acts 9:26–30 describes his first visit. Acts 15 describes his third visit. This is when Paul and Barnabas went to discuss with the apostles and elders if non-Jewish converts to Christianity needed to be circumcised. The timing of Paul's first and third visits to Jerusalem, and his conversion, depends on how these visits relate to the visits mentioned in Paul's letter to the Galatians.

The main question, which New Testament scholars still debate, concerns Paul’s visits to Jerusalem. In Galatians 1:15–2:10, Paul says that he visited Jerusalem twice after his conversion. The first visit was three years later (1:18). The second was 14 years after that (2:1–10). 

All scholars agree that the first visit, three years after his conversion, matches the first visit recorded in Acts 9:26–30. However, opinions differ on whether Galatians 2:1–10 refers to the second visit to Jerusalem during the famine in Acts 11:30. In this case the third visit in Acts 15 is not mentioned in Galatians. Or, Galatians 2:1–10 could refer to the visit in Acts 15. In this case, the famine visit is not mentioned in Galatians.

Supporters of the first reconstruction present six arguments: 

Paul detailed his travels in Galatians 1:15–24 to show he did not learn his gospel from people (1:12). His visits to the Jerusalem apostles were not to receive his gospel. If Paul left out the second Jerusalem visit, it would harm his credibility with the Galatians. The first reconstruction avoids this issue. Leaving out a third visit in Galatians 2:1–10 might mean it had not happened when Galatians was written. 

Galatians 2:1–10 describes a private meeting between Paul, Barnabas, and the "pillar" apostles. The meeting in Acts 15 was public and involved the entire church. So, Galatians 2:1–10 likely refers to a private meeting during the visit in Acts 11:30, which Galatians does not mention. 

Paul's eagerness to help the poor in Galatians 2:10 fits with the second Jerusalem visit, when he delivered aid to the poor (Acts 11:30). 

If Galatians 2 described the same trip as Acts 15, it would likely mention the Jerusalem Council's decision. This is especially likely, since it related to the circumcision issue Paul addressed in Galatians. 

It is unlikely the Jerusalem Council happened before Galatians 2:11–21. This is where Paul rebuked Peter for avoiding fellowship with non-Jewish believers. This would not have been an issue if the church had recently settled the Gentile status issue in Jerusalem.

According to Galatians 1:6, the letter was written "quickly" after Paul founded the Galatian churches. This makes sense if Galatians was written soon after the first missionary journey, just before the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15. This would mean Galatians was Paul's first letter.

Scholars who support the second reconstruction present four arguments: 

The main purpose of Paul's visit in Galatians 2:1–10 seems similar to that in Acts 15:1–20. Both address whether Gentile converts need circumcision (Galatians 2:3–5; Acts 15:1, 5). This similarity is clear, but there is no such clear link between Galatians 2 and Acts 11:30. 

Based on style and content, Galatians resembles Romans and 1 and 2 Corinthians. This suggests it was written much later than the Jerusalem Council. Paul likely would have included a reference to the Jerusalem Council (namely Galatians 2:1–10) in his writings, as its decision supported his view on circumcision. 

Acts 11:30 shows Barnabas as the leader of the Barnabas/Paul team, with his name listed first (as in Acts 12:25; 13:1–2, 7; see also 11:25–26). However, in Galatians 2, Paul describes himself as the leader. Acts portrays Paul as the leader from the first missionary journey (Acts 13:9, 13, 43, 46, 50), including the third Jerusalem visit (15:2). Because of this, it is more likely that Galatians 2 refers to the trip in Acts 15. 

Finally, in Galatians 2:7–8, Paul is recognized as an apostle to the Gentiles, equal to Peter. If Galatians 2 described events from Acts 11:30 before the first missionary journey, the leading apostles could hardly have recognized Paul's authority as an apostle to the Gentiles. It is more likely that Galatians 2 occurred after the first missionary journey, just as Acts 15 did, and that both refer to the same event.

The importance of these arguments for chronology is that, in the first view, Paul's conversion happened 17 years before the famine visit mentioned in Acts 11:30 (see also Galatians 1:18; 2:1). In the second view, Paul's conversion occurred 17 years before the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15. The difference between these views is just one year.

It is useful to consider a likely date for Paul's arrival in Corinth during his second missionary journey (Acts 18:1). On this journey (15:40–18:22), Paul and Silas traveled by land through Syria, Cilicia, Phrygia, and Galatia. They visited churches they had founded earlier. They reached Troas, then moved on to Philippi and continued along the coast through Thessalonica and Berea. 

Paul went to Athens before arriving in Corinth. From Acts 18:12, we know Gallio was a proconsul (governor) in Corinth while Paul was there. An inscription found at nearby Delphi suggests Gallio's term was from mid-51 to mid-52. The event in Acts 18:12–17 likely happened early in Gallio's term, as the Jews sought a ruling against Paul from the new proconsul. Shortly after, Paul left Corinth, probably in the summer or fall of 51. 

According to Acts 18:11, Paul spent 18 months in Corinth, suggesting he arrived in early 50 or late 49. This is supported by Acts 18:2, which mentions that Aquila and Priscilla had recently been exiled from Rome when Paul arrived. A fifth-century historian, Orosius, dated Claudius's official order expelling Jews from Rome to AD 49. Therefore, Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla likely arrived around late 49 or early 50. Early in his 18-month stay, Paul wrote his First and Second Letters to the Thessalonians.

The two fixed dates are 46 or 47 for the famine visit (Acts 11:30) and late 49 or early 50 for Paul's arrival in Corinth (Acts 18:1). Acts 24:27 records an event that helps establish dates for other events in Acts. Porcius Festus replaced Felix as governor of Judea. Evidence from Eusebius, a historian who lived in the fourth century, suggests that this change probably took place in the summer of AD 59.

Paul was arrested in Jerusalem (Acts 21:33) in 57, about two years before Festus arrived. This likely happened in late spring or summer of 57. Paul hoped to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (20:16), which was at the end of May. He was arrested shortly after arriving in the city.

Paul celebrated the Passover festival with the church in Philippi (Acts 20:6), which was 50 days before Pentecost. This likely took place from April 7–14, AD 57. After the feast, he quickly traveled to Caesarea and Jerusalem (20:6–21:16). Before visiting Philippi for Passover, Paul spent three months in Greece (20:3). Based on his travels through Macedonia and visits to the Thessalonians and Bereans, these three months were likely the winter of 56–57 (Acts 20:3; compare 1 Corinthians 16:6). He probably spent this time in Corinth, the main church of Greece, where he partly wrote the Letter to the Romans.

Five years passed between Paul's departure from Corinth on his second missionary journey (Acts 18:18) in autumn 51 and his arrival in Corinth on the third journey (20:2) in late winter 56. We cannot date all his activities exactly. Paul mentioned working in Ephesus for three of those years (20:31; see also 19:1–20:1). Considering travel time before and after, he likely stayed in Ephesus from 52 or 53 to summer 55 or 56 (see 1 Corinthians 16:8). During his long stay in Ephesus, Paul wrote his First Letter to the Corinthians. On his way to Corinth in 56, he wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia.

Festus became governor in the summer of 59, after Paul had been in prison in Caesarea for two years. A few days later, Paul was tried before Festus (Acts 25:1–12). Paul did not want to be handed over to the Jewish authorities, so he appealed to Caesar (verse 12), meaning he would go to Rome. Acts does not mention any delays, so the journey likely started in the summer or fall of 59 (27:2). 

Luke reported that when Paul, a prisoner, reached Fair Havens on the island of Crete, the weather was dangerous for sea travel because the fast had passed (Acts 27:8–9). An ancient writer noted that sailing was risky between mid-September and mid-November, and impossible until spring. The fast likely referred to the one before the Day of Atonement, which in the year 59 was on October 5. 

Fourteen days after leaving Fair Havens, Paul's ship was wrecked on the coast of Malta, south of Sicily (verses 27–44). Three months later, Paul sailed for Rome again on a ship that had wintered in Malta (28:11). Soon, Christians in Rome welcomed him (verse 15). Paul arrived in Rome in early AD 60. The book of Acts ends by noting, "Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house" (verse 30). The New Testament does not mention the outcome of his trial. Traditionally, during this time, he wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon.

Eusebius recorded a tradition that after defending himself, Paul was sent out to preach again, and that when he returned to Rome a second time, he was killed under Nero. Nero, the Roman emperor from 54 to 68, executed many Christians in Rome soon after a major fire in July 64, according to the Roman historian Tacitus. 

Some early Christian writings, like those by Clement, suggest that Peter and Paul were both killed in Rome during this brutal persecution. If this is true and Eusebius was correct, Paul may have spent the years 62 to 64 freely ministering in the eastern provinces. Many conservative scholars believe Paul’s First Letter to Timothy and his Letter to Titus were written during this time. Second Timothy was probably written from Rome shortly before Paul was killed for his faith in 64. It was likely his final letter (2 Timothy 2:9; 4:6).

In Jerusalem, within three years after Paul had been taken to Rome, James the brother of Jesus was stoned to death by the Jewish authorities. Josephus records this event happening in 62. Soon after, Eusebius notes that the church in Jerusalem received a prophecy. It warned them to leave the doomed city and move to Pella, one of the cities of the Decapolis (“ten cities”) east of the Jordan. When war began between the Jews and Romans in 66, most Christians escaped the violence. The war ended in 70 with the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple (see Mark 13:2; Luke 21:24).

CHRONOLOGY OF THE BIBLE (Old Testament)

Old Testament chronology is the study of the dates and order of events in the Old Testament. Scholars examine evidence, theories, and assumptions to decide when events may have happened and how they relate to one another.

Some questions do not have a clear answer. Scholars may need to choose between different theories, even when none of them solves every problem.

Chronology is an important part of biblical studies because it helps people understand the historical setting of biblical texts. In general, scholars understand the order of Old Testament events well enough to support the basic historical accuracy and sequence presented in Scripture.

Students studying Old Testament timelines use both the Bible and sources from outside the Bible. Biblical information includes: 

genealogies (lists of family relationships) that show connections between families and tribes;

specific numbers given by biblical authors to show a person's age, a king's reign, or the length of an event; and

statements that date an event in a specific year of a king's reign or link it to a well-known natural event at the time (for example, Amos 1:1; Zechariah 14:5).

With so many chronological passages in the Old Testament, you might think setting dates and sequences would be easy. However, each type of biblical material has unique problems that need solving first.

Many nonbiblical sources help us understand Old Testament timelines. New sources continually add to what we know as they are discovered. These include: 

official records of important events such as military campaigns from countries like Egypt or Babylonia;

official inscriptions that dedicate or celebrate a major victory;

annals (official yearly records) that list a ruler's major achievements each year; and

ostraca (inscribed pieces of pottery) containing letters, tax transactions and economic records, military dispatches between field leaders and command headquarters, or other information.

Ostraca may be dated archaeologically and are often used to supplement the biblical record.

Chronologists study information from the Bible and from outside the Bible to find connections between the sources. These connections create a system that fits the greatest number of facts. New evidence might require changes to this system. While the main framework of biblical chronology appears stable, many details may shift with new discoveries.

Generally, the older the historical period, the less certain we are about the exact dates. For example, in the second millennium BC, many dates have a 100-year range. By the time of David and Solomon (around 1000 BC), scholars debate dates within a decade. 

As we move closer to the present, the date range narrows. By the middle of the ninth century BC, most dates are accurate within one or two years, except for a few problematic periods. Keep these limitations in mind when studying major periods of Old Testament history.

Before the Patriarchs

This period covers the time before Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the early ancestors of Israel. 

Evidence from the Bible

The first 11 chapters of Genesis follow a specific timeline of events that include: 

stories about the creation of the world in chapters 1–2,

the fall of humanity in chapter 3, 

Cain and Abel in chapter 4,

the flood in chapters 6–9, and

the tower of Babel in chapter 11.

According to Genesis 5, ten generations passed between the creation of the world and the flood. The people listed lived an average of 847 years each. However, only 1,656 years passed from Adam to the flood.

According to Genesis 11, ten generations passed from the flood to Abraham's time. This comes from the Septuagint, a third-century BC Greek translation of the Old Testament. The Masoretic Text, the traditional Hebrew text of the Old Testament, lists nine generations. 

In the Septuagint list, people lived an average of 346 years (using 460 years for Arphaxad’s son Cainan, mentioned in verse 13 of the Septuagint; see also Luke 3:36). The total time from the flood to Abraham was only 520 years. If taken literally, this means all of Abraham’s ancestors back to Noah’s son Shem were alive at Abraham’s birth, and 2,176 years passed from the creation to Abraham.

Understanding the Bible's Information

A strict or overly mathematical understanding of the figures requires several assumptions, including:

that no names are missing from the genealogies,

all numbers are in sequence, and

that ancient biblical numbers mean the same as they do today. 

We need to carefully examine each assumption based on other known facts.

A careful look at other biblical genealogies shows that these lists did not always include every person in a family line. For example, Matthew listed 28 generations (two sets of 14) between David and Jesus. However, if you compare this with Old Testament genealogies, you will find that Matthew left out some names. Luke, on the other hand, listed 42 generations for the same period. You can also see missing names when you compare the genealogies in 1 Chronicles 1–8 with those in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, 1 and 2 Samuel, and 1 and 2 Kings.

Ancient people often thought of numbers in a symbolic way. Their use of numbers was very different from how we use them today. We know about these practices from the Bible and from sources outside the Bible. For example, eight Sumerian kings ruled Shuruppak before the "great flood" of the Jemdet Nasr era, around 3000 BC. The list gives each king an average reign of over 30,000 years. Berossus, a Babylonian priest of Marduk from the third century BC, added two more names to this list and said each king ruled an average of 43,200 years. These huge numbers help us understand the numbers in Genesis.

The ages given for the ancestors before Abraham in Genesis probably had real meaning for the people who preserved these records. However, we should not use these numbers as exact figures for calculating the length of each generation. The Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch (an early form of the first five books of the Bible used by the Samaritan community) also give different numbers in many places. These differences show that the numbers in Genesis were difficult to understand even for some of the earliest scholars of Scripture.

Evidence from Outside the Bible

Archaeology does not offer evidence to date the creation or any events in Genesis 1–11. The flood story highlights some challenges. Experts in science, geography, and theology have claimed that archaeology proves the Genesis flood story. However, no city excavated in Palestine and Syria, even the oldest ones, shows archaeological evidence of the flood.
