From Abraham to Moses

This period begins with the patriarch Abraham and continues through the time of Moses.

The Patriarchal Age

The patriarchal age is the time of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the early ancestors of Israel. It also includes Jacob's sons, who became the ancestors of the tribes of Israel.

The date of Abraham is a debated topic among biblical scholars, even those who agree that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were historical people. Some scholars believe the patriarchal age was from 2086 to 1871 BC. Others think Abraham lived around 1400 BC. Each view claims to match the biblical information, so examining both perspectives is important.

Many Old Testament passages suggest that Abraham lived a long time ago. First Kings 6:1 calculates 480 years back from the start of the temple in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign (961 BC, according to the early-date view) to the exodus from Egypt, dating it to 1441 BC. The Israelites stayed in Egypt for 430 years (see Genesis 15:13; Exodus 12:40), which takes the timeline back to 1871 BC. The total of 215 years includes:

Abraham was 75 years old when he entered Canaan (Genesis 12:4);

Isaac was born 25 years later (Genesis 21:5);

Jacob was born 60 years after Isaac (Genesis 25:26); and

Jacob was 130 years old when he met the pharaoh (Genesis 47:9).

These 215 years added to the previous total suggest Abraham entered Canaan in 2086 BC and was born in 2161 BC.

This calculation does not use all the chronological evidence in the Old Testament, so the date for Abraham is debatable. The 480 years between the exodus and Solomon’s fourth year as king include the time for: 

the wilderness wanderings,

Joshua's leadership,

the judges,

Samuel,

Saul, and

David. 

The Old Testament does not specify the lengths of Joshua's, Samuel's, or Saul's leadership. However, even a simple estimate suggests these events together require about 600 years.

Additionally, the length of time the Israelites stayed in Egypt is challenging to determine. The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint both interpret the number 430 (in Exodus 12:40) to include the years in Egypt as well as the years Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob spent in Canaan.

Paul likely followed the Septuagint tradition when he dated the giving of the law 430 years after God's promise to Abraham (see Galatians 3:15–18). This means the Septuagint's number is significant and should not be ignored.

The late dating of Abraham (around 1400 BC) relies on two ideas: 

The patriarchal society described in Genesis is similar to one described by cuneiform tablets from Nuzi. Nuzi is a town in northeastern Mesopotamia about 175 miles (282 kilometers) north of Baghdad.

Since these tablets are from the 15th and 14th centuries BC, the patriarchal age likely occurred during the same time.

People who support the late-date view know their timeline for Abraham does not match the numbers used by the early-date view. They refer to other information from the Old Testament. Joseph, who was an important Egyptian official when Jacob moved to Egypt, lived to be 110 years old (Genesis 50:26). Moses was the great-grandson of Levi, Joseph’s older brother. Joseph lived to see his great-grandchildren, who were likely younger than Moses. So the late-date view suggests Joseph might have been alive when Moses was born. 

The genealogy of Moses (in Exodus 6:16–20; Numbers 3:17–19; 26:58–59; and 1 Chronicles 6:1–3) lists four generations: 

Levi, 

Kohath, 

Amram, and 

Moses. 

This seems complete according to Genesis 15:16, which predicted that Abraham’s descendants would be freed from Egyptian slavery "in the fourth generation."

However, dating Abraham to around 1400 BC does not match other biblical information. This includes the long stay in Egypt mentioned in Genesis 15:13 and Exodus 12:40, and the 40-year wilderness period. Some usually moderate scholars shorten the wilderness time to two years to support their later date for Abraham.

In summary, the late-date theory aligns with some biblical evidence, like the genealogies of Moses. The early-date theory matches other evidence, such as specific years mentioned in Genesis and Exodus. The late-date theory suggests genealogies are more generally reliable in Semitic societies. In contrast, the early-date theory takes the years in the biblical account more literally.

Due to issues with both dating positions, many scholars choose a middle ground for the patriarchal age. They argue that Abraham's life fits well in the early second millennium BC, but is less compatible with later time periods. By placing Abraham between 1800 and 1600 BC, they can combine all available evidence into a workable timeline. Archaeology offers four key pieces of evidence for an early second-millennium patriarchal era:

The Nuzi tablets provide a clear example of patriarchal social life. Other tablets from different towns and earlier times show similar customs found in both Nuzi and Genesis. The Nuzians, who were Hurrians, possibly migrated to northeastern Mesopotamia from Armenia. Their social customs likely began much earlier than the time of the tablets we have today. Therefore, the 15th-century BC date of the Nuzi tablets does not rule out an earlier date for Abraham.

Some of Abraham's ancestors named in Genesis 11 are now linked to towns in northern Mesopotamia near Haran. This is the city Abraham left to go to Canaan (Genesis 11:31–12:3). Haran was a thriving city in the 19th and 18th centuries BC.

Shortly after 2000 BC, Semitic nomads from the desert invaded the Fertile Crescent's civilized communities. These invaders, known as Amorites in the Old Testament, settled in several cities in northern Syria and Mesopotamia. One Amorite city was Babylon, ruled by Hammurabi around the early 18th century BC. Although King Amraphel from Genesis 14:1 is not the same as the Babylonian king Hammurabi, as earlier scholars thought, the events after the Amorite invasion still match the general timeline of stories in Genesis.

Mari, an Amorite town, is famous for over 20,000 tablets found in its royal palace and archives. Mari was near Haran. The tablets date back to the 18th century BC. Zimri-Lim, an 18th-century king of Mari, exchanged many letters with Hammurabi of Babylon. The Mari tablets provide valuable information about tribal and ethnic groups and their movements in the region. Some documents from Mari are important for dating the Genesis stories. They include personal names similar to Abraham (Abi-ram), Jacob, Laban, and other West Semitic names.

Archaeological evidence does not confirm or deny the existence of Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob. Everyone agrees on this point. However, archaeology offers a context that makes the biblical stories of these patriarchs more plausible.

Date of the Exodus

Determining the time period of the patriarchal age is linked to dating the Israelites' exodus from Egypt. Since we cannot determine when exactly Abraham lived, we also cannot determine when Joseph or Jacob entered Egypt. Additionally, the Bible does not provide an exact duration for the Israelites' stay in Egypt.

For many years, biblical scholars used 1 Kings 6:1 to establish a firm date for the exodus. They could fix Solomon’s fourth year to a ten-year range, from 967 to 958 BC. By adding 480 years, they could date the exodus with similar accuracy. However, other biblical information challenges this simple method. The Bible covers events from the exodus to the founding of Solomon’s Temple, from Numbers to 1 Kings 5:18. The total years given are closer to 600, not 480.

The evidence is not enough to pinpoint the exact date of the exodus, so scholars have two main theories. Some evidence supports a 15th-century exodus. The timeline in 1 Kings 6:1 seems to match a passage in Judges 11:26. It says Israel lived near Heshbon for 300 years before Jephthah's time. If Jephthah lived around 1100 BC, this suggests an exodus in the mid-15th century. Additionally, three generations of pharaohs in the 16th and 15th centuries had no male heirs. This makes it more likely that Moses could have been adopted by a royal princess during one of those generations. In contrast, all the kings of Egypt’s Nineteenth Dynasty, from 1306 to 1200 BC, had recognized male heirs.

A 15th-century date suggests a link between the Habiru invasion of Canaan around 1400–1350 BC and the Hebrew invasion described in the Old Testament book of Joshua. The Amarna letters, found in Tell el-Amarna, Egypt, describe the Habiru invasion. Additionally, the Merneptah Stele, a stone pillar from around 1220 BC, mentions "Israel." This suggests that the people Merneptah encountered during a Canaanite military campaign had existed for some time. Lastly, archaeologist John Garstang dated the destruction of Jericho to around 1400 BC.

Other evidence suggests the exodus happened in the 13th century, not the 15th. Many scholars date it between 1290 and 1275 BC based on this evidence: 

The 480 years mentioned in 1 Kings 6:1 might represent 12 generations, as shown in 1 Chronicles 6:3–8. If each generation averaged 25 years instead of 40, the 480 years would reduce to 300 actual years, suggesting an exodus around 1266 BC. 

Archaeological evidence shows destruction at the assumed sites of several cities like Lachish, Debir, Bethel, and Hazor, conquered by Joshua, dating to the late 13th century. 

The Bible does not mention Egyptian military campaigns, such as Merneptah’s in 1220 BC. Israelites in Canaan before the active pharaohs Seti I, who ruled from 1319 to 1301 BC, and Ramses II, who ruled from 1301 to 1234 BC, would have been affected by such campaigns. 

Exodus 1:11 mentions the city of Rameses, built by Ramses II, according to his inscriptions. 

Archaeological findings show that Transjordan and the Negev Desert were unoccupied by settled people between 1900 and 1300 BC. The Bible states the Israelites faced strong opposition in that region, suggesting they entered after 1300 BC. 

The term “Habiru” seems to have had a much broader meaning, possibly “trespasser.” It is probably not related to the word “Hebrew” in either its origin or meaning.

Garstang’s work at Jericho was revised by archaeologist Kathleen Kenyon. She showed the walls Garstang dated to about 1400 BC were actually destroyed in 1800 BC or earlier.

It has been difficult to precisely choose between the two centuries suggested for the exodus. Most Old Testament scholars, including more moderate or conservative ones, support the 13th-century option. However, many other conservative scholars still prefer the 15th-century date. Being too certain is not justified because both options have unresolved issues.

Following the majority view, this article uses a date of about 1290 BC for the exodus when discussing related questions.

Conquest and Settlement of the Land

The conquest and settlement of the land is the period when the Israelites entered Canaan, took control of parts of the land, and began living there.

The challenge is to fit the Old Testament events, mainly recorded in Joshua and Judges, between the exodus (around 1290 BC) and the time of David and Solomon. David's lifetime can be put around 1000 BC, and Solomon died in 930 BC. This means fitting about 550 years of biblical events between Moses and David into a 290-year period.

Setting an early date for the exodus, around 1447 BC, might simplify things a bit, but adding about 157 years does not solve everything. Neither date provides enough time for all the Old Testament events from Joshua to David to happen one after the other. Supporters of both dates assume that some judges ruled at the same time rather than one after another. The main difference is how much overlap each view allows.

The book of Joshua provides most of the Old Testament evidence about the Israelites' conquest of Canaan. Unfortunately, it does not include any timelines for Joshua's career. There are also no biblical references to major events elsewhere in the ancient world that could help date these events. Instead, the book gives a condensed account of the fall of Jericho and Ai, followed by southern and northern campaigns. After these victories, the Israelites divided the land of Canaan among their tribes. Each tribe was responsible for destroying any remaining Canaanite inhabitants in their area. However, the book does not mention how long these events took.

In the book of Judges, the situation is a bit different. The Old Testament provides a detailed list showing the lengths of foreign oppression, judgeships, and peace periods. The total number of years for that time is 410, but this does not include the time for many "minor" judges. It seems clear that most judges were local leaders who ruled at the same time as others, at least for part of their rule. Unfortunately, the book of Judges does not offer a system to show which judges were contemporaries. The best approach might be to use general guidelines to understand the timeline between Moses and David.

There are two important points to remember: 

Archaeological evidence suggests the conquest began around 1250 BC, not 200 years earlier. If we assume the judges served at the same time, we can fit the Old Testament figures into the timeline suggested by other evidence.

Ancient scribes often used a 40-year or generation-based timeline. This practice continued until the divided kingdom, when they started using a regular dynastic timeline. Many careers were assigned exactly 40 years, but these numbers do not match biblical or archaeological evidence. Most scholars believe the number 40 was not meant to be exact. This view allows some flexibility to fit biblical and other evidence into a general timeline.

The United and Divided Kingdoms

The period of the united kingdom refers to when Israel was one kingdom under Saul, David, and Solomon. After Solomon’s death, the kingdom divided into Israel in the north and Judah in the south.

Types of Evidence

There is plenty of chronological evidence from the time of the Israelite kingdom. The Old Testament aims to give all the needed details about the timeline of the period, including:

a complete list of all the kings in Israel and Judah, both before and after the kingdom split;

the age of each king (except Saul) when they began their rule;

timelines showing which year each king started ruling in relation to the other kingdom; and

exact lengths of each king’s reign. 

Additionally, some key events are dated by linking them to other events, while others are matched with events in non-religious history.

Outside the Old Testament, there is a lot of material that helps us understand the timeline of the period. The most important source is a collection of Assyrian limmu lists. In Assyria, they kept a record of each king’s reign on a special type of annal (yearly record). Each year was named after a high-ranking court official. The first year was named after the king, the second after the next highest-ranking official (though that name appears to have been selected by lot originally), and so on, until the king died. The word limmu introduced the name of the official for whom the year was named, which is why they are called "limmu lists."

Assyrian limmu lists align exactly with the solar year, making them very reliable. These lists date many events in Assyrian history and notable natural events. For instance, Assyrian scribes recorded a solar eclipse in the limmu year of Bur-Sagale, which astronomers calculated as June 15, 763 BC. Starting from 763 BC and moving both backward and forward, historians have compiled a complete list of Assyrian limmu officials from 891 to 648 BC.

The Assyrian limmu lists are accurate and supported by many sources. They are reliable for reconstructing the timeline of biblical history. This is particularly useful when a biblical writer connects an event in Israel or Judah to a specific year in an Assyrian king's reign. The limmu list shows the exact years of that king's rule.

Records from Chaldean (Babylonian) king lists and later Greek historians also exist. For example, in the second century AD, Ptolemy provided dates for Babylonian kings starting from 747 BC and continued with dates for Persian, Greek, and Roman rulers up to AD 161. Finally, inscriptions on monuments, stone tablets, and other objects from Assyria and nearby regions provide useful information.

Dating the Reigns of Israel’s and Judah’s Kings

The limmu list of Assyrian King Shalmaneser III helps compare dates among Assyria, Israel, and Judah. In the limmu of Daian-Assur, during Shalmaneser's sixth year as king, Ahab of Israel was one of the kings who fought against the Assyrians at the battle of Qarqar. Scholars date this battle confidently to 853 BC.

Assyrian records show that Shalmaneser III met an Israelite king named Jehu in 841 BC, 12 years after a previous encounter. These records help match biblical events. After Ahab's death, which is not precisely dated in Assyrian records, his two sons ruled. Ahaziah ruled for two years (1 Kings 22:51). Joram (also called Jehoram) ruled for 12 years (2 Kings 3:1). Because of the way Israelites counted years back then, the 14 years can be seen as 12 actual years. This suggests Ahab fought Shalmaneser III and died in 853 BC. His sons ruled for a total of 12 years before Jehu took over, aligning with his meeting with Shalmaneser III in 841 BC. Additionally, Jehu killed both the king of Israel (Jehoram) and the king of Judah (Ahaziah) at the same time (2 Kings 9:24–27). This event provides a fixed date that connects the timelines of the two kingdoms in 841 BC.

The first nine kings of Israel ruled for an apparent total of 98 years, or an actual total of 90 years when considering the method of counting reigns. Zimri, who ruled for only seven days (1 Kings 16:15–18), is one of these nine kings but does not add an extra year to the total. Jeroboam I became king in 930 BC. Rehoboam of Judah started his rule in the same year. Solomon's 40-year reign, as mentioned in 1 Kings 11:42, suggests he became king in 970 BC. This timing also marks David's death, though there might have been a short period when David and Solomon ruled together. Saul's reign likely occurred in the late 11th century BC.

In Judah, from Solomon's death in 930 BC to Ahaziah's murder by Jehu in 841 BC, six kings ruled for a total of 95 biblical years. Calculating this period in Judah is more complex than for the Israelite kings. This complexity comes from: 

the change around 850 BC from one method of counting reigns to another,

at least two shared reigns (Jehoshaphat with Asa and then Jehoram with Jehoshaphat), and

calendar differences between the kingdoms. 

To align Judah's timeline with Assyrian and Israelite records, the 95 biblical years must be adjusted to 90 actual years.

After the year 841, the next biblical event confirmed by sources outside the Bible is the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. This date comes from the records of Sargon II of Assyria, who ruled from 722 to 705 BC. He was ruler of Assyria after Shalmaneser V, who ruled from 727 to 722 BC. Although this date is only 120 years after 841 BC in Israelite history, the timeline for this period is hard to interpret accurately. In the past, scholars had to speculate about how to understand this time, including assumptions about shared reigns, possible confusion by scribes over calculation methods, and other theories.

Despite these challenges, scholars have aligned all the biblical and Assyrian dates for most of the period of the divided monarchy. Four figures related to the final years of the Israelite kingdom, all linked to the complex reign of Hoshea, are the exception.

Judah After the Fall of Israel

After Samaria fell in 722 BC, Old Testament chronology focuses only on Judah, the southern kingdom, for 135 years until its destruction. Two key events help establish a timeline for this period: 

Sennacherib of Assyria's siege of Jerusalem in the late eighth century.

Jerusalem's fall to the Babylonians in the early sixth century.

Sennacherib Attacks Judah

The Assyrian invasion took place during the reign of Sennacherib, from 704 to 681 BC. It is mentioned in 2 Kings 18:13–16. Verse 13 dates it to the 14th year of King Hezekiah. Sennacherib’s own records give more details, dating it to 701 BC, which suggests Hezekiah became king in 715 BC. 

This seems straightforward, but there are issues. For instance, 2 Kings 19:9 says Sennacherib contacted Ethiopian King Tirhakah, who ruled from around 690 to 664 BC, during his campaign. The campaign included a siege of Jerusalem. Since Tirhakah became king in 690 BC at the earliest, this contact could not have happened in 701 BC. It is possible Sennacherib invaded Judah twice, first in 701 BC and again later. The date of this second invasion is uncertain, but 2 Kings 19:35–37 might suggest Sennacherib was killed soon after leaving Jerusalem. Since his son Esarhaddon took over in 681 BC, the second invasion likely happened in the late 680s BC.

Some scholars disagree with the idea of a second invasion of Jerusalem by Sennacherib. They propose that Tirhakah, who became king in 690 BC, might have led troops against Sennacherib as early as 701 BC, before he became king. The mention of King Tirhakah in 2 Kings 19:9 might use the title he received later so that people would recognize him.

The number of invasions may be unimportant. Sennacherib definitely invaded Judah in 701 BC, during Hezekiah's 14th year as king. This timing suggests Hezekiah became king in 715 BC, but that creates another issue. Samaria fell in 722 BC, and 2 Kings 18:10 dates this event to Hezekiah’s sixth year as king. The likely explanation is that Hezekiah started ruling alongside his father, Ahaz, six years before Samaria's fall. 

The possibility for confusion arises from the fact that one verse, 2 Kings 18:13 (repeated in Isaiah 36:1) links Sennacherib’s 701 BC invasion to Hezekiah’s 14th year ruling alone. Another verse, 2 Kings 18:10, connects Samaria's fall to the start of Hezekiah’s co-rule. So, from about 728 to 715 BC, Hezekiah ruled with Ahaz. From 715 to 697 BC, he ruled alone. From 697 to 686 BC, his son Manasseh ruled with him.

According to several verses in 2 Kings, 128 years and six months passed between Hezekiah becoming king in 715 BC and King Jehoiachin's capture in 597 BC. This creates a problem because the biblical totals seem to demand over ten extra years. The best explanation is that Manasseh started ruling in 697 BC as co-regent (joint ruler) with his father, Hezekiah. Manasseh died in 642 BC after a 55-year reign, as stated in 2 Kings 21:1. Hezekiah, who became king in 715 BC, ruled for 29 years (2 Kings 18:2), meaning he was king until 686 BC. This is about 11 years after Manasseh would have started his reign to complete 55 years by 642 BC.

The Fall of Jerusalem

Babylonian records from that time provide valuable information about the final years of the kingdom of Judah. The Babylonian Chronicle, a formal record of Babylonian state affairs, covers the years 626–623, 618–595, and 556 BC. This chronicle, along with other cuneiform documents from that time, helps establish three key dates in Judah's history. The first is the death of Josiah in 609 BC. The second is the battle of Carchemish in 605 BC. The third is the end of Jehoiachin's reign. This is dated by the Babylonian Chronicle to the second day of Adar in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, or March 16, 597 BC.

After Jehoiachin was taken captive, Zedekiah ruled Judah for 11 years as a king under Babylon’s control (2 Kings 24:18). On the tenth day of the tenth month in Zedekiah’s ninth year as king (2 Kings 25:1), the Babylonian army began the final siege of Jerusalem. This was January 15, 588 BC. On the ninth day of the fourth month in Zedekiah’s 11th year, after almost 18 months of siege, the wall of Jerusalem was breached (2 Kings 25:3–4). The temple was burned on the seventh day of the next month, the fifth month.

After 586 BC

This period covers events after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and brought the kingdom of Judah to an end in 586 BC.

The Old Testament records several later events. Jeremiah 52:30 mentions a third group of Jews being taken to Babylonia in the 23rd year of King Nebuchadnezzar (582 or 581 BC). Both 2 Kings 25:27 and Jeremiah 52:31 report the release of King Jehoiachin from prison. The Babylonian Chronicle dates this event to 27 Adar, or March 21, 561 BC.

In 539 BC, the Babylonians faced defeat. That year, Cyrus the Great, a Persian ruler, successfully attacked Babylon and its king, Nabonidus. Cyrus took control over the exiled Jews and other groups previously conquered by Babylonia. He quickly started a policy of tolerance toward his new subjects. In his first year, Cyrus issued an order allowing Jews to return to their homeland (Ezra 1:1). On the first day of the next year, 1 Tishri (Ezra 3:6), an altar was set up in Jerusalem. In Iyyar of the following year (April/May 536 BC), work began on the temple itself (Ezra 3:8).

After several frustrating delays, the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah motivated the Jews to finish the temple. They resumed work in 520 BC (Ezra 4:24; Haggai 1:1, 15) and completed it on 3 Adar, or March 12, 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). The last parts of Old Testament history focus on Ezra and Nehemiah. Traditionally, Ezra's time is in the seventh year of Artaxerxes I (458 BC) and Nehemiah's in the 20th (445 BC).

See also Conquest and Allotment of the Land; Dispersion of the Jews; Exodus; History of Israel; Period of the Patriarchs; Postexilic Period; Wandering in the Wilderness.

CHRYSOLITE

Chyrsolite is a yellow-green or olive-green precious stone. Today, the name chrysolite usually refers to a gem-quality form of olivine. Olivine is a mineral made mainly of magnesium, iron, silicon, and oxygen.

The Greek word chrysolithos appears only once in the New Testament. The exact identity of the stone named in the Bible is uncertain. It is the seventh foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20). 

See also Minerals and Metals; Precious Stones.

CHRYSOPRASE, CHRYSOPRASUS

Chyrsoprase is a light-green or apple-green form of chalcedony, which is a type of quartz. Small amounts of nickel give the stone its green color. People often use chrysoprase to make jewelry.

Revelation 21:20 mentions it as one of the gems in the foundation wall of the New Jerusalem. The King James Version uses the name “chrysoprasus.” 

See also Minerals and Metals; Precious Stones.

CHUB

The King James Version spelling of Kub, a place in Ezekiel 30:5 identified as Libya. 

See Kub.

CHUN

Chun is the King James Version spelling of Cun, a city from which David took a lot of bronze, in 1 Chronicles 18:8. 

See Cun.

CHURCH

The word "church" refers to a group or assembly of people who come together for a specific purpose. Although the term is only mentioned twice in the Gospels (Matthew 16:18; 18:17), it appears often in the book of Acts, most of Paul's letters, and other New Testament writings, especially in the book of Revelation.

In the Old Testament, one way to describe the people of Israel was by calling them “the congregation.” Some groups who believed they were the true Israel called themselves "the congregation." They believed they were not Israel by birth. This term was used by the writers of the Dead Sea Scrolls and by early Christians, and it is what the word “church” originally meant. Christians often referred to themselves as “the church” or “the congregation” (with “of God” being understood without saying it). 

The term "church" could mean all believers worldwide or any local group of them. It represented the presence of God’s people in a specific place. That is why the New Testament often uses the singular "church." It does this even when talking about many groups of believers (Acts 9:31; 2 Corinthians 1:1); the term “churches” is rarely found (Acts 15:41; 16:5). Each group or the whole group was the place where God was present (Matthew 16:18; 18:17). The congregation was something God had purchased with the blood of his Son (Acts 20:28). 

Different Ways "Church" Is Used in the New Testament

The word "church" in the New Testament also has connections to the Greek world. In Greek, the word translated as "church" meant an assembly, a meeting. It referred to a political gathering or any group coming together. The word is used this way in Acts 19:32, 39, 41.

The Christian use of the word "church" in the New Testament varies widely:

As a Church Meeting: Sometimes, like in the Old Testament, it refers to a church meeting. For example, Paul tells the Christians in Corinth, “When you come together as a church” (1 Corinthians 11:18). This means that Christians are especially seen as God’s people when they gather for worship.

As the Entire Group in One Place: In passages like Matthew 18:17, Acts 5:11, 1 Corinthians 4:17, and Philippians 4:15, “church” refers to the entire group of Christians living in one place. The local nature of a Christian group is often highlighted. For example, in phrases like "the church in Jerusalem" (Acts 8:1), “in Corinth” (1 Corinthians 1:2), and “in Thessalonica” (1 Thessalonians 1:1). 

As House Churches: In other texts, small groups of Christians who met in someone’s home are called churches, such as those who met in the house of Priscilla and Aquila (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19). 

As the Universal Church: Throughout the New Testament, “the church” can also mean the universal church, which includes all believers (Acts 9:31; 1 Corinthians 6:4; Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18). Jesus’ first mention of the founding of the Christian movement in Matthew 16:18 uses the term in this larger sense: “I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.”

Paul often refers to the church as “the church of God” (1 Corinthians 1:2; 10:32) or “the churches of Christ” (Romans 16:16). This gives a common Greek word a distinct Christian meaning. It sets the Christian assembly apart from other groups, both secular and religious.

The New Testament as a whole makes it clear that the Christian community saw itself as the community of the end times. They believed they were called into existence by God’s final act of revelation and divine presence in Jesus of Nazareth. Paul tells the Christians in Corinth that they are those “on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). This means that God had visited his creation and called out new people from both Judaism and the non-Jewish world. These people were empowered by God’s Spirit to be present in the world, sharing the Good News of God’s radical, unconditional love for his creation (Ephesians 2:11–22). 

The Gospels tell us that Jesus chose 12 disciples who became the foundation of this new people. The connection to the 12 tribes of Israel is clear. It shows that the church was seen as both rooted in Judaism and as God's plan to make Israel "a light to the nations" (Isaiah 49:6; Romans 11:1–5). Because of this, Paul can call this new Gentile-Jewish community, this new creation, “the Israel of God” (Galatians 6:15–16). In this new community, traditional divisions of race, class, and gender were broken down. They had separated and ranked people into inferior and superior groups. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). This one group is called “the body of Christ.”

The Church as the Body of Christ

Paul is the only New Testament writer to call the church Christ's body (Romans 12:5; 1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 1:22–23; 4:12; see also 1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 12:12–13). He also describes the church as “the body” of which Christ is the “head” (Ephesians 4:15; Colossians 1:18). The exact origin of this way of speaking about the church is not clear, but two ideas are particularly helpful for understanding Paul’s thinking:

Paul’s Damascus Road Experience: According to the accounts in Acts 9:3–7; 22:6–11; 26:12–18, Jesus identified himself with his persecuted disciples. When Paul persecuted these early Christians, he was actually fighting against Christ himself. Reflecting on this experience may have led Paul to believe that the living Christ was so closely identified with his community that it could be called his “body,” meaning the real, physical expression of his presence.

The Hebrew Concept of Corporate Solidarity: Corporate solidarity is the idea that a group can be represented by one person. Paul was deeply Jewish, and Jewish ideas shaped his thinking (Philippians 3:5). In this context, the individual is seen as closely connected to the nation as a whole. The individual does not truly exist apart from the whole people. 

At the same time, the whole people can be represented by one individual. For example, “Israel” is both the name of one person and the name of a whole people. The “servant” in Isaiah 42–53 can be both an individual (Isaiah 42:1–4) and the nation of Israel (Isaiah 49:1–6). This idea of corporate solidarity (or unity) is the background for the close connection Paul makes between "the first Adam" and sinful humanity. It also connects "the last (or second) Adam" (Christ) with renewed humanity (1 Corinthians 15:45–49; see also Romans 5:12–21).

Paul expresses the close relationship between Christ and his church by comparing it to the unity and working together of a physical body (Romans 12:4–8; 1 Corinthians 12:12–27). For Paul, the Lord’s Supper is a specific example of this reality: “The bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.” (1 Corinthians 10:16b–17). Because of this, Paul argues, every function within the body has its rightful place. 

Division within the body (meaning the church) shows that something is not right. Paul’s repeated call for unity within the Christian community is based on this image of the church as “the body of Christ.”

CHURCH MEETINGS

Gatherings of believers. In the New Testament, the Greek word ekklesia (usually translated as “church”) is used primarily in two ways: 

It is used to describe a meeting or an assembly. 

It is used to refer to the people who take part in these gatherings—whether they are actually meeting at the time or not. 

The New Testament mentions a few non-Christian Greek assemblies (Acts 19:32, 41). Every other instance refers to Christian gatherings. 

Sometimes ekklesia means the actual meeting of Christians. This is what Paul meant in 1 Corinthians 14:19, 28, and 35, where the Greek phrase en ekklesia must mean “in a meeting” and not “in the church.” Translating this phrase as “in the church” (as is done in most modern English versions) is misleading. Most listeners or readers will think it means “in the church building.” The New Testament never calls the place where people meet a “church.” 

Apart from these few instances where the word means the actual gathering of believers, ekklesia is most often used to describe:

The believers who are part of a local church (such as the church in Corinth, the church in Philippi, and the church in Colossae); or

All the believers (past, present, and future) who are part of the universal church, the complete body of Christ.

When hearing or reading the New Testament, Christians need to be aware of the various ways in which the word ekklesia (“church”) is used. The most basic meaning of ekklesia is any gathering of believers. Ekklesia can also refer to an organized local group—including all the believers in one place, led by a group of elders. The ekklesia is also the universal church whose members are all the believers who have ever been, are now existing, and will ever be. 

The word ekklesia was used by the New Testament writers with these various aspects of meaning. Sometimes it is hard to tell which meaning is intended. However, being careful about this can help avoid confusion when studying the New Testament. Some people teach that the smallest part of the church is the local church. But those who wrote the New Testament sometimes used the word “church” to mean a small group meeting in a home. 

Others confuse the local church with the universal church. But some things in the New Testament are addressed to a local church that do not necessarily apply to the whole church. Some great things are said about the universal church that could never be achieved by any particular local group. For example, in Paul's letter to the Ephesians (which was actually meant for several churches), he talks about the church in ways that a local church could never fully achieve. No local church could become fully like Christ.

There is much to be said about how interpreters have confused the local church with the universal church, but this article is focused on clearly explaining what constitutes the smallest unit of the church—the local church, or what could be called the house church or home gathering.

The New Testament shows that a local church (all the believers in one area led by one group of elders) could have several ekklesiai—“meetings” or “assemblies” in different homes. Thus, the smallest unit to comprise a “church” was one of these home meetings. 

However, the New Testament does not say that each of these home meetings had its own separate leaders or or was completely separate from other ekklesiai (“gatherings”) in the same area. According to Acts 14:23 and Titus 1:5, elders were appointed for every local church and not for every house church (compare the expressions “appointed elders in every church” and “appoint elders in every city”). Even so, it seems that every local church of some size had several such ekklesiai (“meetings”) happening within that area.

The church in Jerusalem must have had several home meetings (see Acts 2:46; 5:42; 8:3; 12:5, 12), as did the church in Rome (see Romans 16:3–5, 14–15). A small local church may have had only one home gathering—as was probably the case with the church at Colossae (see Philemon 1:2). But this would have been impossible for large local churches like those in Jerusalem, Rome, and Ephesus, in which there must have been several “house churches” (see 1 Corinthians 16:19–20 [1 Corinthians was written from Ephesus]). We can better understand the idea of “house church” from these passages: Romans 16:3–5, 14–15; 1 Corinthians 16:19–20; Colossians 4:15–16; and Philemon 1:1–2.

Romans 16:3–5, 14–15

In the last chapter of Romans, Paul asked the believers in Rome, to whom he had written this epistle, to greet Priscilla and Aquila and the church that met in their home (16:3–5). The entire church in Rome could not have met in Priscilla and Aquila’s home, for the church was much too large to have gathered in a single home. Rather, the church in Priscilla and Aquila’s home must have been one among several such “house churches” in Rome. The following discussion supports this idea.

Paul wrote his letter to the Romans to “all in Rome who are loved by God” (Romans 1:7), not to “the church in Rome.” When he wrote this, Paul had not been to Rome, and no other apostle had either. The church in Rome probably started when Jewish Romans visited Jerusalem during Pentecost (Acts 2:10) became believers in Jesus, and then went back to Rome. Since no apostle had started the church, there might not have been any official leaders (elders) in Rome. There were likely several groups of believers meeting in different parts of Rome and nearby areas.

Paul knew some of the saints in Rome (whom he addressed by name in the last chapter). So he wrote to all the believers in that area, instead of to the church as a whole—which is what he usually did (see 1 Corinthians 1:1; 2 Corinthians 1:1; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Even so, “all in Rome who are loved by God” would make up “the church in Rome” (compare Philippians 1:1, in which Paul addressed his letter to all the saints in Philippi).

In the final chapter of Romans, Paul asks all the believers in Rome (which equals the “local” church in Rome) to greet the church in Priscilla and Aquila’s house. Later in the chapter, Paul asks the church to greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brothers with them. And then again he asks the church to greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympas, and all the saints with them (Romans 16:14–15). 

Evidently, Paul was identifying two other groups of believers who must have met together. (And perhaps Paul was referring to two more groups in 16:10–11, which in the Greek could mean the ones of Aristobulus’s and Narcissus’s households or the ones of their fellowships.) It seems that the church in Rome, like the church in Jerusalem and Ephesus, had several home ekklesiai (meetings).

Paul wrote his letter to the Romans around AD 58. The time when Nero badly hurt Christians (known as the Neronian persecution) began around AD 64. Nonreligious historians such as Tacitus tell us that a large number of Christians were tortured and killed during this persecution (Annals 15.44). Another writer, Seutonius (in his book Nero, chapter 16), said that the fast growth of Christians in Rome made them unpopular. 

Indeed, at the time Paul wrote his letter to the Romans he said their faith was known throughout the world (1:8). This indicates that the church in Rome had already made an impact on the Mediterranean world. When Paul came to Rome three years later in AD 61, he came to a city that had a large church there already. From Romans 15:23, we know that the church had been in existence for many years even before Paul wrote his letter to them. 

In short, the church in Rome was a large church around the time Paul wrote his letter to them. The whole church could not have met in Aquila and Priscilla's home. They were tentmakers and would have had only a medium-sized house. Also, Paul greeted more than 25 people by name in chapter 16—and he had not even been to Rome yet!

There must have been several ekklesiai in Rome, meaning several home churches that together made up the one local church in Rome. For example, the Christians in Rome apparently worshiped in many homes such as Priscilla and Aquila’s. Other churches in homes are mentioned in Colossians 4:15 and Philemon 1:2. Groups of Christians met in houses of important believers or in other available rooms (compare Matthew 26:16; Acts 12:12; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 1:2). 

The church in Priscilla and Aquila’s house is the first of five groups of believers in Paul’s list, but the only one referred to definitely as a church (see Romans 16:5, 10–11, 14–15). Priscilla and Aquila opened their home for Christian meetings. The church mentioned there was only a part of the total number of Christians in Rome. Verses 10–11 and 14–15 seem to refer to two other household churches in Rome. There were at least three churches there, and probably more. Each house church could not have been a separate group with a separate church government. Instead, each house church must have been simply one home meeting of some of the saints in the one local church at Rome.

1 Corinthians 16:19–20

In this passage we again see Aquila and Priscilla and again we learn that a church met in their house. According to Romans, their house church was in Rome. According to 1 Corinthians (which was written from Ephesus), their house church was in Ephesus. 

Many scholars think Aquila and Priscilla left Rome around AD 49 when the emperor Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome. They might have already been Christians then. According to Acts 18, they joined Paul in Corinth (where they all worked together as tentmakers) and then went on with him to Ephesus, around AD 51 when the church in Ephesus was first established. Paul continued his second missionary journey, while Aquila and Priscilla remained in Ephesus.

The early church in Ephesus likely first met in their home. Paul returned to Ephesus a few years later and remained there for two years (around AD 53–54). During this time, Paul's teaching about Jesus spread from Ephesus (as a center) to all of Asia Minor (see Acts 19:8–10). As this was going on, the church in Ephesus grew (see verses 18–20).

During these years Paul wrote to the Corinthians. He sent greetings from the churches in Asia, from Aquila and Priscilla—and the church in their house, and from all the brothers (1 Corinthians 16:19–20). In giving this kind of greeting, it seems that Paul was sending greetings from:

 all the churches in Asia Minor, 

the church in Ephesus (equivalent to “all the brothers”), and 

those believers who gathered with Aquila and Priscilla in their home. 

It would be hard to imagine that all the saints in Ephesus met at Aquila and Priscilla’s home. The church probably began that way, but as it grew, so did the number of home meetings. 

From other parts of the New Testament, we learn that there must have been several home meetings in Ephesus because there were so many saints there. This is true of 1 Timothy, which was written around AD 64 by Paul to Timothy while Timothy was leading the church in Ephesus. There must have been a large number of saints in Ephesus—young men, young women, older men, widows, and so forth (1 Timothy 5–6). 

Many believers must have hosted a church meeting (ekklesia) in their home. (Aquila and Priscilla left Ephesus around AD 56/57 and went back to Rome, where they again hosted a church in their home. Others in Ephesus would have opened their homes.) But each home meeting didn't have its own leaders. Instead, all of the church in Ephesus was under one group of leaders—led by Timothy, Paul’s coworker.

Colossians 4:15–16

In this part, we again read about a church existing in the home of one called Nymphas. In his final remarks to the church in Colossae, Paul asked the saints in Colosse to send his greetings to:

 the brothers that are in Laodicea, 

Nymphas in particular, and

the church in Nymphas’s house. 

According to the structure of Colossians 4:15, it seems that the first greeting included all the believers in Laodicea (a neighboring church to Colossae), who would comprise the entire church in Laodicea (called “the church of the Laodiceans” in Colossians 4:16). The second and third greetings were to a specific individual named Nymphas in the church in Laodicea and a church meeting in Nymphas’s house. This church meeting in Nymphas’s house would probably be one of several home meetings—all part of the one local church in Laodicea.

There is a problem with the text in this passage that could have some effect on how it is interpreted. Some manuscripts read “his house”; others read “her house”; still others read “their house.” Because it cannot be determined from the Greek text whether Nymphas was male or female, various scribes used different pronouns before “house.” Between the readings “her” and “his,” it is far more likely that the pronoun “her” was changed to “his” than vice versa. 

Some scholars say that “their” refers to “the brothers” at Laodicea. But that does not make sense if we understand that “the brothers in Laodicea” refers to the church in Laodicea. How could the church in Laodicea have the church in their house? 

Other scholars indicate that the Greek word for “their” (auton) refers to the ones with Nymphas—the members of his household. 

Whether the reading was “her house” or “their house,” a particular group of believers within the church of Laodicea met there. Their meeting could legitimately be called an ekklesia—an assembling together.

Philemon 1:1–2

This is the last time we read about a church in a particular home in the New Testament. Paul wrote a short epistle to Philemon, a leader of the church in Colossae. He wrote about Onesimus, Philemon's runaway slave who Paul had led to believe in Christ. 

In his introduction to this short letter, Paul sends his greetings to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in Philemon’s house. Paul did not send greetings to all the saints in Colossae and then to the church in Philemon’s house. This was the pattern in 1 Corinthians 16:19–20 and Colossians 4:15. Instead, he just sent greetings to Philemon and to the church in his house. Therefore, we can assume that the entire church in Colossae must have met at Philemon’s house.

Worship in the Home Meetings and Church Meetings

When the church first began in Jerusalem, the believers met in homes for fellowship and worship. The early Christians met in homes to hear the apostles’ teachings and to celebrate Communion, which is called “the breaking of bread” (Acts 2:42–47 ). 

During these meetings, Christians often shared meals in what was called a love feast (2 Peter 2:13; Jude 1:12). At these meetings, they recited Scripture, sang hymns and psalms, and joyfully praised the Lord (see Ephesians 5:18–20; Colossians 3:16–17). Christians also gathered together in homes to pray (Acts 12:12) and read Scripture.

Small groups of believers met in homes for worship regularly. In a city where there were several such ekklesiai, all the believers would gather together for special occasions. Scripture tells us that all the believers would come together to hear a letter from the apostles read out loud (see Acts 15:30; Colossians 4:16). We can guess from the New Testament record that all the Christians in a city met together once a week on Sunday, which was called the Lord’s Day. 

First Corinthians tells us how the early Christians worshiped together when all the believers in one city met together. We know that 1 Corinthians talks about this larger gathering because in 11:20 Paul spoke of all the believers coming together in one place. Likewise, in 14:23 he spoke of the whole church coming together in one place.

Paul used this letter to correct how the Corinthians were behaving in two areas:

When they celebrated the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17–34) 

When they used spiritual gifts during church meetings (1 Corinthians 14)

Paul's corrections show us what he thought a good Christian meeting should be like. He probably based this on his experience in other church meetings. 

Paul told the Corinthians to celebrate the Lord's Supper together in a way that matched how Jesus started this meal. They were to remember the Lord and how he died for them, and they were to eat the bread and drink the wine in a serious way. At the same time, they were to be aware that they were members of the same body of Christ—joined to one another, and also to Christ.

In chapter 14, Paul says this “body awareness” should be evident in the way the believers worshiped together. One’s personal experience and freedom should not stop the group from worshiping God together. Thus, when the believers used their spiritual gifts it should be done it in an orderly way and to help the whole group grow, not just themselves. These spiritual gifts include:

Prophesying (sharing messages from God)

Speaking in tongues (speaking in special languages)

Interpreting tongues (explaining what was said in tongues)

Teaching

When all the church gathered together to worship God, it should demonstrate spiritual unity.

See also Church.

CHURCH OFFICERS

Church officers are leaders who serve in official positions within a church, helping to guide the congregation and provide leadership in areas such as teaching, administration, and pastoral care. The specific roles and titles vary among Christian traditions, but most churches have a recognized leadership structure based on roles mentioned in the New Testament.

CHUSHAN-RISHATHAIM

Chushan-rishathaim is the King James Version spelling of Cushan-rishathaim, a Mesopotamian king and oppressor of Israel, in Judges 3:8–10. 

See Cushan-rishathaim.

CHUSI

Cushi was a place near Acraba and beside the Mochmur River (Judith 7:18). It was probably located south of modern Nablus in Israel.

CHUZA

The steward of Herod Antipas and a powerful and influential man. Chuza was either a manager of Herod's property or a political appointee. He was married to Joanna, whom Jesus healed. She then traveled with Jesus and his disciples (Luke 8:3).

CILICIA

A province of the Roman Empire, located in southeastern Asia Minor. The capital city was Tarsus, Paul’s hometown (Acts 21:39; 22:3). This is why Paul had Roman citizenship even though he was a Jew (16:37).

History of Cilicia

Antiochus the Great settled 2,000 Jewish families in the Asia Minor regions of Lydia and Phrygia in the second century BC (Josephus’s Antiquities 12.3.4). This may be the origin of the Jewish population in the area.

In the Old Testament, Cilicia was called Kue. The region formed a bridge between the country now known as Turkey and Syria. The country was divided between Cilicia Tracheia and Cilicia Pedias. 

Cilicia Tracheia is the mountainous region in the western half. Cilicia Tracheia was territory Mark Antony had given to Cleopatra in 36 BC. By the time of Paul, the Greek King Antiochus IV of Commagene ruled this area. He was king from AD 38 to 72. The Cilician Gates, a narrow pass in the Taurus Mountains, provided entry into Turkey. 

Cilicia Pedias was the plains to the east. Cilicia Pedias was connected to the province of Syria (about 38 BC). The New Testament refers to Syria and Cilicia as one region (Galatians 1:21). 

In AD 72, the Roman emperor Vespasian united the two areas into one Roman province called Cilicia.

Cilicia in Early Christianity

Jews from Cilicia participated in the persecution of Stephen (Acts 6:9). After Paul converted to Christianity, he returned to Tarsus. Paul later traveled with Barnabas to Antioch (Acts 11:25–26). Because of Paul's story, Syria and Cilicia became the first major center of non-Jewish Christianity. Christianity spread from this area to the rest of the gentile population of the Roman Empire.

See also Kue.

CINNAMON

A spice made from the dried inner bark of several trees that come from tropical Asia. The bark has a pleasant smell. It can be ground and used as a spice. The cinnamon mentioned in Exodus 30:23, Proverbs 7:17, Song of Songs 4:14, and Revelation 18:13 is certainly from the Cinnamomum zeylanicum tree.

The cinnamon tree is relatively small, never growing taller than 9.1 meters (30 feet). It has smooth, ash-colored bark, wide-spreading branches, and white flowers. Its shiny, beautifully veined evergreen leaves grow about 22.9 centimeters (9 inches) long and 5.1 centimeters (2 inches) wide.

The Jewish people considered cinnamon a deliciously fragrant substance and valued it highly both as a spice and a perfume. It was one of the main ingredients used to make the precious ointment, or "holy oil," that Moses was commanded to use in the tabernacle. This oil was used for anointing the holy vessels and the priests who served there. Cinnamon was certainly very expensive and highly treasured.

See Food and Food Preparation.

CINNEROTH

CIRCUMCISION

Circumcision is the surgical removal of the foreskin of the male reproductive organ. In Bible times, circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant (a binding agreement) with Abraham (Genesis 17:1–14). 

Circumcision began as an ancient tribal or religious practice. In some Western countries, it has also been performed on newborn boys for reasons of health and hygiene. Where circumcision is performed for medical reasons, it carries no religious meaning.
