The same applies to geography. The writer mentioned many places. His use of place names seems correct. He referred to Cana, a village not mentioned in earlier literature known to us. This suggests the reference probably came from someone familiar with the place. He precisely located Bethany about 15 stadia from Jerusalem (about 3.2 kilometers or 2 miles, John 11:18).

The writer of the Gospel of John mentioned several places in or near Jerusalem, including:

Bethesda (John 5:2),

Siloam (John 9:7), and

the Kidron Valley (John 18:1).

This does not rule out someone who lived at the same time as John. But it makes it hard to think of the writer as someone writing much later and far from Palestine. The evidence suggests the writer was a Jew living in Palestine during the time of Jesus.

Many scholars believe the Gospel of John seems to come from someone who witnessed the events. For example, Jesus was teaching "near the treasury" (John 8:20). This detail is not necessary for the story, but it feels like a memory from someone who visualizes the scene while writing. The fact that the house filled with "the fragrance of the perfume" when the woman broke the jar does not change the story much (12:3). But it is a detail someone present would remember.

The author noted that the loaves used to feed the crowd were made of barley (John 6:9). The tunic Jesus wore "was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom" (19:23). He mentioned that the branches used to greet Jesus were from the palm tree (12:13). He noted that it was night when Judas left (13:30).

These details appear throughout the Gospel of John. They seem more like signs that the author participated in the events rather than just trying to make the story seem real.

The early church believed John wrote the Gospel of John. The early church fathers Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and Tertullian all considered the apostle John to be the writer of the Gospel of John. Theophilus of Antioch was the first to quote the Gospel of John by name around AD 180.

Some people who disagree with John writing the Gospel of John focus on its differences from the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke). They argue that if Jesus was like the Messiah in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, he could not be like the Messiah in John's Gospel. This argument has its basis in personal opinion and overlooks that different people see great individuals in different ways.

The church has long believed that Jesus was complex enough to inspire both "portraits." In other words, the Synoptic Gospels do not tell us everything about Jesus. There is no contradiction. John emphasizes other aspects of the life and teachings of Jesus. We cannot prove for certain that John the apostle was the writer of the Gospel of John. But there is more reason to believe this than any other view.

When and Where Was the Gospel of John Written? Who Was It Written For?

Scholars usually date this writing to the late first century or early second century AD. Some scholars date it to the mid-second century AD, but this is rare. Notably, there is strong agreement among scholars on the date the Gospel of John was written.

Scholars used to think the Gospel of John relied on the Synoptic Gospels. Because of this, they assumed John must have written it later. However, many scholars no longer hold this view. John contains many unique elements not found in the Synoptic Gospels. 

Similarly, the Synoptic Gospels have content that it seems John would have included if he had known about it. This makes it hard to believe John had access to the Synoptic Gospels as he was writing, or even that he had read them. The similarities that do exist are probably because of shared oral traditions.

Some scholars argue that John's theology (what he teaches about God) is very developed. This suggests it needed time to develop. While John's Gospel is indeed profound, it does not mean it must date to the end of the first century AD. 

The theology in the letter to the Romans is also developed, and yet it is not dated later than the AD 50s. Therefore, there is no reason to date the Gospel of John later than the letter to the Romans. Development is not a reliable argument because it occurs at rates that one cannot measure. We cannot know how quickly it happened where the author lived.

Other arguments for a late date are not decisive. For example, some say the church system in John's Gospel is too late for his time. The system related to "sacraments" in John chapters 3 and 6 needed time to develop. But John does not mention any sacrament. Many scholars indeed think these chapters refer to baptism and the Lord’s Supper, but the fact is that John mentions neither.

Some scholars believe that the Gospel of John was written before the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70. They argue that traditional reasons for dating the book later are not convincing. They also point to several details that may suggest an earlier date. 

In John 5:2, the author says that there “is” a pool called Bethesda, rather than saying there “was” a pool. This may suggest that the pool still existed when he wrote. John also often calls the twelve disciples "disciples of Jesus" or "his disciples." Some scholars believe this reflects an earlier time when Christians needed to distinguish the disciples of Jesus from those of Jewish teachers, who also had disciples. 

John also does not directly refer to the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, or Luke. Some scholars suggest that these Gospels were not yet widely available when John wrote. 

This evidence does not establish exactly when the Gospel of John was written, but some scholars believe it supports a date before AD 70.

The apostle John, who was a Jew, wrote the Gospel of John. However, the writing shows Greek influence. For example, it refers to Christ as "the Word" (Greek ho logos) in John chapter 1 and translates Jewish words like "rabbi" (1:38). Most scholars believe the work originated in a Greek cultural center, with Ephesus being the traditional choice. By the end of the second century AD, Irenaeus wrote that John published the Gospel of John while living in Ephesus.

Some scholars note similarities between the writings of John and the Odes of Solomon, which they think came from Syria. They also find similar things in the language of Ignatius, the bishop of Antioch in the early second century AD. This suggests to them that John wrote in Syria, probably in Antioch.

Others argue that Egypt was the location, citing the discovery of the oldest manuscript fragment of this gospel there. However, there is no real evidence, only probabilities. Many support Irenaeus's evidence, suggesting Ephesus as the origin, but we cannot be certain.

There is no clear indication of the intended destination of the Gospel of John. From John 20:31, we learn that John wrote the book so his audience "may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing … have life in His name." The purpose of the gospel is to proclaim the good news about Jesus.

However, "believe" might mean "keep on believing" or "continue in faith," rather than "start to believe." This suggests that from the start, the book may have intended to strengthen people's faith. We should not separate these intentions too strictly, as both are probable.

What Is the Background of the Gospel of John?

Scholars have suggested several possible backgrounds for the Gospel of John. The Greek influence is obvious. Some call this the Gospel of the Hellenists (those who promote Greek culture). Some suggest we should look to Greek writings, like those of philosophers or Philo of Alexandria, to understand John's writing.

The scholar Rudolf Bultmann took this approach. He believed that the Gospel of John was influenced by Gnosticism, a religious movement that emphasized special knowledge as the way to salvation. Bultmann argued that one of John's sources was a collection of teachings that came from a non-Christian Gnostic tradition. Few scholars have accepted his specific theory, but some have suggested that ideas similar to those later found in Gnosticism may have influenced the religious setting in which John was written.

While some scholars propose these views, there are some substantial objections:

Despite some scholars' confident claims, no one has proven that Gnosticism is a predecessor to Christianity. Historically, it appears as a Christian heresy, and a heresy must follow the original faith.

There is a fundamental difference between the two systems. Gnosticism focuses on knowledge (the word "Gnosticism" comes from the Greek word gnosis, meaning "knowledge"). Its "redeemer" brings knowledge from heaven. However, John does not believe that knowledge saves people. The true Redeemer comes to remove the world's sin (John 1:29).

Gnosticism tells people that life is an upward struggle. Christianity tells of a Savior who came down to raise them up.

It is difficult to see any form of Gnosticism as the essential background to Christianity.

The Gospel of John also shows a strong connection to Jewish language, culture, and religious traditions. The Old Testament is especially important for understanding John's message. Both Jews and Christians accepted these writings as sacred Scripture. 

John often draws on Old Testament words, ideas, and events. He also shows familiarity with the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament. Many passages in the Gospel of John reflect the language and ideas found in this translation. Understanding these connections helps explain what John meant.

In modern times, important discoveries have been made at Qumran, near the Dead Sea. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls found in the caves at Qumran, there are several that are similar to the Gospel of John. The scrolls have more similarities with the Gospel of John than with any other part of the New Testament. This is hard to explain if John wrote later and far from Palestine.

We must examine the similarities to the Qumran writings carefully, as they often share language but differ in meaning. For example, both use the phrase “the Spirit of truth.” But where John means one of the persons of the Trinity, the scrolls speak of “a spirit of truth” and “a spirit of error” striving in the souls of people. The connection is real, but John is clearly not dependent on the scrolls for his thinking. 

The Dead Sea Scrolls provide further evidence that the Gospel of John reflects Jewish beliefs and traditions found in first-century Palestine. Understanding this historical and religious background helps explain the message of the Gospel of John.

Some scholars have suggested that the Gospel of John was influenced by other religious writings, including the Hermetic writings. These writings were attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a figure associated with the Egyptian god Thoth. Although some ideas in these writings are similar to those in John, the connections are limited. The Gospel of John has much stronger connections to Jewish beliefs and traditions from first-century Palestine. For this reason, many scholars consider John's Jewish background more important for understanding his Gospel.

Why Was the Gospel of John Written? What Does It Teach Us About God?

The writer explained that Jesus performed many miracles not recorded in the text. However, the ones included are there "so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name" (John 20:31). John wrote to prove that Jesus is the Christ (the promised Messiah) expected by the Jews. He wanted to do more than share interesting facts.

John wanted his audience to see this knowledge as a challenge to their faith. By believing, they would have eternal life. John's goal was to lead people to Jesus Christ, with the purpose of proclaiming the good news of God's kingdom. However, his words also hold meaning for those who already follow Jesus. It is important for believers to have a right knowledge of Jesus and that they continue to believe.

The main teaching of John's Gospel is that God sent his promised king, Jesus. He is the Son of God and brings eternal life (John 3:16). Jesus told the woman at the well he was the Messiah, but this is not often stated directly. The term "Messiah" (or "Christ") had political meanings for many Jews. They expected a Messiah who would fight and defeat the Romans, and create a world empire with Jerusalem as its capital.

This was not what Jesus intended to do, so he avoided language that suggested it. Although he avoids traditional terms about the Messiah, John plainly shows Jesus as the one God chose as king. He often depicts Jesus fulfilling roles of the Messiah. For example, in John chapter 6, Jesus is "the bread from heaven," fulfilling the expectation that the Messiah would renew the manna mentioned in the Old Testament. In giving sight to the blind man (chapter 9), Jesus performs another function of the Messiah (see Isaiah 35:5).

Along with teaching about the greatness of Jesus, John also emphasizes his humility and complete dependence on God the Father. Jesus said he could do nothing without the Father (John 5:30). His purpose is to do the Father's will (John 4:34). He lives through the Father (John 6:57). The Father gives him his disciples (John 6:37, 44; John 17:6). The Father also testifies about him (John 5:32, 37).

John emphasizes that Jesus is not independent of the Father. In the mission of Jesus, John sees Jesus as fulfilling the Father's purpose.

What Is the Content of the Gospel of John?

Introduction and Chapter 1

John starts with an introduction that is unique to the Gospel of John (1:1–18). He calls Jesus "the Word," a term that is connected to both Greek and Hebrew ideas. John uses this term to show that Jesus reveals the thoughts and purposes of God the Father.

John describes the Word as God (1:1). He sees the Word as active in creation (1:3–5). The writer presents John the Baptist’s testimony about the Word (1:6–8), speaks about the Word coming into the world (1:9–14), and ends with the greatness of the Word (1:15–18).

This section briefly introduces major themes that will develop throughout the Gospel of John. It serves as a grand introduction to the entire work.

Next, it presents the start of the public ministry of Jesus (1:19–51). John the Baptist's work came before the work of Jesus. The writer first describes John the Baptist's testimony about Jesus. Witness is one of his important concepts, and witness is all that John the Baptist does in this Gospel.

From this testimony, we see how the first disciples came to Jesus. We learn how Andrew and Peter met the Lord. John also tells us about Philip and Nathanael. The Synoptic Gospels say little about them.

The Signs and Teachings (2:1–12:50)

The Gospel of John describes the public ministry of Jesus in a unique way. John includes a long section where he recounts several miracles Jesus performed, combining them with various discussions (John chapters 2–12). Sometimes Jesus speaks to groups, and other times he talks with individual people.

Some scholars refer to this part of the Gospel of John as the "Book of Signs," emphasizing the important place given to seven miracles. For John, these are not just wonders. They are meaningful and truly significant.

The first miracle is when Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding in Cana of Galilee (2:1–11). The water in question is connected with Jewish rites of purification (verse 6). The story teaches us that Jesus transforms life. He changes the water of the law of Moses into the wine of the good news of God's kingdom. Because of this "sign," his disciples believed in him (verse 11).

John then describes how Jesus went to Jerusalem and drove the traders out of the temple. They were selling animals for sacrifice and exchanging money. Their business took place in the Court of the Gentiles, the only temple area where a non-Jewish person could come to meditate and pray.

The first teaching is about being "born again" (3:1–21). Jesus spoke with Nicodemus, a religious leader of the Jews from the Pharisee group. They talked about the need for becoming totally renewed to enter the kingdom of God. Jesus referred to God's work of transformation, not human efforts.

After this, John describes a disagreement between some of John the Baptist's disciples and a Jew about purification. This leads to a section that emphasizes Jesus as superior to John the Baptist, as confessed by John himself (3:22–36).

The second teaching is really a long conversation Jesus had with the woman of Samaria, whom he met by a well (4:1–42). It focuses on "living water," a term not fully explained in this chapter but later refers to the Holy Spirit (7:38–39). This leads to the story of the second sign, the healing of the son of a noble (4:46–54). This healing is notable because Jesus healed from a distance.

The third sign is the healing of the disabled man by the pool of Bethesda (5:1–18). This man had waited many years for healing when the water moved. Jesus told him to get up and walk, and he did. Because it happened on a Sabbath day, the Pharisees objected.

This leads to the third teaching, which was about the divine Son (5:19–47). Here, Jesus emphasizes his close relationship with God the Father. John emphasizes the role Jesus has in judgment. There is also emphasis on the variety of witnesses who encountered Jesus. This shows it is reasonable to accept him as God’s Son.

John's fourth sign is the only miracle, besides the resurrection, found in each of the four Gospels. This is the feeding of the 5,000 (6:1–15). Next follows the story of Jesus walking on water (verses 16–21). This is probably the fifth sign, although some scholars disagree. If they are correct, there are only six signs.

Next is the fourth teaching, the important speech on "the bread of life" (6:22–59). Jesus is this "bread," which he offers to all who believe in him. There are mentions of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, which refer in a mystery to his death (verses 50–58).

Some scholars believe that these words refer to the Lord’s Supper, also called Communion. However, Jesus spoke these words before he established that practice. In the same teaching, Jesus also says that those who believe in him will receive eternal life (6:35, 47). It seems Jesus means that people must believe in him as the one who would die for them to have life.

There is a section detailing Peter’s affirmation of loyalty in the face of some who drifted away from the Master (6:67–71). Next is the fifth teaching about God's Spirit who gives eternal life (7:1–52). John explains that "the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified" (verse 39). The full measure of the Spirit depends on Christ completing his work through his death and resurrection.

The sixth teaching describes Jesus as "the light of the world" (John 8:12–59). The sixth sign clearly shows this part of the identity and work of Jesus. This is when he heals a man born blind (chapter 9). The account is full of action as the healed man boldly defends Jesus against the Pharisees, who speak against him.

In the seventh teaching (chapter 10), Jesus uses the picture of a good shepherd to explain his relationship with those who follow him. Just as sheep depend on their shepherd for care and protection, the followers of Jesus depend on him. But Jesus goes even further than an ordinary shepherd. He willingly gives his life to save those who belong to him.

The final sign is the raising of Lazarus (John 11:1–44). Lazarus had been dead for four days. This story shows the power Jesus has over death and his desire to give life. Jesus calls himself "the resurrection and the life" (verse 25). Death cannot defeat him. He gives life to both the spiritually dead and physically dead, like Lazarus.

John notes the reactions to this miracle. Some believed, while others opposed Jesus (11:45–57). He includes a notable saying by Caiaphas, the high priest, that one man should die for the people (verses 50–52). Caiaphas was speaking as a cynical politician. He was suggesting one innocent man should die rather than for the whole nation to encounter trouble. However, John considered it to have a deeper meaning. He believed the death of Jesus would bring salvation to many people.

John concludes his account of the ministry of Jesus with several events, including:

a woman pouring oil on Jesus in Bethany,

the entry of Jesus into Jerusalem in triumph,

the coming of some Greeks to Jesus, and

a final summary of what Jesus had taught (chapter 12).

The Last Supper

The account of what happened in the upper room the night before the death of Jesus on the cross is the most detailed in all four Gospels. It is interesting that John does not mention the start of the Last Supper. However, he describes how Jesus washed the disciples' feet (13:1–17). This shows the spirit of humble service that would soon be evident on the cross. Then, there is the prophecy that Judas would betray Jesus. This began the events leading to the death of Jesus on the cross (verses 18–30).

In the discussion that follows, Jesus answered some questions asked by his disciples. He went on to teach them some important truths. Jesus explained that he is "the way and the truth and the life" (14:6). He described himself as "the true vine," with his disciples connected to him like branches. The branches must stay connected to the vine to have life (15:1–16). Jesus also spoke about suffering, offering guidance for times of persecution (verses 17–25).

He then discussed the Holy Spirit (15:26–16:15). This passage is important because it contains more about the Holy Spirit than we find in other teachings of Jesus. Jesus calls the Holy Spirit the "Paraclete," a Greek term that can mean someone who comes alongside another person to offer help or support. The term was sometimes used in legal settings for someone who speaks on behalf of another person. Jesus uses it to describe the Holy Spirit as one who helps, encourages, and guides his followers.

Jesus went on to speak of his coming departure from the disciples and to prepare them for the difficult time ahead (16:16–33). This section of the Gospel ends with the prayer of Jesus in 17, often called his High Priestly Prayer. Jesus asks his heavenly Father to protect his disciples and help them remain united as one.

The Cross and the Resurrection

When the soldiers came to arrest Jesus, he stepped forward to meet them. They fell to the ground (18:1–11). He surrendered to them. They did not overtake him. At the start of the story of his suffering, John emphasized that Jesus is in control. These events did not defeat Jesus. He was fulfilling the Father’s will.

John is the only one who tells us that they took Jesus to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the current high priest (18:12–14, 19–24). He also describes Peter's three denials of Jesus (verses 15–27). John does not focus much on the Jewish trial. But he provides more details than the other gospel writers about the Roman trial.

John obviously had special knowledge of what happened before Pilate. John presents a powerful image of Jesus discussing the idea of what a king is with Pilate. The Son of God talks with the Roman emperor's representative about the nature of power (18:33–40).

In his account of the death of Jesus, John includes unique details. He describes how Jesus committed his mother Mary to the beloved disciple's care (19:26–27). He notes that Jesus cried out, "It is finished," as he died (verse 30). He also mentions a soldier stabbing the side of Jesus with a spear (verses 31–37).

John continues with the story of the burial and the empty tomb (19:38–42; 20:1–10). John describes how the risen Lord appeared to Mary Magdalene (verses 11–18) and to the disciples, both without Thomas (verses 19–23) and with Thomas (verses 24–29).

The final chapter serves as a conclusion to the Gospel of John. It describes how Jesus helped his disciples catch a large number of fish (John 21:1–14). It continues with the special story of Peter declaring his love for Jesus three times and how Jesus restored him after the denials.

See also John the Apostle.

GOSPEL OF JUDAS ISCARIOT

This ancient Gnostic writing probably came from a group called the Cainites. The only reason we know about it is because early Christian writers quoted from it, especially Bishop Irenaeus of Lyons. Because Irenaeus wrote about it in the second century AD, the Gospel of Judas must have been written before that time.

The text probably included secret teachings that Judas Iscariot was said to have received from Jesus. It may have summarized the “true” or “higher” knowledge that this Gnostic group claimed to possess. The gospel gives its own explanation of the “mystery of the betrayal,” saying that Judas’s actions made salvation possible for everyone. According to this view, Judas either protected the truth of Christ or prevented evil powers (called Archons) from stopping the crucifixion, which they feared would destroy their power.

See also Apocrypha; Gnosticism; Judas Iscariot.

GOSPEL OF LUKE

The Gospel of Luke is the third book of the New Testament. It is one of the three Synoptic Gospels: Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

Preview

Who Wrote the Gospel of Luke?

When and Where Was the Gospel of Luke Written? Who Was It Written For?

What Is the Background of the Gospel of Luke?

Why Was the Gospel of Luke Written? What Does It Teach Us About God?

What Is the Content of the Gospel of Luke?

Who Wrote the Gospel of Luke?

According to tradition, the apostle Luke, a companion of the apostle Paul and a respected physician, wrote the Gospel of Luke (Colossians 4:14). The Gospel of Luke does not name its author, but early Christians seem to have known him well. He had obviously been gathering information for his project for some time. In both Luke and Acts the recipient is identified as Theophilus.

The book of Acts also provides evidence that Luke may have written both books because they are closely connected. In three sections of Acts, the author uses the word “we,” suggesting that he was present during the events he describes (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16). These sections may come from a record of the author’s travels with Paul. The last section places the author in Rome with Paul. By considering who traveled with Paul, some scholars conclude that Luke was the most likely author.

Where and When Was the Gospel of Luke Written? Who Was It Written For?

Scholars disagree about when Luke wrote his Gospel. Some believe he wrote it after AD 70, when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem. However, this view raises questions about whether Jesus was predicting Jerusalem’s destruction in Luke 21:20. Others believe Luke wrote his Gospel before Paul’s death, traditionally dated to about AD 64. This earlier date could help explain why the book of Acts ends with Paul still under house arrest in Rome.

Luke may have written his Gospel in Rome, but its place of writing is uncertain. Some scholars suggest that he wrote it in Asia Minor or Greece. An early Christian document called the Monarchian Prologue to Luke supports Greece as the place of writing, but scholars question how reliable this document is. Rome is another possibility because Luke may have had time there to complete his Gospel.

Luke wrote to Theophilus. "Theophilus" means "beloved of God." He was probably a real person, so the name was not a general term for all Christians. He did not seem familiar with Palestine's geography. Luke often explains it in detail.

However, Theophilus understood the Greek-Roman world well. Luke assumes he knows about it. Luke also avoids using terms that might confuse a non-Jewish audience, like "hosanna" during the triumphal entry of Jesus into Jerusalem.

The Gospel of Luke was probably written in Rome while Paul awaited trial, on or before AD 64. Luke dedicated it to the “most excellent Theophilus” (Luke 1:3). This follows a common custom of the time. Theophilus was a prominent non-Jewish Christian. Luke intended to instruct him and others more thoroughly in the Christian faith.

What Is the Background of the Gospel of Luke?

Jesus spent his life in an area about 80.5 kilometers (50 miles) wide and 241 kilometers (150 miles) long. It went from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south. Besides Jerusalem, the places he visited are not important to the region's secular history. He grew up in the small village of Nazareth and lived there until he was about 30 years old.

Capernaum became the center of his work in Galilee. He sometimes traveled through Samaria and also worked in Perea. Judas betrayed him and the Romans crucified him in Jerusalem. He rose in triumph on the third day.

Luke wrote his account of the life and ministry of Jesus many years after these events took place. By then, Christianity had spread beyond Israel into the Roman Empire. The early church had grown from a mainly Jewish community into one that included many people who were not Jewish. Christian worship was no longer centered on the temple in Jerusalem, and believers were spreading the good news about Jesus to other nations. Luke described the life and ministry of Jesus with these changes in mind. He showed how the words and actions of Jesus helped prepare the way for the growth and mission of the early church.

Why Was the Gospel of Luke Written? What Does It Teach Us About God?

Simeon expressed the theme of salvation in Luke’s Gospel with beauty when he held Jesus in his arms and shouted, “my eyes have seen Your salvation … a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel” (Luke 2:30–32). He identified Jesus as the savior awaited for a long time, the hope for both Jews and non-Jews (Gentiles).

Luke emphasized the role of the Holy Spirit in the life and ministry of Jesus. The Holy Spirit conceived Jesus (Luke 1:35). The Spirit descended on him at his baptism (3:22). The Spirit led him into the desert to defeat the devil's temptation (4:2).

The Spirit "anointed" him for his ministry (Luke 4:18). The Spirit remains in the background during the later work of Jesus. But their connection is plain even when not mentioned.

Luke emphasized the joy associated with the Messiah. The army of angels announced the birth of Jesus with the words, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!” (Luke 2:14). Then, as he approached Jerusalem, the crowd with him began to praise God, saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” (19:38).

All this suggests that the theme of salvation in Luke's Gospel is complex. It identifies Jesus as the Christ (God's chosen king, the promised Messiah). It invites a positive response from both Gentiles and Jews. It includes the Holy Spirit’s power for the ministry of Jesus and for the work of his disciples. It emphasizes the joy that comes with proclaiming the gospel. These are variations on Luke's single design of salvation.

Luke also emphasizes other concerns. Luke's focus on historical accuracy is one. His need to defend his beliefs is another. He also emphasizes prayer. The list could go on.

What Is the Content of the Gospel of Luke?

Introduction (1:1–4)

The gospel starts with a formal introduction. Luke intended to record in an organized way what others passed down as a faith tradition. He wanted to show the historical basis of the faith and assure his audience of its truth.

Birth and Early Life of Jesus (1:5–2:52)

None of the Gospels is a complete biography of Jesus. However, Luke focused on historical events, especially regarding the birth and childhood stories. He described ten episodes, including:

the announcement of John the Baptist's birth as the forerunner of Jesus;

the announcement of the birth of Jesus to Mary,

Mary's visit to Elizabeth,

the birth of John the Baptist,

John the Baptist's time in the wilderness,

the birth of Jesus,

the visit of the shepherds,

the circumcision of Jesus,

the presentation of Jesus in the temple, and

the visit to the temple as a youth.

John the Baptist gained attention from the beginning. Luke noted that during Herod the Great's rule from 37 to 4 BC, Zechariah the priest served in the temple. Priests worked in 24 groups, each serving two weeks a year. They cast lots to choose who would burn incense. Once a priest performed this task, he could not do it again.

As Zechariah prepared to burn incense, an angel appeared. The angel told him that he and his wife, Elizabeth, would have a son named John. John would live as a Nazirite.

A Nazirite was a person dedicated to God. See Numbers 6:1–4. He would prepare the way for the Messiah. Zechariah doubted this because of their old age. So, the angel made him unable to speak until the birth God promised.

We next hear about John when Mary visits Elizabeth. The baby moved in Elizabeth’s womb when she heard Mary’s greeting (Luke 1:41). Luke then describes the birth of John the Baptist. Zechariah named the child as instructed, regained his speech, and prophesied about the coming Messiah and his son's role in preparing the way. The child grew strong in spirit and remained in the wilderness until his public ministry began.

Luke shared the nativity story from Mary's perspective. The angel Gabriel visited her and announced she would give birth to the Messiah (Luke 1:26–38). She would conceive by a miracle from the Holy Spirit. Luke presents Mary as willing to accept God’s plan.

The birth occurred when Quirinius governed Syria. People traveled to their home towns so the Roman king could count the population (census). Mary gave birth in a stable or cave in Bethlehem. Angels announced the birth to shepherds, who left their flocks to see the child. Mary reflected upon these events and continued to think about their importance.

After Mary completed her 40 days of ceremonial purification, she and Joseph went to the temple to present Jesus to the Lord (Luke 2:21–40). There, Simeon and Anna, two elderly and dedicated Israelites, recognized the infant as the Messiah promised by God. Simeon concluded that Jesus would cause many in Israel to fall and rise, and would bring deep grief to Mary's heart.

The stories of the birth and childhood of Jesus end with his visit to the temple at age 12 for the Feast of Passover. Joseph and Mary left Jesus behind, thinking he was with relatives or friends. They went back and found him in the temple talking with the Jewish rabbis (religious teachers with authority). He listened to them and amazed them with his understanding. Luke concluded by saying, "Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man" (Luke 2:52).

Beginning of the Public Ministry (3:1–4:30)

Luke then record the events related to the start of the ministry of Jesus, including:

the ministry of John the Baptist,

the baptism of Jesus,

the family line of Jesus,

the temptation in the wilderness, and

the public announcement of his ministry in Nazareth.

Luke identified when John the Baptist began his ministry by naming six rulers and religious leaders who held positions of authority at that time, including:

Tiberius Caesar, the Roman emperor;

Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea;

Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee;

Philip, the ruler of Iturea and Trachonitis;

Lysanias, the ruler of Abilene; and

Annas and Caiaphas, Jewish high priests.

John came preaching a baptism of repentance in preparation for the coming of the Messiah. Multitudes came out into the wilderness to hear him and to be baptized by him.

Jesus also came to be baptized by John. Luke does not mention John's protest that Jesus should baptize him instead. Nor does Luke mention that Jesus insisted that the baptism was necessary. This act was probably to identify with the people and point to his death as a sacrifice for them. The baptism marked the start of the public ministry of Jesus. Luke included a list of the ancestors of Jesus that some scholars believe traces his family line through Mary. This would fit with Luke’s earlier account, which often tells the events surrounding the birth of Jesus from Mary’s point of view.

The temptation of Jesus tested his role as the Messiah. The phrase “If You are the Son of God” was intended to make him doubt the words from his baptism, “You are My beloved Son” (Luke 3:22; 4:3, 9). Satan wanted Jesus to fulfill his mission without dying on the cross. Each time, Jesus countered the temptation with a quote from Scripture.

Jesus returned to Galilee and went to the synagogue (local Jewish place of worship) in Nazareth. There, he announced his public mission using words from the Jewish Jubilee observance ("the year of the Lord's favor"), associated with the time of the promised Messiah (Luke 4:18–19; see also Isaiah 61:1–2).

These words showed both the religious focus and the wide social impact of his future work. The announcement offered hope to those who were treated badly and rejected by society. When people questioned his authority, Jesus said, “no prophet is accepted in his hometown” (Luke 4:24). When they tried to throw him off a hill, he walked through the crowd and continued on his way.

The Ministry in Galilee (4:31–9:50)

Jesus shifted his main activities to Capernaum. Luke describes many events from the ministry in Galilee that followed. He mentions about 30 instances. Around a third of these events involve extraordinary events, including: 

healing, 

driving out demons, 

resurrecting the dead, or 

feeding large crowds. 

These events were associated with the time of the promised Messiah.

It was the teachings of Jesus that first caused people to pay attention. Unlike the rabbis, who relied on tradition, he taught with the authority of his role as the Messiah. Luke included many of these teachings in his narrative. There is a fairly extended section on observing the Sabbath (Luke 6:1–11). But it is less prominent than the sermon Jesus gave "on the plain." This sermon includes comments on blessings and punishments, loving enemies, judging others, recognizing people by their actions, and wise and foolish builders (6:12–49).

Jesus often taught through stories called parables. Luke recorded two of these stories, one about a farmer planting seeds and another about a lamp (Luke 8:1–18). In the parable of the sower, the seed represents God's word, and the soil represents how ready people are to receive it. This helps the disciples understand the mixed outcomes of the ministry of Jesus and their own ministry. However, some people did not understand the meaning of the parables.

Luke described how Jesus called certain disciples. He mentioned Peter, James, and John, and later Levi (Luke 5:1–11, 27–32). Peter, James, and John left their fishing boats, while Levi left his tax booth. Jesus called all of them to follow him in his mission across the countryside of Galilee.

Later, when there were 12 disciples, Jesus sent them to preach about the kingdom and heal the sick (Luke 9:1–11). Many people probably helped with this mission. Luke noted that certain women traveled with them and “were ministering to them out of their own means” (8:3).

There is growing excitement about the mission in Galilee. It starts with Jesus working quietly by himself and ends with a loyal group who followed him. Many people were eager to hear his words, and he became famous throughout the area. The section reaches its high point with the apostle Peter declaring Jesus as the Messiah and the story of Jesus becoming transfigured (Luke 9:10–36). Moses and Elijah's presence shows that the law and prophets are secondary to the Messiah.

The scene suddenly shifts to the bottom of the mountain. The disciples fail to heal a boy possessed by a demon. Jesus emphasizes the need for spiritual strength to meet the kingdom's needs. Later, in response to the disciples arguing about who is the greatest, he emphasizes the importance of humility.

The Journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27)

Luke then reported on the ministry of Jesus while Jesus was traveling to Jerusalem. Some call this the Perean ministry, assuming much of it occurred across the Jordan River in Perea. Others describe it as “the road to the crucifixion.” The number of events is similar to the previous section, but the text is about a quarter longer.

Opposition appeared at the beginning. Jesus sent messengers ahead to prepare for his arrival at a Samaritan village. However, the villagers did not welcome him because he was going to Jerusalem. There was a long-standing conflict between the Jews and Samaritans.

The Samaritans had settled in the land during the Assyrian occupation and introduced foreign religious and social customs. This mix of beliefs upset the Jews. Some disciples asked if Jesus wanted them to call down fire from heaven on the village to destroy them. But Jesus criticized them. He showed a more peaceful attitude.

Luke again introduced the Samaritans in a story Jesus tells (Luke 10:25–37). Thieves attacked a man and left him for dead. First, a Jewish priest and then a Levite walked by on the other side of the road. Another person passed by and took pity on the injured man. He wrapped his wounds and brought him to an inn for care, paying for his expenses.

Jesus mentioned that the man who stopped to help was a Samaritan. He understood that a neighbor is someone we choose to help, not just someone who helps us. The Samaritans appear again in the story of 10 lepers who were healed. Only a Samaritan returned to give thanks (Luke 17:11–19).

The story of the Good Samaritan shows the opposition Jesus encountered from the religious leaders in Jerusalem. As the crowds grew, Jesus said, “The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here” (Luke 11:31). Similarly, the men of Nineveh will condemn this generation because they asked God to forgive them when Jonah preached. Now someone greater than Jonah is here.

Jesus gave his strongest criticism to the Pharisees who challenged him all the time. Jesus and the Pharisees often moved in the same social circles. Some Pharisees supported his message, but they were few. Jesus described the Pharisees as those who were strict about following the rules (Luke 11:37–44).

Events were reaching a high point. Jesus had prophesied his own death and resurrection. He was determined to go to Jerusalem. When some concerned Pharisees warned him about Herod Antipas's plan to kill him, Jesus refused to be scared (Luke 13:32–33).

This section of Luke's Gospel contains many parables, including:

the Good Samaritan,

the mustard seed,

the yeast (or leaven),

the narrow door,

the invitation to a marriage feast,

the great feast,

the one who builds a tower,

the king who goes to war,

the lost sheep.

the lost coin,

the Prodigal Son,

the unjust manager,

the rich man and Lazarus,

the Pharisee and the tax collector, and

the ten minas.

These parables generally fit into three categories, although not always perfectly:

One category involves accepting those who sin. In the Synoptic Gospels, "sinners" refers to Jews who do not obey the law, even though Scripture shows we are all sinners. A classic example is the story of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32).

The second category consists of kingdom parables. They show that the kingdom starts small but will greatly increase. They also warn that not everything that appears to be part of the increase truly belongs to the kingdom. You can see these points by comparing the parables of the mustard seed, yeast, and narrow door (Luke 13:18–30).

The third category is about management. As they neared Jerusalem, Jesus told a parable (Luke 19:11–27). It was about a noble who traveled to a distant country. He left his servants with ten minas each. A "mina" was about three months' wages for workers.

They were to invest the minas so the man would earn a good profit when he returned. When the noble came back, he asked his servants for an account of what they did with the minas. Those who were loyal with small tasks received greater opportunities. However, the one who failed lost even the little he had.

The Gospel narrative includes some special scenes. One shows Jesus welcoming little children (Luke 18:15–17). Another describes a rich ruler asking Jesus how to obtain eternal life (verses 18–30). Yet another episode involves a tax collector named Zacchaeus (19:1–10). These stories help us appreciate the variety in the ministry of Jesus.

Jesus gradually made his way toward Jerusalem. As he traveled, more people opposed him. He knew that he would soon suffer and die on the cross. Until then, he continued teaching and helping people.

The Death and Resurrection of Jesus (19:28–24:53)

Luke ended his account of the ministry of Jesus by describing the final week before his death. He began with the triumphal entry into Jerusalem (Luke 19:28–44). As Jesus and those following him came over the top of the Mount of Olives, they praised God for the miracles they had witnessed: 

“Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” (19:38). 

The crowd's joy is in sharp contrast to the sadness Jesus felt that the city would not ask God to forgive them and the destruction it would encounter.

When Jesus entered the temple area, he began to drive out those selling goods. He said God's house should be a house of prayer, but they had turned it into a cave of thieves. Jesus continued to teach daily in the temple, while the religious leaders plotted to kill him without angering the people.

Chapters 20–21 record several events and teachings with leaders and people, including:

a challenge to the authority of Jesus,

the parable of the evil tenants,

a question about paying taxes to Caesar,

another question about the resurrection,

a question Jesus asks about how the Messiah can be both a descendant of David and David’s Lord, 

a warning against the teachers of the law,

comments on a widow's offering, and

a discussion on the end of the age.

These events and teachings are connected to the ongoing debate about whether Jesus is the promised Messiah.

Luke presents the problem as more of a moral issue than an intellectual one. The religious leaders wanted to keep their position of privilege at any cost. This rabbi from Galilee posed a serious threat that they needed to stop. They only had to wait for the right moment. That moment came when Judas Iscariot offered to betray Jesus (Luke 22:1–6).

The Last Supper and the all-night prayer session in the garden of Gethsemane happened between the leaders' plot and the arrest of Jesus (Luke 22:7–46). Jesus and the disciples left the upper room and crossed the Kidron Valley to the Mount of Olives. There, Jesus prayed to prepare for the coming crucifixion. The disciples, tired from the day's demands, fell asleep.

Soon, Judas arrived to identify Jesus. Soldiers took him to the high priest. The apostle Peter denied knowing Jesus because he feared for his life. The Sanhedrin (high Jewish council) condemned Jesus. Some commentators debate whether this was a formal meeting of the Sanhedrin.

The Sanhedrin sent Jesus to the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, then to Herod Antipas, and back to Pilate. Pilate found no reason to execute Jesus. But the crowd, influenced by Jewish leaders, demanded crucifixion. Pilate yielded to their demands when he could not find another way.

He sent Jesus away to be put to death on a cross. Only Luke mentioned those who showed grief for Jesus (Luke 23:27). Jesus advised them to show grief for themselves and their children instead. Throughout, we see the concern Jesus had for others during his own suffering. He showed concern for those crucifying him, the thief who asked Jesus to forgive him, and his mother, Mary.

Luke describes a mixed reaction to the crucifixion. The people stood watching, seemingly frozen by the rapid events. They may have felt unable to help, even if they could have. Some religious leaders made fun of Jesus, saying, "He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One!" (Luke 23:35). One thief joined in mocking Jesus while the other asked for mercy.

Darkness covered the scene. The temple curtain tore, suggesting access was now available to all through the shed blood of Christ. Jesus committed his spirit to the Father and took his last breath. They laid his body in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea. Women prepared spices and sweet-smelling liquids for burial. But they rested on the Sabbath day to obey the commandment.

Early on the first day of the week, the women went to the tomb. They found the stone moved away and the body of Jesus missing. Suddenly, two figures in bright clothes appeared. They told the frightened women, “He is not here; He has risen!” (Luke 24:6).

The women went back to tell the apostles. Peter ran to check and found the linen strips still there. But the body was gone. Peter wondered what had happened.

On the same day, two disciples were going to a village called Emmaus. They were discussing what had happened in Jerusalem when Jesus joined them. They did not recognize him until later, when he broke bread with them. They quickly returned to Jerusalem to assure the group that the Lord had risen.

While they were talking, Jesus appeared among them. “Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.” (Luke 24:39).

Then Jesus helped the two disciples understand what had happened. He told them, “This is what is written: The Messiah will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things. And behold, I am sending the promise of My Father upon you. But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:46–49).

Luke ends his gospel with the story of Jesus going up to heaven (Luke 24:50–53). As Jesus blessed them, he rose before their eyes. They worshiped him as the Lord taken to heaven by God. They returned to Jerusalem with great joy. There, they stayed in the temple area. They were praising God and waiting for the Holy Spirit to empower them to witness to the world.

See also Book of the Acts of the Apostles; Teachings of Jesus Christ; Luke (Person); Synoptic Gospels.

GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

The Gospel of Matthew is the first book in the New Testament. It tells the story of Jesus's life, teachings, death, and resurrection.

Preview

• Who Wrote the Gospel of Matthew?

• When Was the Gospel of Matthew Written?

• Why Was the Gospel of Matthew Written?

• What Is the Message of the Gospel of Matthew?

Who Wrote the Gospel of Matthew?

The text of Matthew does not clearly state who wrote it. However, the ancient church believed the apostle Matthew was the author. Matthew was also known as Levi (see Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27, 29). Before Jesus called him to be his follower, Matthew worked as a tax collector (Matthew 9:9 and following verses). 

It is interesting that Matthew refers to himself as a tax collector in his Gospel, but the other Gospel writers do not call him this. Perhaps Matthew mentioned his former job to show how his life changed when Jesus called him. Tax collectors in those days were hated and considered very low in society. 

The Gospel itself contains details that suggest the writer knew about money and taxes. For example, the Gospel mentions specific coins like the two-drachma tax (in Matthew 17:24), a four-drachma coin (in verse 27), and the various talents (in 18:24; 25:15 and following verses).

When Was the Gospel of Matthew Written? 

Scholars disagree about when Matthew wrote his Gospel. This is primarily because there is still debate about whether the Gospel of Matthew or the Gospel of Mark came first. If Mark wrote his Gospel before Matthew, then Matthew relies on Mark for a lot of material. If Matthew wrote his Gospel before Mark, then Mark relies on Matthew for a lot of material. 

Those who argue that Matthew wrote his Gospel first base it on three facts: 

The early church recognized the Gospel of Matthew as the first Gospel. 

Matthew wrote his Gospel to those who first needed a written story—the Jews. 

When the early church established the New Testament canon (the official list of books that are accepted as Scripture), they placed the Gospel of Matthew at the beginning. 

Whether Matthew came before or after Mark, most scholars believe it was written before Jerusalem was destroyed in AD 70. This is because Matthew 24:15 talks about the temple as if it were still standing. The early church leader Irenaeus wrote that Matthew created his Gospel while Peter and Paul were in Rome. This would mean Matthew was written sometime in the 60s AD.

Why Was the Gospel of Matthew Written?

Defense of the Gospel

Matthew wrote his Gospel for a community of Greek-speaking Jewish Christians. They likely lived in a place like Antioch in Syria. This community was surrounded by Jews who were hostile to the claims about Jesus and opposed the Christian community.

Matthew wrote as a Jew for a Jewish audience. He argues that in Jesus of Nazareth, the Old Testament reached its chosen purpose. Jesus is the Messiah (God's chosen one) that Israel was waiting for. 

In the opening chapter, Matthew says Jesus is "the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Jesus is "God with us" (verse 23). Later in the book, Jesus is shown to be the "Son of Man" described in Daniel 7 and the "Suffering Servant" described in Isaiah 53. Matthew presents the events of Jesus’s life as the "fulfillment" of Old Testament prophecies (Matthew 1:22–27:10). Jesus comes to offer Israel salvation from sin (1:21). 

However, many Jews rejected Jesus as their Messiah, which put them in a dangerous position (Matthew 11:20–24; 21:33–46). One reason Matthew gives for Israel's rejection of Jesus is that the Jewish religious leaders failed to prepare the people for his coming. Matthew strongly criticizes the teachers of the law and the Pharisees. He claims they abandoned the word of God and followed their own traditions instead (chapter 15).

Teaching the Church

Matthew also wrote as a Christian for a Christian audience. He presents Jesus as a new Moses, and even as God (Yahweh) in human form. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus teaches his own law for his followers (Matthew 5). Jesus forms a new community around himself under the leadership of the apostles (10:2–4; 16:18–19; 23:8–10). There is only one way for the Christian church to function properly. 

Matthew believes that for the Christian church to work properly, the teachings of Jesus on moral and spiritual matters must be taken very seriously (chapters 5–7, 18). To help with this purpose, Matthew designed his Gospel like a handbook or textbook for the church. It instructs God's people about who Jesus is and what he did.

To make these teachings easier to remember, Matthew organized his material in a very structured way. He arranges Jesus's teachings in five major sections called "discourses" (which are mixed with stories about Jesus). In these sections, similar types of teachings are grouped together. For example, chapter 10 contains instructions for missionaries, and chapter 13 contains seven parables about the kingdom of God.

The main theological themes in Matthew's Gospel are:

 The Son of God. Jesus is God in a human body, "God with us." Another way of saying this is that Jesus is God incarnate.

The kingdom of God. In Jesus, God enters into history like a victorious king to begin his final rule.

The salvation of God. As the servant-king, Jesus has come to "save His people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21).

The people of God. Jesus has come to build his church. The church is a redeemed community consisting of both Jews and non-Jews (gentiles).

What Is the Message of the Gospel of Matthew?

The Coming of the Savior (1:1–2:23)

The name "Jesus" means "Yahweh saves," which reveals his mission (Matthew 1:1). Jesus is "the son of Abraham," who comes to fulfill God's ancient promises to both Jews and non-Jews (Genesis 12:1–3). Jesus is "Christ [or Messiah]," the son of David (Matthew 1:1), who comes to begin the kingdom of God (4:17). More than that, Jesus is "God with us." This is shown both by prophecy (1:22–23) and by the nature of his conception (verses 18–20). Jesus has come to "save His people from their sins" (verse 21). 

As the son of David, and according to prophecy, Jesus is born in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:1–6). Guided by the star of Israel's Messiah, gentiles come to worship him (Matthew 2:1–12; compare Numbers 24:17). When King Herod tries to kill him, Jesus finds safety in a foreign land. Matthew connects the exodus of Israel (when God led the Israelites out of Egypt) to the person and work of Jesus. God calling his Son out of Egypt marks the beginning of a powerful saving work. It is nothing less than a new exodus under Jesus, the new Moses (verses 13–20). After being born in very humble circumstances, Jesus comes to live in the town of Nazareth (verses 21–23).

The Beginnings of Ministry (3:1–4:25)

John the Baptist warns Israel to repent because Jesus is about to bring judgment (Matthew 3:1–12). When Jesus allows John to baptize him, a voice from heaven speaks. This shows that Jesus is a King who serves his people by taking their sins upon himself (verses 13–17). 

Like Israel during the exodus, the Holy Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness for a period of testing (Matthew 4:1). The devil tries to turn Jesus away from God and from what God has chosen Jesus to do. But Jesus wins this battle by relying on God and his word (verses 1–11). 

Jesus returns to Galilee and chooses to live in an area where both Jews and non-Jews live (verses 12–16). He begins his ministry by preaching (like John, he calls people to repent because the kingdom is coming), teaching (he calls his first disciples), and healing people (verses 17–25).

The Sermon on the Mount (5:1–7:29)

Jesus went up a mountain to teach, similar to how Moses went up Mount Sinai to receive God's law for Israel. Jesus did this both as a new Moses figure and as God in human form. On the mountain, he gave important teachings for people who belong to God's kingdom (Matthew 5:1–2). 

Jesus began with good news, not just rules (gospel not law). He said that God will save people who recognize their sin, trust in God's mercy, follow his commands, and eagerly wait for God to establish his righteous rule on earth (verses 3–12). Jesus taught that his followers should act as a preservative (like salt) and provide guidance (like light) in a sinful world (Matthew 5:3–16). 

Jesus explained that he did not come to remove the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them completely. This means he came to bring in the new age that the Old Testament pointed toward (verse 17). Jesus called his followers to obey God's law faithfully as he now explained it as the Lawgiver himself (verses 18–20). 

Jesus taught that God's commands include both inner thoughts and outward actions. These commands should not be weakened or explained away. They require even more complete obedience now that the final age has arrived (Matthew 5:21–48). 

When giving to others, praying, and fasting, followers of Jesus should avoid being hypocritical by focusing on God rather than themselves (6:1–18). The Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 5:9–13 asks God to honor his name by establishing his rule on earth and to forgive, protect, and provide for his children. Those who follow Jesus should have a God-centered view of life (verses 19–24). There is no cause for anxiety (verses 25–34).

Disciples must be discerning without being judgmental (Matthew 7:1–6). They must depend on God for the power needed to love others (6:7–12). After finishing his explanation of the law in 5:21–7:12, Jesus now calls potential disciples to follow him (7:13–14). He warns against false teachers (verses 15–20). He insists that true disciples do the will of God (verses 21–23).

The Authority of Jesus (8:1–9:38)

After Jesus showed his authority through his teaching, he demonstrated this authority through healing miracles (Matthew 7:28–29). These miracles revealed him as the servant described in the book of Isaiah (8:17). 

Jesus healed several people using just his words: 

a person with leprosy, 

a Roman officer's servant, and 

a woman who had been bleeding for many years (Matthew 8:1–13; 9:20–22). 

With his touch, Jesus cured a fever and brought a dead person back to life (8:14–15; 9:23–25). Sometimes Jesus used both his words and his touch to heal, as when he restored sight to blind people (9:27–31). 

As "God with us," Jesus calls for total allegiance (Matthew 8:18–22). He did not have the basic shelter that animals enjoy (8:20). But Jesus showed his power over nature—proving his divine nature—by calming a storm (verses 23–27). Jesus directly confronted evil spirits and proved his power over them (8:28–34; 9:32–33). Using authority that belongs only to God, Jesus forgave sins (9:1–8). With this same authority, Jesus called sinners to turn from their wrong ways and follow him (verses 9–13). 

The joy about the beginning of God's kingdom was mixed with a desire for its completion (verses Matthew 9:14–17). The summary in 9:35–38 is similar to what was said in 4:23–25, recalls chapters 5–7, and prepares the audience for the next major speech.

Jesus’s Orders to the Missionaries (10:1–42)

After Jesus told his followers to pray for more workers, he gave 12 disciples special authority as apostles and sent them out to work in his harvest field (Matthew 9:37–10:4). In this teaching, Jesus talked about both the apostles' immediate mission (10:5–15). Jesus also talked about the broader mission of the church (verses 16–42). 

For their first mission, the apostles were told to focus on sharing the good news about Jesus with the Jews (verse 6). This would prepare them for the later mission to non-Jewish people (28:19). The "worthy" are those who welcome the apostles and their message. The "unworthy" are those who reject them (Matthew 10:11–15). 

In the wider mission, Jesus warned that there would certainly be persecution (verses 16–19, 24–25). However, this persecution would actually help spread the message (verses 17–23). Jesus promised that God would save his faithful messengers (verses Matthew 10:19–23). But God will judge those who oppress them and who reject Jesus (verses 26–39). Jesus assured them that both those who announce the message and those who accept it would receive a definite reward (verses 37–42).

Christ the Lord (11:1–12:50)

The judgment that John the Baptist prophesied is already happening. How a person would be judged at the end of time would depend on how they responded to Jesus's words and actions (Matthew 11:2–6). Like John the Baptist, Jesus faced widespread rejection and indifference from people (verse 7–19). Because Jesus brought such important grace in his ministry, those who rejected him would face the most severe judgment (verses 20–24). 

Yet, there are others—the humble, those carrying heavy burdens, and those willing to learn. They discover by revelation from God the Father and God the Son that the "Lord of heaven and earth" is also the "gentle and humble" God who comes to give rest to those who trust in him (Matthew 11:25–30). As the one who brings in the new age (12:6), Jesus claims that he is the Lord of the Sabbath (verses 1–8). True rest comes to those who come to Jesus (11:29).

The Pharisees saw Jesus as someone who destroyed the Sabbath, and they claimed his miracle-working powers came from Satan (Matthew 12:22–24). But Jesus explained that the rule he was establishing was defeating Satan's empire (verses 25–29). To reject this truth while fully understanding what one is doing is to commit the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit (verses 30–32). The words of those accusing Jesus showed that they were destined for condemnation (verses 33–37). They asked for a sign from heaven, but Jesus said it would not be given. Jesus's resurrection was the only sign they needed.

The Parables of the Kingdom (13:1–58)

This is the third of Matthew's five major teaching sections. It contains seven parables (stories with deeper meanings). 

In the parable of the sower, four types of soil—hard, shallow, cluttered, and fruitful—show the different ways people respond to Jesus's teaching (Matthew 13:3–9, 18–23). The disciples had accepted Jesus's announcement of the kingdom, so they are given more understanding (4:17). But the crowds must accept that first proclamation before they receive further knowledge (13:10–17, 34–35). 

In both the parable of the weeds in Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43 and the parable of the parable of the net in verses 47–50, Jesus assures his disciples that the final judgment would separate true believers from false ones. He also warns against making hasty judgments too early (compare with (compare 7:1–5). 

The parables of the mustard and the yeast in Matthew 13:31–33 contrast the smallness of the kingdom’s beginnings with the fullness of its completion. The parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl in verses 44–46 show that the kingdom is more valuable than all others (compare 6:33). With Jesus's teaching, the disciples gained new treasures to add to their old ones (13:51–52).In contrast, the people of Nazareth showed the same lack of understanding as the crowds and the same hostility as the Pharisees (verses 53–58).

Spiritual Conflict (14:1–16:12)

In Matthew 14:1–12, John the Baptist's preaching revealed Herod's weakness. The beheading of John anticipates the death of Jesus on the cross (compare 17:12). The true king is not Herod but Jesus. Jesus showed his power over nature itself (14:13–36). As God in human form, "God with us," Jesus fed the hungry crowd in the wilderness (similar to how God provided manna in the Old Testament) and walked on and calmed the sea (see Psalm 89:9). Peter shows us an example of Christian faith, fear, and complete dependence on Jesus (Matthew 14:28–31). 

The Pharisees and teachers of the law appear to worship God. But they are actually devoted to their own traditions. They offered these traditions not as additions to God's Word but as replacements for it (Matthew 15:1–9). In verses 10–20, Jesus teaches that the ceremonial law apart from moral law becomes an empty ceremony. The old difference between ceremonially clean and unclean foods is now outdated (Leviticus 11). The same is true for the difference between Jews and non-Jews (gentiles). To emphasize this point, Jesus enters non-Jewish territory and heals a Canaanite woman (15:21–28). He also feeds a crowd of gentiles (verses 29–39). Despite their many differences, the Pharisees and Sadducees unite in their opposition to Jesus (16:1–12).

The Coming Salvation (16:13–17:27)

While the crowds had respectful but incomplete opinions about Jesus, Peter confesses that Jesus is "the Christ, the Son of the living God." This recognition of Jesus's divine nature came through divine revelation (Matthew 16:13–17; compare 11:25–26). Since God the Son owns and builds the church, Satan and death are defeated rather than victorious.

Jesus said he would build his church on Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. When the apostles decide who can enter the church ("binding" and "loosing"), their decisions depend on God's revelation of apostolic teaching. After hearing Peter's confession and seeing the persistent wrong ideas about what the Messiah (God's chosen one) should be, Jesus predicted for the first time his suffering and future glory (Matthew 16:20, 23; 21–28). 

In anticipation of that glory, Jesus transfigures himself (his appearance was transformed) before certain disciples. Moses and Elijah join God the Father in testifying to the unique glory of God the Son (17:1–8). Jesus later showed his power by casting out evil spirits (verses 14–18). He demonstrates his authority by choosing to pay the temple tax using miraculous means (verses 24–27).

Greatness in the Kingdom (18:1–35)

This is the fourth of Matthew's five major teaching sections. In it, Jesus focuses on the character and attitudes that church members should have.

Jesus called his followers to both become humble like little children and to welcome those who are considered least important (Matthew 18:1–5). He especially instructed leaders to be strict with themselves but gentle with those under their care (verses 6–9). 

Jesus taught that Christians should remember the Father's love for sinners. They should make every effort, through both prayer and personal action, to restore fellow believers who have done wrong. Removing someone from the church should only be used as a last option (verses 10–20). Church members who truly understand the Father's amazing grace will never stop offering forgiveness and compassion to those who harm them (verses 21–35).

Instructions on the Way to Jerusalem (19:1–20:34)

Jesus says that based on God’s rules of creation, divorce is never commanded. God allows it only in the case of sin. This is when unfaithfulness to a spouse has already severed the marriage union (Matthew 19:1–9). As in 5:17–48, Jesus calls his followers to follow God's commands completely (19:10–12). 

Jesus instructs his disciples to become like children (18:1–4). He also embraces children with his love (19:13–15). Jesus also pleads with the rich young man (Matthew 19:16–22). Although this man had kept the commands about loving neighbors, he was too attached to his wealth to give himself completely to loving God. However, Jesus promised that those who give up everything to follow him will receive much greater wealth in the coming kingdom (verses 27–30). These blessings come not from human goodness but from the amazing generosity of our gracious God (Matthew 20:1–16). No one—not even the rich—is beyond the reach of God's grace. But God offers free salvation at great cost to himself (Matthew 20:17–19). 

Jesus confronts competition and ambition among his followers. Jesus teaches them that true greatness comes from serving others, not having authority over them (verses 20–34). He will ultimately demonstrate this in his death as "a ransom for many" (verse 28).

Confrontations in Jerusalem (21:1–22:46)

Jesus enters Jerusalem as the servant-king (compare Matthew 3:17). He comes as the Messiah destined for suffering (compare 16:16–21; 20:28). He does not arrive on a war horse but on the colt of a donkey. He did this because he planned not to fight his enemies but to give himself over to them. Through this apparent defeat, he would achieve victory (21:1–11). 

As Lord of the temple, Jesus demands that business activities stop and that the temple become (as God intended) a place of worship for everyone, including sick people, children, and foreigners (Matthew 21:12–17; compare Mark 11:17). He outsmarts those who refuse to acknowledge the heavenly source of his authority and that of John the Baptist (Matthew 21:23–27). 

Jesus powerfully pronounces judgment upon those Jews who have refused to acknowledge him as the Messiah and Son of God. First, he shows this visually by cursing the fig tree (Matthew 21:18–22). Then, he shows this through his words by teaching three parables (21:28–22:14). From then on, the true people of God would be those who believed in Jesus, whether they were Jews or non-Jews.

Jesus called his people to give their highest loyalty to God. He taught that in the resurrection, what will matter most is one's relationship with God (Matthew 22:23–33). In fact, the person who loves God with their whole being and loves their neighbor as themselves has kept the two most fundamental commandments of the Old Testament (verses 34–40). 

From then on, submitting to God means correctly recognizing Jesus. He is indeed David's son (Matthew 1:1). But more importantly, he is ultimately David’s Lord and the exalted Son of God (22:41–46; compare 16:16).

Woes upon the Scribes and Pharisees (23:1–39)

Jesus gave five reasons for his strong criticism of the Jewish leaders:

Jesus calls the Jewish leaders hypocrites. What they do contradicts what they teach (Matthew 23:1–4). Their outward purity hides an inward corruption (verses 25–28). They seem to defend God’s cause but are really enemies of God’s servants (verses 29–36). 

Their pride causes their hypocrisy (Matthew 23:5–12). 

They take advantage of and threaten those under their care (Matthew 23:13–15). 

They focus on obeying the least important things of the law and ignore the most important things (Matthew 23:16–24). 

They are responsible for the terrible judgment that the whole nation will experience (Matthew 23:33–39).

The Coming of the End (24:1–25:46)

The introduction to this fifth and final major teaching section of Matthew makes it clear that Jesus and his disciples saw a close connection between Jerusalem's coming destruction and the end of the age (Matthew 24:1–3). It is clear that for Jesus and his disciples, there is the closest connection between the two events. 

Jesus first describes the time between his first and second comings:

Natural disasters will occur.

Nations will be at war with one another.

False messiahs will appear.

God's people will face persecution.

The good news about God's kingdom will be preached in all the world (Matthew 24:4–14). 

Then Jesus speaks of the disaster that will soon happen to the Jewish nation. He already prophesied this in Matthew 22:7 and 23:38. This ends with the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70 (24:15–25).

Sometime later, the Son of Man will return in great glory. Only God the Father knows when this will happen (Matthew 24:36). The Son of Man will return with signs that the end has come and he will gather his people (verses 26–31). The current generation will not die before judgment comes against Israel (verses 15–25). So, those listening must take action (verses 32–35). 

The same warning applies to the final coming of the Son of Man (Matthew 24:36–51). Both the certainty that it would happen and the uncertainty about when it would happen called for watchfulness and faithfulness during the waiting period. This event would bring both salvation and judgment.

To emphasize this lesson, Jesus told the parable of the wise and foolish virgins (Matthew 25:1–13) and the parable of the talents (verses 14–30). The final parable of the sheep and the goats (verses 31–46) spoke about the urgent need to respond correctly to the "brothers." This refers to the messengers of Jesus. Those who feed, clothe, and otherwise care for the messengers of Jesus show that they have accepted the apostles' message and their Lord (compare 10:40–42).

The Road to Golgotha (26:1–27:26)

As if responding to Jesus’s own prediction, the main Jewish priests and the leaders plot to murder him (Matthew 26:1–5). Judas will soon help them (verses 14–16).At Bethany, a woman showed her great love for Jesus by anointing him with expensive perfume, which also pointed to his coming death (verses 6–13).

During the Passover meal (described in Matthew 26:17–30), Jesus explained that his death would be a sacrifice to forgive sins (26:26–28; compare with 1:21). This meal marked the beginning of a new exodus, similar to when God freed the Israelites from Egypt (compare with 2:15). Jesus also looked forward to the future day when God's kingdom would be complete and sin and death would be defeated (26:29).

In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus felt great distress about taking the sins of his people upon himself (verses 36–46). Yet he chose to obey his Father's will so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled (Matthew 26:54; compare Isaiah 53). As God's servant who was destined to suffer, Jesus did not try to stop his arrest (26:47–56). 

The Jewish court (the Sanhedrin) and the high priest condemn Jesus as a blasphemer because he claimed to be "the Christ, the Son of God" (26:57–68; compare 16:16). Peter denies knowing Jesus three times, just as Jesus had predicted (26:31–35; 69–75). Judas feels so guilty about betraying Jesus that he kills himself (27:3–10). 

The Jewish leaders give Jesus over to Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:1–2). Pilate is the only person with the authority to sentence someone to death. The Jews know that charging Jesus with blasphemy will not convince Pilate. 

So, they now represent Jesus as a threat to Caesar (the emperor of Rome). In the end, Pilate does not respond to specific accusations or evidence. The crowd pressures him and threatens a riot (Matthew 27:11–25). So, he releases a murderer named Barabbas and sentences Jesus to be crucified (verse 26).

The Death of Jesus (27:27–66)

The Roman soldiers humiliate, mock, and beat Jesus. Then they lead him to the place where they will kill him. Jesus is weak because of the beatings, so he needs help carrying his cross (Matthew 27:27–32). He refuses the pain-relieving drug they offer him, so that he might keep his head clear (verse 34). 

They executed him with criminals (Matthew 27:38). This testifies to the purpose of his death (compare 1:21). The Jews continue to mock and blaspheme him. They disregard the truth of the title above his head, "THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS" (27:37–44). 

Finally, the ultimate horror reveals itself. Out of the darkness, Jesus cries out as if abandoned by God (Matthew 27:45–49). This is the greatest agony of he who bears the sin of the world. In the garden of Gethsemane, this is what he asked the Father to take away if possible. Jesus cries out with a loud voice and dies (27:50; compare John 19:30). 

Right after Jesus died, the saving effects of his death became clear (Matthew 27:51–53). The curtain in the temple tore in two from top to bottom. This curtain had separated the most holy place from the rest of the temple. When it tore, it showed that sinners could now approach God directly because their sins were forgiven through Jesus's sacrifice.

There was also an earthquake, rocks split apart, and some dead believers came back to life. These events showed that Jesus's death brought the hope of resurrection for those who had died.

Just as at the beginning of the Gospel of Matthew (2:1–12), when wise men from the east (gentiles) recognized Jesus, now it is Roman soldiers (also gentiles) who declare, "Truly this was the Son of God!" (27:54; contrast 26:63–65). Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man who had become a follower of Jesus, carefully placed Jesus's body in his own new tomb (27:57–66). Joseph’s actions contrast with the ongoing attempts of the chief priests and Pharisees to resist Jesus’s power (27:57–66).

The Triumph of the Savior (28:1–20)

The victory of the Savior comes with great glory and power and joy. The angels announce it and his disciples testify to it (Matthew 28:1–7). The risen Jesus appears first to the women who stayed with him while he was nailed to the cross (28:8–10; compare 27:61; 28:1). After the guards report what happened, the Jewish leaders become even more desperate to stop the truth from spreading (28:11–15). 

Jesus meets with the 11 disciples on the mountain in Galilee (Matthew 28:16–20). Like Moses who received God's commands on a mountain, Jesus gives his final instructions to his followers. From the very beginning of his Gospel, Matthew has been preparing his audience to understand its purpose of spreading the good news about Jesus The apostles must disciple all peoples by:
