NETHINIM

The Nethinim were temple assistants who helped with the work in God's temple. This term appears only in books written after the Israelites returned from exile (1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah). The word "Nethinim" comes from the Hebrew verb "nathan," which means "to give, set apart, or dedicate." So the term means "those given" or "those set apart for service."

The Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) translates this word as dedomenoi. Some recent translators have followed the Jewish historian Josephus by referring to them as “temple slaves” (Antiquities 11.5.1). The Berean Standard Bible translates it “temple servants.” The New Living Translation translates it "temple assistants."

Before the exile (when many Israelites were taken to Babylon), the Nethinim worked in temple service. First Chronicles 9:2 lists them with the priests and Levites who took possession of their assigned cities. The order in which they are listed—priests, Levites, and Nethinim—shows that they had a role below the Levites (see also Nehemiah 7:73; 11:3, 20–21). They returned from exile as temple servants (Ezra 2:43, 58; 7:7, 24; 8:17, 20; Nehemiah 7:46, 60). They lived in Jerusalem (Ezra 7:7; Nehemiah 3:31; 11:21). They helped repair the city walls (Nehemiah 3:26).

We cannot be completely certain about who exactly the Nethinim were. Numbers 31:47 rells us that the Levites received captives who were given hard and basic tasks. When the Gibeonites were accepted into Israel as servants, they too were assigned to carry water and chop wood for the entire community and for the altar of the Lord (Joshua 9:9–27). King David increased the number of people serving at the tabernacle by assigning prisoners of war to perform these duties (Ezra 8:20). When the temple was completed, more workers were needed for temple services, and King Solomon added to their number. This new group became known as “the servants of Solomon.” 

Ezra records that 392 Nethinim returned from exile to Jerusalem (2:58). They performed the duties in the rebuilt temple that their ancestors did before the exile. The Israelites considered the Nethinim full members of the restored covenant community. The Nethinim devoted themselves to God (Nehemiah 10:28).

NETOPHAH, NETOPHATHITE

Netophah was a place near Bethlehem in the Old Testament. A Netophathite was someone who came from that place.

Two of David’s thirty mighty warriors came from Netophah (2 Samuel 23:28–29; 1 Chronicles 11:30; 27:13–15). Seraiah, one of the army leaders who met Gedaliah after Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC, was also a Netophathite (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8).

Later, 56 men from Netophah returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Joshua (Ezra 2:22).

Levites also lived in the villages of the Netophathites (1 Chronicles 9:16). Temple singers came from villages around Jerusalem, including those near Netophah (Nehemiah 12:28). These verses suggest that Netophah was not just a town but part of a larger area or district.

Netophah was likely located near Bethlehem (see 1 Chronicles 2:54; Nehemiah 7:26). We do not know the exact location, but many believe it was at Khirbet Bedd Faluh, about 4.8 kilometers (3 miles) southeast of Bethlehem.

NETTLE

The nettle is a plant with toothed leaves covered with tiny hairs that release a stinging liquid when touched. Four types of nettle grow in Israel and the surrounding areas:

The common or great nettle (Urtica dioica)

The Roman nettle (Urtica pilulifera)

The small nettle (Urtica urens)

Urtica caudata, which is similar to the small nettle

Some nettles can grow as tall as 1.5 to 1.8 meters (five to six feet). They are common weeds found in abandoned areas and fields. They often grow in places that were once farmed but have since been neglected (Isaiah 34:13; Hosea 9:6).

NEW

New describes something that has recently come into existence. It often replaces what existed before, making the old new.

That the second part of the Bible is called the New Testament shows how important the idea of "new" is to biblical revelation. Many important theological ideas include the concept of new: 

new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17),

new birth (John 3:3),

new man (Ephesians 2:15; Colossians 3:10),

new commandment (John 13:34),

new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31),

new life (Romans 6:4), and various others.

The Expectation of the New

The totality of the expectation of the new is best expressed in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and the Psalms. The reference in the Psalter to the "new song" to be given to the people to sing is a central metaphor (For example, Psalms 33:3; 40:3; 149:1; compare also Isaiah 42:10). Jeremiah speaks of the day when God will make a new covenant (special agreement) with the house of Israel (Jeremiah 31:31–34; compare Ezekiel 34:25–31; 37:26–28). In contrast with the old, this new covenant will be internal, written upon the heart. Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:22–32) also tells of the day when God will cleanse his people and will give a heart of flesh in place of the heart of stone. 

This act of God's holiness will introduce the age of the Spirit. It will bring about a new existence, characterized by security and freedom, where the laws of God are followed. The supreme feature of this new time is the new spirit within people (Ezekiel 11:19). Joel speaks also of that day when the Spirit of God will be poured out on all flesh (Joel 2:28). Isaiah 65:17 states the promise of "new heavens and a new earth." Isaiah's words often reflect national circumstances and hopes (for example, after the exile). However, this promise took on new significance beyond the hope of the nation Israel.

The Coming of the New

The presence of the kingdom in the world through Jesus announces that the promised new age has broken into time in powerful ways. Jesus’s ministry is one of fulfillment. What the prophets promised has begun to take place. John the Baptist had prepared the way for the one who would give the promised Spirit. The giving of this Spirit is the giving of new life. Through faith in Christ, one is born anew (John 3:3–7). But Jesus had to die in order for this new life to be given. The cup of wine Jesus shared with his disciples at the Last Supper symbolized the blood of the new covenant (Mark 14:24).

The early church expressed this significance in using many metaphors: 

This "newness of life" is demonstrated through baptism (Romans 6:4). 

The eucharistic cup is the new covenant through blood (1 Corinthians 11:25). 

An extended discourse on the old and new covenants shows that by the shedding of his blood Christ has become mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 9:15). 

By his blood, Jesus has opened up a new and living way into the Holy Place (10:19–20). 

Paul restates the promise of Ezekiel for a heart of flesh (2 Corinthians 3:3). He then gives an account of the ministry of the new covenant in contrast to the old. 

The church represents the appearance of the new age in the domain of the old.

The one who comes to Christ by faith is declared a new person, a new creation, for whom the old has passed away (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15). 

Jewish-gentile hostility disappears in the resulting "new humanity" (Ephesians 2:15). 

All other social distinctions (such as male-female, slave-free) pass away in the new humanity created in Christ Jesus (Colossians 3:10–11).

The newness of a person in Christ is the foundation for New Testament ethics (Ephesians 4:24; Colossians 3:12). The new commandment (John 13:34; 1 John 2:8) is not really new (1 John 2:7), but now has new possibility and deeper meaning by the power and example of Jesus. Though this new life is a gift of God, the process of being made new continues. Transformation by the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2) realizes the will of God. Paul declares the inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16).

The Realization of the New

As real as the new life of the believer is, Scripture shows a tension between the new age that is not yet realized. The time when all things are made new is a future promise (Revelation 21:5). With the end of the old, there is a new heaven and new earth. The new Jerusalem "coming down out of heaven" as the dwelling place of God (verse 2). The people of God receive a new name (3:12) as the old things disappear. 

The people who are the redeemed of the Lord are given a new song to sing. The song is about the Lamb slain from the beginning of creation:

The first line of the song is "Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!" The chorus returns, "To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!" (Revelation 5:12–13).

See also New Commandment; New Covenant; New Jerusalem; Old and New Self; New Creation, New Creature; New Heavens and New Earth; Renewal, Regeneration.

NEW BIRTH

A way of receiving "spiritual life" and becoming part of the kingdom of God. 

Jesus spoke about new birth when he talked with a man named Nicodemus (John 3:3–7). Jesus said that people must be "born again" to see the kingdom of God. This new birth does not come from human parents. It comes from God’s Spirit.

New birth is also called regeneration (a word that means being made new). It happens when God gives someone a new heart and a new spirit.

See Regeneration.

NEW COMMANDMENT

The “new commandment” is Christ’s instruction for Christians to love one another. The phrase appears four times in the New Testament, all in the writings of John (John 13:34; 1 John 2:7, 8; 2 John 1:5). Jesus first gave this command to his disciples on the night he was arrested: “A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another” (John 13:34). This command appears in other places in the Bible (John 15:12, 17; Romans 13:8; 1 Peter 1:22; 1 John 3:11, 23; 4:7, 11–12), but is not called “new” in those passages.

Love as a Commandment

Jesus had already told his disciples to love their enemies (Matthew 5:43–45) and to love their neighbors as themselves (Luke 10:25–37). The “new commandment” demanded that Christians love each other. It did not replace the other two love commands. Jesus intended this command to create a strong and convincing testimony for those outside the church. This would clearly show three things:

that his followers lived like Christ by loving one another;

that true human community is built on Christ; and

that this love confirms that what Jesus said about himself and his work is true (John 13:35; 17:21–23).

Jesus chose the word used to describe the Old Testament law. By doing this, he gave his new commandment the same level of authority. The Old Testament law also included commands to love (Leviticus 19:18, 34; Deuteronomy 10:19). The apostle Paul referred to love as the “law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2), and James called the love command the “royal law” (James 2:8) and “the perfect law of liberty” (1:25; 2:12).

The word “commandment” had another meaning as well. Many Jews in the time of Jesus wrongly thought that obeying commandments would make them worthy of God’s blessing (Romans 8:3; Galatians 3:2). Jesus made it clear, however, that love was a natural result of God’s blessing, not a necessary condition for it. For Jesus, the commandment showed how the blessed should behave. Disciples were commanded to love in the same way that branches are “commanded” to bear fruit: by staying connected to the vine (Jesus), Christians can love (John 15:4).

What Made the New Commandment New?

The new commandment gets its special character from the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). Jesus established the new covenant at the Last Supper. Under the new covenant, God “writes” his law on the hearts of believers (Hebrews 10:16). This means he actively works in them through the Holy Spirit (Ezekiel 36:27; 2 Corinthians 3:3). God gives them a new desire to obey him (Romans 8:4; Galatians 5:16). 

The new commandment to love is the main part of the new covenant (Romans 13:8, 10; Galatians 5:14). Obedience is therefore a gift, because “love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God” (1 John 4:7). Love is the result of faith (1 John 3:23) and is part of the gospel itself (1 John 3:11).

The close relationship between the new covenant and the new commandment helps explain why the command to love is called new. Christ’s incarnation inaugurated a new age. As John writes, “The darkness is fading and the true light is already shining” (1 John 2:8). In the context of his departure (John 13:33–35), Jesus gave his disciples a defining commandment (mutual love) that would characterize life in this new age. Obedience to this commandment was to identify them as the disciples of Jesus during his absence (John 13:35; 17:21–23). In this sense, the love commandment is new not because love itself was previously unknown, but because it now functions as the central mark of allegiance to Christ in the inaugurated new age, oriented toward its final consummation

What made the era new was that Jesus Christ’s coming revealed God the Father in a way that had never been seen before (John 1:18; 10:30; 17:6–8). No prophet had ever been able to say, “Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Therefore, the command from Jesus that his disciples love each other “as I have loved you” (John 13:34) was new and shocking by any human standard. No one had ever loved perfectly as Jesus did (John 13:1). Following his example of love was a new commandment. 

The greatness of the love of Jesus led him to “lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Similarly, John concluded that “we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John 3:16). Love means not refusing to help a fellow Christian who is in need (1 John 3:17). Love means gladly sacrificing one's own good for another's benefit.

See also Ten Commandments; Biblical Concept of Law.

NEW COVENANT

The new covenant is a special promise that God made through Jesus Christ to rescue people from the effects of sin. It replaces and completes the old covenant, which was based on the laws God gave to Moses. The Bible mainly talks about this new covenant in the New Testament

The idea of a new covenant is found in several places in the Old Testament (Ezekiel 34:23–31; 37:24–28; Joel 2:12–32). The actual phrase occurs only once (Jeremiah 31:31–34). 

In this passage, Jeremiah describes how God's new covenant would be different from the old covenant he made with Moses. The main difference is where God would put his laws. In the old covenant, God wrote his laws on stone tablets (Exodus 31:18; 34:27–32; Deuteronomy 4:13; 5:22; 9:11; 10:3–4). It was also written in a book (Exodus 24:7; compare the phrase “the old way of the written code,” Romans 7:6). 

But in the new covenant, God would write his laws directly in people's hearts. This would help people understand more clearly what God wants. People would be able to actually do what God asks (see Romans 8:2–4). Other prophets also talked about how God would work inside people's hearts (Ezekiel 11:19–21; 36:26–27). The prophet Joel said that one day God would give his Spirit to all kinds of people: “I will pour out My Spirit in those days” (Joel 2:28–32).

Another difference is how God’s people know him under the two covenants. Israel knew God under the old covenant. God had revealed himself to Israel, but sometimes they forgot him (Judges 2:10; Hosea 4:1, 6). The prophets wrote that the new covenant would be different: each person would be able to know God personally.

Lastly, the two covenants differ in how God deals with people's sin. Jeremiah said God would forgive his people's bad actions and remove their sins. The people of Israel already knew that God was merciful and forgiving (Exodus 34:6–7). But now Jeremiah was telling them something new: God would never think about their sins again (Jeremiah 31:34). Under the old covenant, people were reminded of their sins every year (Hebrews 10:3). But under the new covenant, God removes all memory of sin (10:14).

A New Covenant

The term “new covenant” appears at least six times in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Hebrews 8:8, 13; 9:15; 12:24) According to some manuscripts, it is likely Luke 22:20, also uses the phrase. In some Greek handwritten copies of Matthew 26:28 and Mark 14:24, the word “new” was added to “blood of the covenant.” These scribes likely added this based on other stories of the Lord’s Supper in 1 Corinthians or possibly in the Gospel of Luke.

Since the word “new” was not in the best Greek copies of the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Mark, it likely was not in the original writings. It is clear from all four stories that Jesus saw the Lord’s Supper as starting a different and therefore “new” covenant. Jesus's death made this new agreement with God official. This was similar to how God had made his first agreement official when Moses offered animal sacrifices (Exodus 24:6–8). 

The cup in the Lord’s Supper stands for the blood of Jesus's sacrifice, sealing the new covenant God has made with his people. The church remembers this new covenant, made firm by Jesus's death, each time it celebrates the Lord’s Supper.

When Jesus started the Lord’s Supper, he did not explain what was “new” about the covenant. In other places, he spoke about “baptism with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1:5; 11:16; compare. Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:8; Luke 3:16; and John 1:33). In the Gospel of John, John the Baptist makes the promise (compare 1 Corinthian 12:13). Both Old Testament predictions refer to the same new covenant that God would make in the future, as shown in 2 Corinthians 3:6. There, Paul stated that God “has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant” (compare. Jeremiah 31:31), not “of the letter but of the Spirit” (compare Joel 2:28–32), for “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

Why Is the New Covenant Better?

In 2 Corinthians 3, Paul explains the difference between the old and new covenants. The old covenant, which God gave through Moses (3:14), was written on stone and brought death (3:7). But the new covenant that Jesus started is different and better (3:8–9). In this new covenant, God's Spirit writes his laws directly on people's hearts (3:3).

The book of Hebrews in the New Testament explains the new covenant more completely than any other book in the Bible. Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34, which is the longest Old Testament quotation found in the New Testament. In Hebrews 12:24, a different Greek word for “new” is used, but the meaning is the same. 

The new covenant is one of the main topics in Hebrews. The book was written to help Christians who were having doubts about their faith. It shows them why their new faith in Jesus was better than their old Jewish beliefs and practices.

The book of Hebrews explains several ways that the new covenant is better than the old covenant, which was no longer needed.

The new covenant has a better priesthood. In the old covenant, priests would serve God's people by speaking to God for them. But these priests were human and would eventually die, so new priests were always needed to replace them (Hebrews 7:23). 

The new covenant is different. Jesus is our priest, and he lives forever. He never needs to be replaced, and he is always there to speak to God for his people (7:24–25).

Jesus is a better priest than the priests of the old covenant. The old priests had to offer animal sacrifices again and again. They had to make these sacrifices first for their own sins because they too were sinful people. Then they would make sacrifices for everyone else's sins.

But Jesus was different. He never sinned, so he did not need to make sacrifices for himself. And instead of making many sacrifices, he gave his own life as one final sacrifice that would work forever (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:12).

The new covenant has a better sacrifice. In the old covenant, priests had to kill animals as sacrifices for sin. But these animal sacrifices could only partly cover people's sins, and they had to be repeated over and over (10:2–3). 

Jesus's sacrifice was different. When he gave his life, it was one perfect sacrifice that worked completely and forever (9:11–14; 10:1–10).

The new covenant is built on “better promises” than the old (8:6).

The old covenant was not complete and had weaknesses (8:7). This is why it was replaced by something better (8:13). But the new covenant is complete and perfect, and it will last forever (13:20).

The old and new covenants are different in how people can approach God. Under the old covenant, people could not come to God directly. They needed priests to go to God for them (9:6–8). Under the new covenant, everyone can come to God directly. When we do this, God cleanses our hearts and takes away our guilt (compare 9:14 with 9:9).

The new covenant has a better guarantee, a promise made by God himself (7:20–22).

In the new covenant, God promises that his Holy Spirit will live in everyone who believes in Jesus. God gives his Spirit to all his people (6:4). Paul tells us that the Holy Spirit is proof ("seal") that we belong to God and a promise ("pledge") that we will receive everything God has promised us (see 2 Corinthians 1:22; 5:5; Ephesians 1:13–14).

Conclusion

The new covenant completes what God started in the old covenant. It also comes with a new command to love others God puts his laws inside people's hearts through his Holy Spirit. God's Spirit lives in believers and gives them the power to follow his new command (Romans 8:2–4; Galatians 5:16–25). This power from God's Spirit is one of the most important differences between the old and new covenants. The Spirit helps believers do what God asks of them.

See also Covenant.

NEW CREATION, NEW CREATURE

"New creation" refers to God's work of renewing and restoring everything he has made. "New creature" refers to a person who has been transformed through faith in Jesus Christ. Together, these ideas express the Bible's message of redemption, which develops throughout the Old Testament and New Testament and will reach its fulfillment at the second coming of Jesus Christ.

One of the most important truths in the Bible is that God created heaven and earth and continues to sustain and rule over everything he has made (for example, Genesis 1; Psalms 33:6–11; 104; Matthew 6:25–32). The Bible also teaches that humans are creatures made in God's image (Genesis 1–2). Because of this, the Bible's message of salvation can only be understood correctly when we understand God as Creator.

Human sin is serious because people have turned away from the Creator. Instead, they have "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). God is the Redeemer because he is also the Creator. The people he saves are his creatures who have rebelled against him. Along with humanity, the whole created order suffers under the effects of sin and is subject to frustration and decay (Genesis 3:17–18; Romans 8:20–21).

New Creation in the Old Testament

The connection between creation and salvation is especially clear in Isaiah 40–66. Here, the prophet talks about God's ultimate redemption for Israel. This future salvation often highlights God as the Creator of heaven, earth, and Israel (see Isaiah 40:12–31; 44:24; 45:18; 48:13; 51:16; 64:8).

Isaiah speaks of "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). This idea of a new creation shows that the salvation God promises is for everyone, not just Israel. God’s work of recreation and restoration at the end connects to his work of creation in the beginning (Isaiah 48:12). What God will do at the end for all things is as significant as what he did when he created everything from nothing. This new creation order will lead to eternal happiness for the faithful. New Testament writers continue to develop these themes.

New Creation and Christ

The New Testament connects creation and redemption (God's work of saving people). Several writers compare Christ's saving work with his role in creation or show how the two are related (John 1:3; Colossians 1:15–18; Hebrews 1:2–3; Revelation 3:14). TWhat Christ did at the end of history, "when the time had fully come" (Galatians 4:4; Ephesians 1:10) and "in these last days" (Hebrews 1:2) is based on what he did at the beginning. The redemption Christ accomplished is a work of new creation.

Paul clearly connects new creation with Christ's work when he calls Christ the "last Adam" and "second man" (1 Corinthians 15:45–47; compare verse 22; Romans 5:14). This description is very similar to "Son of Man," the title Jesus often used for himself. By calling Christ the "last Adam," Paul emphasizes the contrast between Adam and Christ (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 15). Adam's disobedience brought sin into the world, and sin led to condemnation and death. In contrast, Christ's obedience brought righteousness (a right relationship with God), resulting in justification (being made right with God) and life.

Paul explains more of the contrast between Adam and Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:42–49. He compares the believer's present body, which is weak and subject to death, with the body believers will receive at the resurrection (when God raises the dead). He summarizes this contrast by calling one body "natural" and the other "spiritual." 

Adam and Christ represent these two kinds of bodies. At the same time, Paul presents them as representatives of two different orders of life. Adam, the first man, is the representative head of the natural, earthly order. Because of his sin, this order became subject to corruption and death (Romans 5:12–19). Christ, the second and last Adam, is the representative head of the spiritual, heavenly order, which is marked by life, power, and glory. Ultimately, this passage contrasts two stages in God's plan: the present creation and its future completion in the new creation. Each begins with an Adam.

Two other points are important for understanding Paul's teaching about the new creation, as well as the teaching of other New Testament writers.

The believer's resurrection depends completely on Christ's resurrection. As the last Adam, Christ became the life-giving Spirit through his resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:45). The main emphasis is the close connection between Christ's resurrection and the resurrection of believers (compare with 1 Corinthians 15:12–20; Colossians 1:18). 

In the New Testament message, Christ's resurrection is the great saving act that corresponds to creation itself (Romans 4:17). According to the New Testament, the new creation is already a present reality because Christ has been raised from the dead.

When 1 Corinthians 15:45 says that the last Adam became a life-giving Spirit, it points to the unity between the exalted Christ and the Holy Spirit in giving life. The Holy Spirit is the power of the new creation (compare Hebrews 6:5). Wherever the Holy Spirit is at work as the gift of the glorified Christ, the new creation is present.

The new creation is the fulfillment of what the Old Testament promised and looked forward to in the last days. It has already begun through Christ's work as the last Adam, especially through his death and resurrection. It will be completed when he returns.

Until then, believers live in a time when both the old creation and the new creation exist side by side. The new creation has begun, but the old creation is still passing away (1 Corinthians 7:31). The idea of the new creation is closely related to the kingdom of God. In the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke), the kingdom of God is the central theme of the teaching of Jesus. Jesus announced that the kingdom was both present through his own person and work (Matthew 12:28; 13:11, 16–17) and still future (Matthew 8:11; 25:34). 

Jewish people in the time of Jesus often spoke of two ages: the present age and the age to come. Jesus and the early church also used this way of speaking about God's plan (for example, Matthew 12:32; Ephesians 1:21). The new creation is this long-awaited age to come.

The term "new creation" emphasizes how complete this future reality is. God's work of redemption (saving and restoring his people) involves nothing less than the renewal of all things (Revelation 21:5).

New Creation and the Church

According to the New Testament, salvation depends completely on union with Christ (being joined to Christ by faith). Through this union, believers share in all the benefits of Christ's once-for-all work of redemption.

Because Christ died and was raised from the dead, everyone who is in Christ already shares in the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:15). This truth is not only about individual believers. It also has a wider meaning that includes all creation. The surrounding verses emphasize reconciliation (God restoring relationships that sin has broken) and show that its effects reach far beyond individuals (2 Corinthians 5:17–19).

The only other New Testament use of the expression "new creation" is found in Galatians 6:15. Here, the idea includes both the individual believer and the wider created order. In this new creation, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. What matters is God's new work of renewal. The new creation stands in contrast to the world, to which believers have died through their union with Christ (Galatians 6:14; compare Colossians 2:20). “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Resurrection is not only a future hope for believers. It is also a present reality. Through their union with Christ, believers have already been raised with him (Ephesians 2:5–6; compare Colossians 2:12–13; 3:1). As a result, believers are “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:10). 

The church is also the new covenant community of the "new man," made up of both Jews and Gentiles (Ephesians 2:15). Even now, believers are being renewed inwardly (2 Corinthians 4:16). Through the work of the Spirit of the Lord, they are being changed to become more like Christ, the last Adam, in his glory (2 Corinthians 3:18; 4:4–6; compare Romans 8:29; Ephesians 4:24; Colossians 3:10). When Christ returns, believers will also share his image in their resurrected bodies (1 Corinthians 15:49). 

The strongest reason for holy living is not simply gratitude for the forgiveness of sins. It is the reality that believers have become a new creation. New Testament ethics (teaching about how believers should live) comes from this new creation identity (Romans 12:2; Colossians 2:20).

The Future of the New Creation

The new creation is not only a present reality. It is also a future hope. As they wait for its full completion, believers live "by faith, not by sight" (2 Corinthians 5:7). Like Isaiah, who looked forward to God's future promises, believers look forward to Christ's return. They await "a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells" (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–4. In that future world, sin and all its effects will be gone

This hope raises an important question: What is the relationship between the final, eternal creation and the original creation?

Some passages seem to suggest a complete break between the two. For example, 2 Peter 3:10–12 describes destruction by fire, and Revelation 21–22 includes images such as the absence of the sun, moon, and night (compare Revelation 6:12–14). However, other passages show that this language is symbolic and points to a transformed creation rather than its complete destruction.

Paul's teaching about the resurrection helps explain this. Although there are great differences between the present body and the resurrection body, they are not two different bodies. The same body that is now subject to corruption, dishonor, and weakness will be raised incorruptible, glorious, and powerful (1 Corinthians 15:44). 

The same principle applies to creation. All creation now suffers under the effects of sin and decay. Yet creation is not waiting to be destroyed. It is waiting to be set free from its bondage to decay and to share in the freedom and glory of God's children when their bodies are redeemed through resurrection (Romans 8:19–23). 

The new creation is therefore not simply a return to the way things were in the beginning. It is the renewal and completion of creation. It brings to fulfillment God's purposes, which he established before the beginning of the world and accomplished through Christ, the last Adam, despite the effects of human sin.

See Adam (Person); Creation; Eternal Life; Old and New Self; New; New Heavens and New Earth.

NEW GATE

The New Gate was one of the temple gates during the prophet Jeremiah’s ministry (Jeremiah 26:10; 36:10).

NEW HEAVENS AND NEW EARTH

The concept of a new or renewed universe first found in the book of Isaiah. God declares, “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind. … For just as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, will endure before Me. … so your descendants and your name will endure” (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22).

Some scholars believe that, before Isaiah's time, many cultures thought the end of history would be like its beginning. This would lead to a universal restoration. The Bible describes a supernatural world renewal. It occurs in a higher, different realm.

The belief that God is the Creator of the heavens and the earth is central to all biblical teachings. “In the beginning You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands” (Psalm 102:25). Since God created the heavens and the earth, it is fitting that, once they have served their purpose, God can do with them as He wishes. “They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment. Like clothing You will change them, and they will be passed on” (Psalm 102:26). The same metaphor is found in Isaiah 51:6, where the earth is described as wearing out like a garment.

The Bible discusses the end of the old order. It speaks of a time when heaven and earth will vanish (Isaiah 34:4; 51:6; Matthew 24:35; Revelation 21:1). Several phrases express this idea: 

“The world is passing away” (1 John 2:17)

“The earth will wear out like a garment” (Hebrews 1:11; compare Psalm 102:26; Isaiah 51:6)

“But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare” (2 Peter 3:10)

This destruction by fire will occur at the time of final judgment. It will be “the day when God will set the heavens on fire and the elements will melt away in the flames” (2 Peter 3:12)

This judgment, which brings an end to the old order, prepares the way for new heavens and a new earth. Peter continues, “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). It will be so wonderful that no one will even remember the old (Isaiah 65:17). 

Peter, preaching in Solomon’s Colonnade, says that Jesus will remain in heaven until the time comes for establishing all that God spoke by his holy prophets (Acts 3:21). The created order eagerly awaits this recovery or renewal. Paul writes, “For all creation is waiting eagerly for that future day when God will reveal who his children really are” (Romans 8:19) because “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God” (Romans 8:21).

The renewed heaven is not God's presence. It is the starry universe, the heaven of human existence. The book of Revelation says the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven to earth (Revelation 21:2, 10). It is the eternal home of God and his people. The new earth will be a place of perfect righteousness (Isaiah 51:6), divine kindness (Isaiah 54:10), eternal relationship to God (Isaiah 66:22), and total freedom from sin (Romans 8:21).

See also Eschatology; Heaven; Kingdom of God, Kingdom of Heaven; New; New Creation, New Creature.

NEW JERUSALEM

The phrase “New Jerusalem” appears only twice in the Bible. Both times, it appears in the book of Revelation—once near the beginning and once near the end (Revelation 3:12; 21:2). 

In the first major vision of Revelation, the risen Christ speaks to his people while they face conflict in this world. He promises that those who remain faithful will one day belong to the new Jerusalem. This promise describes a future identity and place of belonging for God’s people.

At the end of Revelation, this promise is fulfilled. John sees the victorious people of God and the city that will be their home. The new Jerusalem represents life with God in a renewed world, where God lives with his people forever.

This does not, of course, answer the question “What is the new Jerusalem?” A description of what it is like would be relatively simple. An explanation of what it is would be more complicated.

Description of the City

An angel takes John to a high mountain to show him the new Jerusalem. What follows is a detailed vision (Revelation 21:10–22:5). 

The first thing John notices is the light of the city. It shines like a great, jewel-like lamp. This light is “the glory of God” (21:11). John then describes the city's walls and gates (Revelation 21:12–14). The 12 gates have the names of the tribes of Israel, and the wall between each gate forms a single “foundation,” or block, with the name of one of the 12 apostles of Christ. 

Next, John gives the measurements of the city (Revelation 21:15–17). The city is about 2,220 kilometers (1,400 miles) wide, long, and high. Its wall is 65.8 meters (216 feet) thick or perhaps high. While these modern measurements are helpful, they may miss what mattered most to John.

According to biblical measurements, the city is 12,000 stadia wide, and its wall is 144 cubits thick. These numbers are symbolic. They are multiples of 12, indicating perfection, as do other occurrences of the number 12 in Revelation (for example, Revelation 7:4–8).

After this, John describes the materials used to build the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:18–21). The city wall is made of jasper. The foundation layers are covered with many precious stones. The gates are made of pearls. The streets and buildings inside the city are made of "pure gold, clear as glass." 

John then lists several important things the city does not have (Revelation 22–27). There is no temple, because God himself lives with his people. There is no sun or moon, because God’s glory gives light. There is no night, the gates are never closed, and nothing evil is present.

Finally, John describes three wonderful things the city does have (22:1–5). There is the river of the water of life, which brings life from God. There is the tree of life, which provides healing and renewal. Most important of all, God himself is present. His throne is there, and his people live with him forever.

This is how John describes the new Jerusalem. However, his main purpose is not simply to help us imagine what the city looks like. He wants us to understand what the new Jerusalem means and what it shows about God’s final plan for his people.

Background of the City

Old Testament history presents the city of David, old Jerusalem, as the center of God’s rule and presence among his people. In that city stood the temple, where the priests served God. It was also the place of the king’s throne, where rulers governed as God’s representatives. Jerusalem was the main city, or “mother city,” of Israel, the people of God.

However, the Bible as a whole tells the story of God redeeming a people for himself from all nations and all times. This larger people of God goes beyond Old Testament Israel. Israel was the beginning, or first part, of this greater people.

Because of this, it makes sense that the Bible’s final revelation shows a vision of this greater people of God. They are finally at home in the true mother city. This city is the new and greater Jerusalem.

The Old Testament prophets saw the decline of old Jerusalem. They watched with sorrow and anger as the city failed to live up to its calling. Sin and foolishness spread through the city. Its kings and priests increasingly turned away from the role God had given them.

Because of this, some prophets began to hope for a different Jerusalem. They looked forward to a city that would one day become what God intended. The prophet Ezekiel imagined Jerusalem and its temple rebuilt in great detail (Ezekiel 40–48). The prophet Isaiah described this future Jerusalem in even more vivid and hopeful language (Isaiah 52, 60–66). 

The visions of Ezekiel and Isaiah closely connect with John’s vision in Revelation 21–22. Together, they point toward a renewed Jerusalem that fully reflects God’s purpose for his people.

In the time between the Old Testament and the New Testament, many Jewish writers became even more disappointed with the situation in Jerusalem. Because of this, they shifted their hope. Instead of expecting the earthly city to be renewed, they began to describe a heavenly Jerusalem.

These writers believed this heavenly city already existed. At the end of the age, God would cause it to come down from heaven. It would be the main city of God’s people. It would be full of life and beauty, and it would be the place of God’s temple and throne.

In many ways, what these apocalyptic writers imagined is very similar to what John later describes in Revelation. Their hopes and visions prepared the way for the picture John presents of the new Jerusalem.

Jesus takes all these earlier ideas and reshapes them in a striking way. He does more than predict the final destruction of Jerusalem and its temple (Mark 13; Luke 19:41–44). If that were all he said, an important question would remain unanswered.

Old Jerusalem existed for a purpose. It was meant to be the place of God’s rule and presence. If the city and its temple are destroyed, how will that purpose be fulfilled? Where will God’s people then find God’s throne and God’s dwelling place among them?

Jesus answers that, since the Incarnation (when God became human), God now rules through him, and God’s presence is seen in him (Matthew 28:18; John 14:9). In Jesus, God is present with his people in a new way. Because of this, some Christians understand Jesus as fulfilling what Jerusalem and the temple once represented. 

There are two different Greek words that English Bibles translate as “new.” After the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, the emperor Hadrian built a “new” Jerusalem. That kind of “new” meant only the latest version of a city built on the same site.

John’s vision uses the other meaning of “new.” This word means fresh, clean, and truly different. It does not describe a replacement of the old city. It describes something transformed and renewed. The New Testament uses this same word when it speaks of the new covenant and the new commandment (John 13:34; Hebrews 8:8), and of the new creation and the new person in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17; Ephesians 2:15). 

John shows what this kind of “new” means by listing seven things that will exist “no more” in the new heaven and new earth. There will be no more sea, death, sorrow, crying, pain, curse, or night (Revelation 21:1, 4; 22:3–5). In these ways, everything will be truly new and different.

Five other passages in the New Testament help explain the background of Revelation 21. In Galatians 4:26, Paul speaks of “Jerusalem above.” This city is the mother city of all who receive salvation by faith. He contrasts it with the old Jerusalem, which represents those who try to please God by obeying the law (Galatians 4:25). In Ephesians 5:25–32, Paul describes the “bride of Christ,” meaning the church. In John’s vision, this same bride is described as a city, the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:9–10). In Philippians 3:20, Paul says that believers already have their citizenship in heaven. This means the heavenly city is not only a future home. It is also the place to which believers already belong. Hebrews 12:22 makes the same point. Those who believe have already come to the “heavenly Jerusalem.” This language shows that the city is real in the present, not only in the future.

Taken together, these passages show that the Jerusalem John sees is the home of all God’s people. This includes Jews and non-Jews (gentiles), and believers from both Old Testament and New Testament times. In some way, this city already exists, even though its full reality still lies ahead. This raises an important question: how should we understand John’s vision of the new Jerusalem?

Meaning of the City

Some Christians expect a future millennium. This refers to a one-thousand-year earthly reign of Christ between his second coming and the final defeat of Satan.

Some Christians who hold this view believe the new Jerusalem belongs to the millennium. They base this view on details they think fit that period better than the eternal state that follows it (Revelation 21:24–26; 22:2). They imagine the new Jerusalem as a literal, physical city. Because its length, width, and height are equal, they suppose it may be shaped like a cube, or possibly a pyramid. Some even imagine it floating above the earth, like a very large structure suspended in the air (that is, not resting on the ground).

Most Christians who believe in a future millennium, and also many who do not hold that view, think John is describing the city as it will be in eternity. Some of them understand the description in a literal way. Others think John uses detailed images (the city’s size, shape, and materials) because this is the only way to speak about something that is beyond full human description. In this view, the city is real, but its reality goes beyond what human language can fully explain

In line with the message of the whole book of Revelation, many understand the new Jerusalem as the ideal city of God. In this view, it belongs not only to the future but also to the present. The new Jerusalem exists now because it is a spiritual reality, not a physical city made of material things. It is “coming down out of heaven” because it comes to people “from God” (21:2). 

At the same time, everything John describes in the final chapters of Revelation belongs to a new world. This world will appear only after the first heaven and the first earth have passed away. From our present point of view, that world is still future.

When we consider all these passages together, we come closest to understanding the new Jerusalem as the community of Christ and his people. This community will be revealed in its full perfection only when this present age comes to an end.

At the same time, Christians already belong to it in a real sense. The new Jerusalem gives them an ideal to live toward in this world and a hope to look forward to in the world to come.

Development of the New Testament Canon

The New Testament was written over about 50 years, several hundred years after the Old Testament was completed. Some modern scholars question both parts of this statement. They believe that each Testament took longer to complete. However, the writer of this survey is confident that this statement is historically true. This survey’s explanation of how the Old and New Testaments became accepted as Scripture is based on these two beliefs.

Inspiration as the Basic Principle

In one sense, we have stronger confirmation of the Old Testament canon than of the New Testament canon. The canon is the collection of books accepted as Scripture. Jesus himself confirmed the authority of the Hebrew Scriptures by using them as the word of God.

However, Jesus Christ also pointed ahead to the content of the New Testament. He promised that the Holy Spirit “will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you” (John 14:26). He also said that the Spirit “will guide you into all truth” (16:13).

From this, we can identify the basic principle for recognizing the New Testament canon, the books accepted as Scripture. This principle is the same as the one used for the Old Testament: a writing belongs in the canon if God inspired it.

This applies both to the Old Testament prophets and to the apostles and their God-given coworkers in the New Testament period. Their writings had authority because people recognized these authors as true messengers of God when they wrote. A writing is fully God’s word only if it is “God-breathed,” or inspired by God.

The church in the time of the apostles accepted these books when an apostle confirmed that they were inspired. Some New Testament letters were not recognized in every region at the same time. This may be because the apostles’ confirmation was first known only in certain places. In the end, the church accepted all 27 books of the New Testament. According to this view, their final acceptance shows that the church carefully examined the evidence and confirmed that the books had proper apostolic approval (that is, an apostle had confirmed that the writing came from God).

Tertullian was an important Christian writer during the first 20 years of the third century. He was one of the first people to call the Christian Scriptures the “New Testament.” This title had appeared earlier, around AD 190, in a work written against Montanism, a Christian movement. The author of that work is unknown. This title was important because it placed the New Testament Scriptures on the same level of inspiration and authority as the Old Testament.

The available evidence shows that the church gradually moved toward full and official recognition of the 27 books of the New Testament. This process continued into the fourth century AD. This does not necessarily mean that the church had failed to recognize all these books before that time. Rather, the church did not have an urgent need to define the canon officially until the fourth century.

The New Testament was written over a much shorter period than the Old Testament. However, its books were written across a much wider geographic area. This helps explain why churches did not immediately recognize the exact contents of the New Testament canon. Different churches first received different parts of the New Testament. Because these churches were far apart, some regions took longer than others to recognize certain books. This also led to some uncertainty about those books.

Five Periods of Development

To understand how the New Testament books became part of the canon, we must review the available evidence. This will help us see how and why the early Christians accepted the 27 books now included in the New Testament.

This historical process was gradual and continuous. However, it will be easier to understand if we divide the period of nearly 350 years into shorter sections. Some writers describe three main stages in the formation of the canon. However, this may wrongly suggest that the process developed through clear and separate steps. Other writers give a long list of the people and documents involved. This approach can make it hard to see how the process developed over time.

For this reason, this discussion divides the process into five periods. These divisions are somewhat artificial. Throughout the whole period, knowledge of the sacred writings continued to spread. At the same time, Christians continued to grow in agreement that these writings were authentic and inspired Scripture.

The five periods are:

First Century

First Half of the Second Century

Second Half of the Second Century

Third Century

Fourth Century

These five periods are not clear and separate stages. However, the main developments in each period can help us understand the process.

During the first period, the New Testament books were written. Christians also began to copy them and share them among the churches.

During the second period, more churches came to know and value these writings. Christians also began to quote them as authoritative.

By the end of the third period, these writings had gained a recognized place beside the Old Testament as “Scripture.” Christians also began to translate them into local languages and write commentaries on them.

The fourth period took place during the third century AD. Christians began to collect the books into one “New Testament.” They also worked to distinguish these books from other Christian writings.

In the fifth period, church leaders in the fourth century stated that the church had reached agreement about the canon. In the strict and formal sense, the canon was now fixed.

We will now examine in more detail the people and influences that produced the written evidence for this important process. Through God’s providence (his wise care and guidance over history), this process gave us the New Testament we have today.

Period One: First Century

The New Testament writings themselves show why the early church recognized their authority. Several passages tell believers to read the apostles’ messages aloud in public.

At the end of 1 Thessalonians, which may be the first New Testament book written, Paul says, “I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers” (1 Thessalonians 5:27). Earlier in the same letter, Paul praises the Thessalonians for accepting his spoken word as “the word of God” (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Paul says the same thing about what he writes. He insists that his readers recognize his written message as a commandment from the Lord himself (1 Corinthians 14:37). We see similar instructions in Colossians 4:16 and Revelation 1:3. 

In 2 Peter 3:15–16, Paul’s letters are included with “the other Scriptures.” Because Peter’s letter was written for a broad audience, this suggests that Paul’s letters were already widely known. 

Paul does something similar in 1 Timothy 5:18. He introduces two quotations with the words “the Scriptures say.” The first is the command “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4). The second is the saying “the worker is worthy of his wages,” which also appears in Luke 10:7. This suggests that Paul treated an Old Testament passage and a New Testament Gospel as having equal authority as Scripture.

Around AD 95, Clement of Rome wrote a letter to the Christians in Corinth. In this letter, he freely quoted or paraphrased material from the Gospels of Matthew and Luke. His writing also shows a strong influence from the Letter to the Hebrews. In addition, he was clearly familiar with:

Romans, 

1 and 2 Corinthians, 

Ephesians, 

1 Timothy, 

Titus, and 

1 Peter.

Period Two: First Half of Second Century

One of the earliest known New Testament manuscripts is a fragment of the Gospel of John found in Egypt. It is called the John Rylands Papyrus. This fragment shows that Christians respected and copied John’s writings by about AD 125, only 30 to 35 years after his death.

Evidence also suggests that within 30 years of John’s death, all four Gospels and Paul’s letters were known and used in every major Christian center from which evidence has survived.

Some churches continued to question the authority of a few shorter letters for about another 50 years. This was mainly because they were uncertain about who had written them. This suggests that councils did not force churches to accept these books. Instead, churches accepted them as they learned more about their authorship and apostolic approval. In places where this information was uncertain, acceptance took longer.

The first three major church fathers (Clement, Polycarp, and Ignatius) used most of the New Testament writings in a natural and informal way. They did not argue for the authority of these writings. Instead, they treated the recognized Scriptures as already authoritative.

Their writings clearly refer to nearly every New Testament book. The exceptions are:

Mark (which closely follows much of the material in Matthew),

2 Peter,

2 and 3 John, and

Jude.

The Epistles of Ignatius, written around AD 115, contain several phrases that are similar to passages in the Gospels. They also seem to use language from several of Paul’s letters. The Didache, also called The Teaching of the Twelve, may have been written even earlier. It refers to a written Gospel. Most importantly, Clement, Barnabas, and Ignatius clearly distinguish their own writings from the inspired and authoritative writings of the apostles.

The Epistle of Barnabas, written around AD 130, gives the earliest known example of the phrase “it is written” being used for a New Testament book. In Barnabas 4:14, the phrase introduces words from Matthew 22:14. 

Even before this, Polycarp combined a quotation from the Old Testament with one from the New Testament. Polycarp had personally known people who had seen and heard Jesus during his ministry. In his Epistle to the Philippians, Polycarp refers to Paul’s teaching in Ephesians 4:26. In that verse, Paul quotes Psalm 4:4 and adds further words. Polycarp introduces this material with the phrase “as it is said in these Scriptures” (Epistle to the Philippians 12:4). 

Papias was the bishop of Hierapolis around AD 130–140. In a work later preserved by Eusebius, Papias names the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. He also uses them as the basis for explanation. This suggests that he accepted them as part of the canon.

The Gospel of Truth, written around AD 140, also provides important evidence. This work reflects Gnostic teaching, a religious movement that claimed special spiritual knowledge. Valentinus probably wrote it. The work uses many New Testament writings and treats them as authoritative. This evidence supports the conclusion that Christians in Rome at that time had a collection of New Testament books that was very similar to the one used today. The Gospel of Truth includes citations from:

the Gospels, 

Acts, 

Paul’s letters, 

Hebrews, and 

Revelation.

Around AD 140, the heretic Marcion (a teacher whose views the church rejected as false) created his own limited canon. This prompted orthodox Christians (those who held the church’s accepted teaching) to define more clearly which books they accepted as Scripture. Marcion rejected the entire Old Testament. He accepted only the Gospel of Luke, but he removed chapters 1 and 2 because he believed they were too Jewish. He also accepted Paul’s letters, except for the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus). An interesting detail is that Marcion used the name “Laodiceans” instead of “Ephesians.” This is especially noteworthy because of Colossians 4:16.

Near the end of this period, Justin Martyr described the worship services of the early church. He placed the writings of the apostles on the same level of authority as the writings of the Old Testament prophets.

Justin said that the voice speaking through Christ’s apostles in the New Testament was the same voice that spoke through the prophets. It was the voice of God. It was also the same voice that Abraham heard and obeyed in faith. Justin also often used the phrase “it is written” when he quoted from New Testament Scriptures.

Period Three: Second Half of Second Century

Irenaeus began his Christian training under Polycarp, who had learned from the apostles. Later, while serving as a church leader in Lyons, Irenaeus worked with Bishop Pothinus. Pothinus had also known Christians from the first generation of the church.

Irenaeus quoted from almost every New Testament book and treated these writings as authoritative. He also taught that God had given the apostles power from heaven. They were, he said, “fully informed concerning all things, and had a perfect knowledge … having indeed all in equal measure and each one singly the Gospel of God” (Against Heresies 3.1.1). 

Irenaeus also explained why there are four Gospels. “The word,” he says, “gave us the Gospel in a fourfold shape, but held together by one Spirit.” In addition to the four Gospels, Irenaeus referred to:

Acts,

all of Paul’s letters except Philemon,

1 Peter,

1 John, and

Revelation.

Tatian, a student of Justin Martyr, combined the four Gospels into one continuous account called the Diatessaron. This work shows that the church regarded all four Gospels as having equal authority by about AD 170. Other writings called “gospels” also existed by that time, but Tatian accepted only these four.

The Muratorian Canon also dates from about AD 170. In 1740, the librarian L. A. Muratori discovered and published an eighth-century copy of this document. The manuscript is damaged at both the beginning and the end. However, the surviving text suggests that Matthew and Mark were included in the missing opening section.

The surviving list includes:

Luke, 

John, 

Acts, 

13 letters of Paul, 

1 and 2 John, 

Jude, and 

Revelation. 

It then says, “We accept only the Apocalypse of John and Peter, although some of us do not want it to be read in the church.” Scholars are not certain what this sentence means, because the manuscript is damaged at this point. The list then rejects several heretical leaders and their writings by name.

Translations of the New Testament already existed by this time. By about AD 170, Syriac translations in the eastern church and Old Latin translations in the western church provide strong evidence for the books Christians accepted. These translations contain the New Testament canon with no added books and only one book missing (2 Peter).

Period Four: Third Century

Origen, who lived from AD 185 to 254, was one of the most important Christian scholars of the third century. He studied and interpreted the Bible in great depth. He also examined the text of the New Testament, alongside his work on the Hexapla, a large comparison of different versions of the Old Testament. Origen wrote commentaries and sermons on most New Testament books. In these works, he emphasized that the Scriptures were inspired by God.

Dionysius of Alexandria, a student of Origen, shows that churches did not agree about every New Testament book. The Western church accepted Revelation from an early time, but churches in the East were less certain about it. The situation was the opposite for the Letter to the Hebrews. Churches in the East accepted it more readily than churches in the West.

Other books were also disputed. These books now appear near the end of the New Testament, from Hebrews through Revelation. Among the General Letters, the letters written to a broad Christian audience, Dionysius supported James and 2 and 3 John. However, he did not support 2 Peter or Jude.

This shows that the church had still not reached full agreement about certain books at the end of the third century. The situation was the same as it had been at the beginning of that century.

Period Five: Fourth Century

Early in this period, the situation became clearer. Eusebius lived from AD 270 to 340. He became the bishop of Caesarea before AD 315, and he was an important church historian. In his Ecclesiastical History (3.3–25), he described the status of the New Testament canon in the early fourth century.

He divided the books and writings into three groups:

Books accepted by all as part of the canon:

the four Gospels, 

Acts, 

Paul’s letters, 

1 Peter, 

1 John, and 

Revelation. 

Eusebius included Hebrews among Paul’s letters, though he noted questions about whether Paul wrote it.

Books accepted by most Christians but disputed by some: 

James, 

2 Peter, 

2 and 3 John, and 

Jude. 

Eusebius himself accepted these books. Second Peter faced the strongest disagreement.

Other Christian writings: 

Eusebius called the Acts of Paul, the Didache, and the Shepherd of Hermas “spurious,” meaning that he did not accept them as part of the canon. He described other writings as “heretical and absurd.”

However, the New Testament canon received its full and final form during the second half of the fourth century.

In his Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria, listed the books Christians should accept as Scripture. He also warned against using certain apocryphal books, writings that were not accepted as part of the canon. His letter says, “Let no one add to these; let nothing be taken away.” This is the earliest surviving document that lists all 27 New Testament books without qualification.

Near the end of the century, the Council of Carthage met in AD 397. It declared that only the canonical Scriptures should be read in church as divine Scripture. Its list also included the same 27 books of the New Testament.

Christianity grew rapidly under Emperor Constantine after the Edict of Milan in AD 313. This growth played an important role in the Eastern church’s acceptance of all the New Testament books.

Constantine asked Eusebius to prepare “fifty copies of the Divine Scriptures.” Eusebius knew which books Christians regarded as sacred and for which many believers had been willing to die. By choosing the books for these copies, he helped establish a standard that included the books that had once been disputed.

In the Western church, Jerome and Augustine had a strong influence on the final acceptance of the canon. The publication of all 27 New Testament books in the Latin Vulgate largely settled the matter.

How the Church Recognized the Canon

By its nature, Holy Scripture (both the Old Testament and the New Testament) comes from God. It is not simply a human creation. The key question in recognizing a book as part of the canon is whether God inspired it.

For this reason, the church did not choose from many possible books. According to this view, there were no other true candidates. Instead, the church received the authentic writings and gradually recognized them as more people learned the facts about their origin.

In one sense, the Montanist movement encouraged the church to define a closed canon of God’s written word. The church of that time declared Montanus’s teaching heretical in the middle of the second century.

Montanus taught that the gift of prophecy would continue permanently in the church. He also claimed to be a prophet. The need to respond to Montanism increased the search for a clear and reliable authority. As a result, apostolic authorship or approval came to be seen as the sure standard for recognizing God’s revelation. Even in the New Testament, first-century prophets were under apostolic authority (see 1 Corinthians 14:29–30; Ephesians 4:11).

During the Protestant Reformation, Christians reexamined many teachings and practices. Some Reformers also looked for ways to reassure themselves and their followers about which books belonged in the Bible.

The writer considers this concern unfortunate in some respects. According to this view, God had already guided his people to recognize the fixed contents of Scripture. That recognition had become a fact of history and did not need to be repeated.

Even so, Martin Luther used a theological test to judge biblical books, and he questioned some of them. He asked, “Do they teach Christ?” John Calvin used a different test. He taught that the Holy Spirit gives each Christian an inner witness about which writings are God’s word. According to Calvin, the Spirit does this in every period of church history. The writer regards both approaches as subjective because they depend on personal judgment or experience.

The first acceptance of the written word of God was not based on intuition or personal feeling. Scripture and history do not support that view. Instead, believers accepted these writings because they obeyed the known commands of Christ and his apostles.

As noted earlier, Jesus promised that he would give everything necessary through his chosen messengers (John 14:26; 16:13). The apostles knew that they had this responsibility and authority when they wrote.

Paul explains this in 1 Corinthians 2:13. He says that the apostles did not use words chosen by human wisdom. They used words taught by the Holy Spirit to explain spiritual truths.

The early church had closer links to the apostles and more information than we have today. Church leaders examined the testimony of earlier Christians. They identified authentic and authoritative books by asking whether those books came from the apostles or had apostolic approval.

Mark was connected with Peter, and Luke was connected with Paul. These relationships gave their writings apostolic approval. Books such as Hebrews and Jude were also closely connected with the apostles’ message and ministry.

The consistent teaching found throughout the books, including those that were sometimes disputed, may also have served as a secondary test. However, the main historical process was the acceptance of books that trusted and informed church leaders confirmed as authentic.

Another important factor was the response of the first readers. They accepted these writings, and later Christians continued to recognize and use them. This ongoing acceptance helped shape the New Testament canon.

The Church Received, Not Created, the Canon

The church’s understanding of the canon first grew from its deep respect for the Old Testament Scriptures. It was also based on the belief that the apostles had unique authority to speak in the name of Jesus Christ, who has all authority.

The next steps followed naturally. Those who heard Jesus in person were under his authority. Jesus himself confirmed the truth of his words to his followers. These same believers also knew that Jesus had authorized the apostles to speak in his name, both during his earthly ministry and, even more importantly, after it.

The church therefore accepted the apostles’ teaching as the message of Christ, whether the apostles spoke in person or wrote letters. Both the spoken words and the written letters of an apostle were understood as the word of Christ.

The generation after the apostles received the testimony of people who knew that the apostles had authority to speak and write in Christ’s name. As a result, second- and third-generation Christians looked back to the apostles’ writings as the words of Christ.

This is the meaning of canonization: recognizing the word that God had already confirmed as authoritative. The church did not create the canon. Instead, believers recognized the authority of Christ’s word and testified about which writings belonged in the canon.
